domains.note: No pooled results.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: No risk of bias was assessed, so none is carried into the interpretation. The statement that high-quality evidence is scarce rests on counts of reporting features, not on a quality appraisal.

No results were pooled, so there is no heterogeneity of results to explain; the Discussion explains how the diversity of exposures, outcomes and units prevents synthesis and proposes standardised reporting.
No pooled results.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding by the State of Colorado, the role of the funder and the authors’ interests are reported as printed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: items 4 and 7 can be judged only from the Appendix and the OSF project, which were not opened, so both are recorded as no information. AMSTAR 2 is built for reviews that pool the effects of an intervention. Applied as written to this scoping review and evidence map, two critical items are “no” (no risk-of-bias assessment of the included studies, which scoping methods omit by design, and so no account of risk of bias in the interpretation), which gives critically low confidence whatever items 4 and 7 turn out to be. That rating is a mechanical result of what the review set out to do, not a finding that the mapping is careless: a protocol was published, seven databases were searched with a peer-reviewed strategy, full-text selection was in duplicate, the funding of included studies was extracted and counted, and the conclusions stay within what a map can show. The review may be cited for what has been studied and how it was reported (counts of studies, exposures, outcomes, funding) and for the gaps it identifies; it should not be cited for any effect of high-concentration products.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC10632847 (abstract, plain-language summary, Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, Conclusions, acknowledgments, conflicts of interest, reference list and the author-information panel read as text; Figures 1 to 3 are images, their legends were read and the PRISMA numbers were taken from the text; the Appendix (search strategy, Appendix Table A), the interactive evidence map and the OSF protocol were not opened)

key_findings.finding: Searches identified 49,729 unique records, 5,828 full-text reports and 452 included studies: 225 observational studies, 142 randomized trials, 51 case reports and 34 case series. The earliest was published in 1971 and 60% (269) in 2017 to 2022.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st (unlabelled) paragraph; Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Few studies give data that could support synthesis: 54 (12%) examined a direct association between concentrates and a health outcome and 189 (42%) a direct association between THC concentration and an outcome; 114 (25%) and 62 (14%) examined indirect associations; 212 (47%) had a control group; effect estimates were reported in 184 (41%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Potential for Evidence Synthesis, paragraph
key_findings.note: Counts of study features; they say nothing about what the studies found.

key_findings.finding: Strengths studied: when THC was given as a percentage (172 studies, 349 exposures) the median was 12% (mean 17.4%, range 0% to 100%, interquartile range 3.6% to 24%); when given in milligrams (113 studies, 143 exposures) the median was 15 mg (mean 37.4, range 0.3 to 500, interquartile range 7.5 to 26). Median reported THC was below 50 mg or 25% for every outcome domain. Units and indices varied.
key_findings.locator: Results › Exposures, 3rd paragraph; Results › Outcomes, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The authors state that THC concentration is not the same as dose (Methods › Study Selection Criteria › THC concentration of products, 2nd paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Most studies concerned generic cannabis types (284, 63%); products typically high in concentration (oils, concentrates, hash, extracts, skunk, resins) were examined in approximately 2% to 10% of all studies. Route was reported in 393 studies (87%): inhalation 62%, ingestion 38%, sublingual 9%, topical 7%. Frequency was reported in 384 (85%), most often daily (177, 39%); duration in 371 (82%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Exposures, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Outcome domains: mental health 180 studies (40%), neurologic 134 (30%), pain 133 (29%), cardiometabolic 110 (24%), gastrointestinal 101 (22%), psychosocial 98 (22%), sleep 94 (21%). A single outcome such as depression was measured in different ways in different studies.
key_findings.locator: Results › Outcomes, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Funding and interests in the included studies: 24% (109) did not report a funding source and 32% (143) did not report whether authors had conflicts of interest; 25 studies (6%) were funded by the cannabis industry and 58 (13%) had an author who disclosed a financial tie with the industry.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Only 48 studies (11%) included any analysis of a health-equity measure, 41 (9%) analysed or stratified by health-equity subgroups, 6 (1%) focused exclusively on historically excluded populations, and none analysed structural racism or inequalities.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Market strengths the authors cite from other sources: a 2018 survey of products sold in 7 US states found most products between 15% and 30% THC; in Colorado the average THC of flower assayed rose from 14% to 19% between 2014 and 2020 and that of concentrates from 46% to 68%. They describe the median of 12% studied as well below what is currently on the market and attribute the low strengths studied, as likely, to the restriction of research cannabis in the United States to a federal supply that lacks concentrates.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Concentrations Studied, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Market figures are quoted from a published survey and a Colorado market report, not measured in this review; the reason for the low strengths is the authors’ inference.

key_findings.finding: The authors write that most studies failed to capture all the elements of cannabis use needed to estimate exposure dose, and recommend that studies at least report THC concentration, product used, frequency of use and route, in THC units that can be standardised.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Exposure Assessment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: the review supports strong conclusions about the usefulness of the literature for characterising risks and benefits of the current marketplace; there are serious limitations in the generalisability of the studies to the current marketplace or to the people who buy its products; high-quality evidence on whether THC concentration should be regulated is scarce.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Conclusions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Abstract
key_findings.note: “Strong” refers to conclusions about the literature, not about health effects.

key_findings.finding: Stated limits: searches were sensitive rather than specific; relevant studies may have been missed despite AI-assisted screening; heterogeneity of designs did not allow risk-of-bias assessment of individual studies; incomplete and inconsistent reporting left gaps in the extracted data.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract and Conclusions say the review supports strong conclusions concerning the utility of the literature. Read alone, “strong conclusions” can be taken as a conclusion about health effects; the review extracts and reports no effects.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite as an inventory of studies and a statement about gaps; do not cite as evidence of any effect.

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract says one person extracted data and a senior reviewer verified a subset; the Methods say the single extractor’s work was checked by senior reviewers without saying how much.
reporting_issues.consequence: How much of the extraction was independently checked is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: AI-assisted title and abstract screening: the Methods describe training on 1,000 records and continuous re-ranking of the rest but give no recall estimate, stopping rule or count of records screened by people at that stage.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of any shortfall in studies found is unknown; the authors say relevant studies may have been missed.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods name the authors added after the protocol as R. L., J.-P. O. and T. W. K.; the author list and the screening paragraph give T. W. Y.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; no effect on findings.

reporting_issues.issue: Counts for products typically high in concentration are given as a single range (approximately 2% to 10% of all studies) in the text; the breakdown by product type is in Figure 2 and Appendix Table A, neither read.
reporting_issues.consequence: How many studies examined each kind of concentrate cannot be read from the text.

design_detail: Field study that the authors call a cohort study with a between-groups design (JAMA Psychiatry 2020), Colorado, registered as an observational study (NCT03522103). Adults who already used cannabis flower or concentrates regularly were measured before and after using a legal-market product that they bought themselves: within each form (flower or concentrate), the labelled THC strength was assigned by random-number table (flower 16% or 24%; concentrate 70% or 90%), but the form itself was each person’s own choice. After a baseline visit and 5 days of using the product, a mobile laboratory came to the participant’s home; blood, self-rated intoxication and mood, cognitive tests and balance were measured before use, about 13 minutes after use and 1 hour after use, with the person using the product in the way they preferred in between. No placebo or no-use session, and nobody who does not use cannabis.
can_establish: What was measured in 121 regular consumers before and after they used a legal-market product at home: blood THC and its active metabolite 11-OH-THC were higher in the concentrate group than the flower group at every time point; self-rated intoxication and most cognitive tests did not differ by form or by labelled strength within form at the authors’ threshold (P < .01); delayed verbal recall and eyes-closed balance were worse after use in both groups, with balance back to its pre-use level by 1 hour. It gives measured blood levels after naturalistic use of products as sold, which controlled studies with lower-strength study cannabis do not.
cannot_establish: Whether concentrates cause more or less impairment than flower: people chose their own form, the two groups differed at baseline in how often they used concentrates, how long they had used cannabis regularly and in baseline THC metabolite, there was no placebo or no-use session so practice and the passage of time cannot be separated from the drug, and each person chose how much to use. Effects in people who use cannabis less often or are new to it (inclusion required use at least four times in the past month and earlier use of the strongest product without a bad reaction), long-term effects (follow-up was 1 hour), driving or other real-world performance, dependence, mental health, or any effect on the lungs or other organs. Why self-rated intoxication matched despite different blood levels is not shown: tolerance, receptor saturation and individual differences are the authors’ suggestions, untested. Strength was the labelled THC percentage; other cannabinoids and contaminants are not reported.

sample.recruitment: Social media postings and mailed flyers advertising to people who use flower or concentrates (Methods › Participants, 1st paragraph). Participants were paid $50 for the baseline visit and $100 for the mobile-laboratory visit; no funds were provided for buying cannabis, so each person paid for their own study product. Self-selected volunteers.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: age 21 to 70; cannabis at least 4 times in the past month; earlier use, at least once by self-report, of the strongest product that could be assigned (24% THC flower or 90% THC concentrate) with no adverse reaction; no other non-prescription drug in the past 60 days (urine screen); no daily tobacco; alcohol no more than twice a week and no more than 3 drinks an occasion; not pregnant or trying to become pregnant; not treated for a psychotic or bipolar disorder (Methods › Participants, 2nd paragraph). Twelve of the 133 people assessed were removed afterwards because blood THC after use was below 0.02 µg/mL (study mean 0.24, SD 0.35), taken to mean they had not used the product at home and returned at once as instructed (Results › Descriptive Information): 9 of 64 flower (14%) and 3 of 69 concentrate (4%) participants (editors’ arithmetic).
sample.demographics: Analysed: flower group 55, mean age 28.8 (SD 8.1), 42% women; concentrate group 66 (65 with baseline data), mean age 28.3 (SD 10.4), 48% women (Table 1). White 78% and 79%; bachelor’s degree or higher 64% and 45%; prescribed psychiatric medication 4% and 12%. Baseline cannabis use, flower vs concentrate group: days of concentrate use in the past 30 days 3.5 vs 16.5; days of flower use 20.6 vs 15.4; age at start of regular use 20.0 vs 17.7 years; cannabis use disorder symptoms 2.96 vs 3.09; baseline plasma THC 0.004 vs 0.009 µg/mL and THC-COOH 0.044 vs 0.087 µg/mL. Alcohol use 7.4 vs 9.0 days and tobacco use 0.5 vs 1.8 days in the past 30.
sample.attrition: 133 assessed, 12 excluded after the visit because of low post-use blood THC (9%), 121 analysed; the Abstract says these 121 complied with instructions and had complete data across the primary outcomes. One concentrate participant had no baseline demographic data (Table 1 footnote); 30-day use history was missing for some flower participants (41 of 55 present, Table 1 footnote).
sample.selection_effects: Strong. Volunteers who already used cannabis regularly, had used the strongest product before without a bad reaction and agreed to be tested at home; people who were new to cannabis or used it rarely, had had an adverse reaction to a high-strength product, used tobacco daily or other drugs, or were treated for psychosis or bipolar disorder were excluded, so the findings cannot be carried over to them or to people who do not use cannabis. Excluding people because their blood THC after use was very low removes the low end of one of the outcomes themselves, and removed more of the flower group (14%) than the concentrate group (4%). Products came from one dispensary that set aside allotments for the study.

exposure.measurement: Form and labelled THC strength (flower 16% or 24%, concentrate 70% or 90%) as tested by an ISO 17025-accredited laboratory and labelled as Colorado requires; purchase verified by receipt; product weighed before and after use at the session; mode of use recorded (concentrate group: glass rig or tube 92%, hash pen 8%; flower group: pipe 51%, bong 31%, vaporizer 11%, joint 7%). Plasma THC and 11-OH-THC by liquid chromatography with mass spectrometry (Methods › Primary Measures › Blood Cannabinoids).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: A single ad libitum session at home, after 5 days of free use of the study product, with the route chosen by the participant. Product used at the session, mean (SD): flower 0.22 g (0.18), concentrate 0.11 g (0.14) (Table 1); by labelled strength: flower 24% 0.24 g, 16% 0.19 g; concentrate 90% 0.10 g, 70% 0.13 g, reported as not significantly different within form. Mean time away from the mobile laboratory 13.3 minutes (SD 7, range 3 to 47). Other cannabinoids (for example CBD) and contaminants not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Limited by selection: no other non-prescription drug in the past 60 days (urine screen), no daily tobacco, light alcohol use, breath alcohol tested before the session. Tobacco and alcohol use in the past 30 days were low in both groups (tobacco 0.5 vs 1.8 days, alcohol 7.4 vs 9.0 days). Tobacco mixed into joints is not recorded (4 of 55 flower participants used joints).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Asked not to use cannabis on the day of the visit before the first (pre-use) measurement; median pre-use blood THC was 0.003 µg/mL (range 0 to 0.05) (Figure 1 legend).

comparison.controls: No placebo and no no-use session (the authors say placebo products do not exist on the legal market) and no group of people who do not use cannabis. Three comparisons: before against after use within each person; flower group against concentrate group (self-selected, not randomised); higher against lower labelled strength within each form (random assignment).
comparison.matching: None between forms. Each model included the baseline value of the outcome as a covariate; removing it did not change the pattern. Random assignment to strength within form gave groups that did not differ except in race among the concentrate groups (P < .01) (Table 1 footnote).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Tolerance and length of regular use differ between the form groups and are only partly captured (concentrate use on about 16 of the past 30 days against about 3, regular use started about two years earlier, baseline THC-COOH about twice as high). The authors name interactions that were not tested or accounted for: strength and cannabinoid ratio, mode of use, expectancies and smoking technique (Limitations).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Light alcohol and no other drug use by selection; groups similar on alcohol and tobacco days (Table 1).

outcomes.instruments: Plasma THC and 11-OH-THC; Addiction Research Center Inventory marijuana scale (12 items); a 3-item intoxication scale (mentally stoned, physically stoned, feeling high); Profile of Mood States vigor and tension subscales; 30-minute delayed verbal recall (International Shopping List Task); NIH Toolbox inhibitory control (flanker), working memory and episodic memory (picture); quiet-standing balance on a smart device with eyes open, eyes closed, and eyes closed with head tilted back (Methods › Primary Measures). Details are in eMethods (Supplement 2, not read).
outcomes.validity_norms: Intoxication scale Cronbach alpha 0.69. The marijuana effects scale correlated 0.42 with the intoxication scale and 0.46 with tension (Results › Subjective Drug Effects). Validity of the smart-device balance measure is not described in the main text.
outcomes.operationalization: Change from before use to about 13 minutes after use (short-term) and 1 hour after use, tested with linear and quadratic time terms in repeated-measures analysis of variance, with form and form-by-time interactions; strength within form tested in the supplement. Impairment is inferred from change in the same person, with no placebo comparison.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: A fixed, stricter threshold of P < .01 set in advance for the number of outcomes (Methods › Statistical Analysis). Thirteen outcomes, each with five tests in Table 2 (linear time, quadratic time, form, form by linear, form by quadratic), is about 65 tests, plus the strength tests in the supplement; a fixed threshold, not a formal correction (a Bonferroni threshold for 13 outcomes would be about .004). Several results fall between .01 and .05 (verbal recall form by quadratic P = .02; eyes-open balance P = .05).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. Participants were not masked to product strength (federal rules restricted masking, Limitations), and the self-rated outcomes depend on what people expect.

analysis.effect_sizes: Means (SE) before, about 13 minutes after, and 1 hour after use (Table 2). Blood THC µg/mL: flower 0.004, 0.14, 0.02; concentrate 0.01, 0.32, 0.03; form effect F(1,228) = 11.00, P < .01; form by quadratic F = 15.07, P < .001. 11-OH-THC µg/mL: flower 0.001, 0.005, 0.004; concentrate 0.004, 0.011, 0.008; form effect F = 46.82, P < .001. Intoxication scale: flower 0.08, 2.40, 1.93; concentrate 0.14, 2.35, 1.63; form effect F(1,230) = 2.57, P = .11. ARCI marijuana scale: form effect F = 1.84, P = .18. Tension and vigor lower in the concentrate group (P < .01, P < .001). Delayed verbal recall errors: flower 0.65, 2.21, 1.88; concentrate 0.90, 1.50, 2.33; linear change F(1,203) = 32.31, P < .001; form effect P = .65; form by quadratic P = .02. Eyes-closed sway: flower 0.63, 0.73, 0.63; concentrate 0.64, 0.69, 0.64; quadratic time F(1,203) = 18.88, P < .001; form effect P = .85. Inhibitory control higher in the flower group at every time (P < .001); inhibitory control and working memory scores rose over the session (linear P < .001), which the authors suggest may reflect practice; episodic memory no effect. Eyes-open balance quadratic P = .05; eyes-closed head-back no change. Strength within form: no effects in the main text (eResults and eTables, Supplement 2, not read). No confidence intervals or standardized effect sizes.
analysis.covariates: Baseline value of each outcome in every model. Race compared across groups but not entered in any model. No adjustment for the baseline differences between the flower and concentrate groups in recent concentrate use, years of regular use or THC metabolite.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Registered as an observational study at ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03522103; the protocol is Supplement 1 (PDF, not opened) and the registry record was not opened, so whether outcomes, threshold and comparisons match the registered plan was not checked. The paper says a second primary outcome of the larger study, change in inflammation markers, will be reported elsewhere (Methods › Primary Measures › Blood Cannabinoids).
analysis.selective_reporting: All 13 outcomes appear in Table 2 with all five effects each, including null results and results against the hypothesis (for example higher tension and vigor in the flower group). Strength results are only in the supplement. The exclusion of 12 people was decided from the blood result. Not in the main text: confidence intervals, effect sizes, individual-level data.
analysis.power: No power calculation in the main text (protocol and supplement not read). With 55 and 66 people overall and about 26 to 33 per strength group, absence of a significant difference is weak evidence of no difference, and the paper gives no interval showing how large a difference the data rule out.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 121 adults who already used cannabis at least four times a month, blood THC measured about 13 minutes after self-administered use was higher in the concentrate group than in the flower group (mean 0.32 against 0.14 µg/mL), and 11-OH-THC was higher at every time point. Self-rated intoxication, the marijuana effects scale and most cognitive tests did not differ by form, and nothing differed by labelled strength within form at P < .01. Delayed verbal recall and eyes-closed balance worsened after use in both groups; balance had returned to its pre-use level by 1 hour. Tension and vigor were lower in the concentrate group at every time point, and inhibitory control scores were higher in the flower group at every time, including before use. The concentrate group had used concentrates on far more days, started regular use about two years earlier and had about twice the baseline THC metabolite. There was no placebo, so changes after use cannot be separated from repeating the tests; follow-up was 1 hour.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Abstract says short-term use of concentrates was associated with higher THC exposure and that verbal memory and postural stability were associated with THC across forms and strengths, which the data support. The Conclusions add that THC exposure was much higher in the concentrate group, prompting concern about long-term clinical and neurobehavioral implications, and the Key Points describe concentrates as associated with potentially greater risk; neither long-term outcomes nor clinical outcomes were measured. The Discussion reads the lack of a blood-level difference by strength within each form as suggesting self-titration (an inference from non-significant differences in groups of 26 to 33), offers tolerance, receptor saturation and individual differences as untested explanations for equal intoxication at different blood levels, and proposes that balance impairment could mark recent use. The authors state the main limits: no random assignment to form, no placebo, limited control of dosing and masking.

timeline.event: Same group: survey of people who use concentrates on the legal market, with strength and health-related outcomes (Bidwell et al., Addictive Behaviors Reports; cited as reference 6, not read).
This study: naturalistic use of legal-market flower and concentrates, measured in a mobile laboratory; the authors present it as the first of its kind (Discussion, 1st paragraph).
Systematic review of cannabis potency and mental ill health and addiction (Petrilli et al.); not yet readable for this library; will be added.
Scoping review and evidence map of high-concentration cannabis products in this batch (Bero et al.); it maps what has been studied and does not appraise the studies.

replication.where_it_stands: One study from one research group in one state; no second measurement of blood THC and impairment after naturalistic use of concentrates and flower was read for this batch. Controlled studies of smoked and vaporized flower under set dosing (Spindle 2018, this batch) measure a different question in people who rarely use cannabis.

funding.funder: US National Institutes of Health (grant DA039707 to Hutchison) and the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (grant 96947 to Bidwell). The funders had no role in design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, manuscript preparation or the decision to submit (author-information panel, funding and role of the funder).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: Bidwell reports grants from NIH/NIDA and from the State of Colorado (CDPHE); Ellingson reports NIH funding; Klawitter reports CDPHE and NIH; Sempio reports CDPHE and NIH; Bryan reports NIH and the State of Colorado; no other disclosures. No cannabis-industry funding or ties are declared. Participants bought their products from one local dispensary, which set aside allotments for the study; no payment from the dispensary is declared.
funding.affiliations_note: University of Colorado Boulder (Psychology and Neuroscience; Institute for Cognitive Science), University of Colorado Aurora (Psychiatry; Anesthesiology) and Colorado State University; blood assays at the iC42 laboratory, Anschutz Medical Campus. Several authors also wrote the 2018 survey of concentrate use that the paper cites. The Colorado grant comes from the same state health department that funded Monte 2019 (this batch). Recorded as a reason to read closely, not to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A study that follows people over time or assigns the form: for example the same people using flower and concentrate on different days, with measured product content beyond THC percentage, a placebo or no-use session to separate practice from drug effects, people with different amounts of experience including those new to cannabis, and longer follow-up of driving-relevant performance, dependence and mental-health outcomes over months to years.

domains.note: Form was chosen by participants. The concentrate group used concentrates on about 16 of the past 30 days against about 3, started regular use about two years earlier and had about twice the baseline THC-COOH, so tolerance and history differ; these are not adjusted for beyond the baseline value of each outcome. Random assignment to strength protects only the within-form comparison.

Product, labelled strength (laboratory tested), weighed amount and mode of use are recorded, which is better than most field studies; but the amount is each person’s choice, labelled THC is not measured content, other cannabinoids and contaminants are not reported, and 12 of 133 people were removed because blood THC was too low to show they had used the product as instructed.

Self-selected volunteers who already used cannabis regularly and had used the strongest product before without a bad reaction; excluding 12 people by their post-use blood THC, one of the outcomes, removed more of the flower group (9 of 64) than the concentrate group (3 of 69); no one new to cannabis or using it rarely.
Measurements followed a fixed sequence; nothing after use is described that would change outcomes differently by group.

Complete data on the primary outcomes was a condition of analysis (121 of 133); 30-day use history is missing for some flower participants and one concentrate participant lacks baseline demographics; handling of other missing values is not described.

Blood cannabinoids are measured by validated chromatography with mass spectrometry. Intoxication and mood are self-rated by people who knew their product’s strength and the study’s hypothesis (modest scale reliability, alpha 0.69). Tests were repeated three times within about an hour with no placebo or practice-control session, so practice effects cannot be separated from drug effects (the authors raise this for two tasks). Validity of the smart-device balance measure is described only in the supplement.

Registered as an observational study with the protocol in Supplement 1 (not compared here); a fixed P < .01 threshold across 13 outcomes; results between .01 and .05 are described in words as trends or marginal, and not consistently across text and legends; strength results sit in the supplement and a second primary outcome is to be reported elsewhere.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E is applied to a cohort-style field study. Confounding and selection are judged high because the central comparison (flower against concentrate) is between self-selected groups that differ in prior use and probably tolerance, there is no placebo or no-use session, and 12 people were removed using the blood result; the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. Against that: laboratory-tested products, weighed use, blood cannabinoids at three time points, a registered design, a deliberately strict significance threshold, and null results shown in full. It can be cited for measured blood THC after naturalistic use of legal-market flower and concentrates in regular consumers, and for the absence of detectable differences in self-rated intoxication and short-term tests at one hour; it cannot be cited for long-term outcomes, for people who use cannabis less often, or for a causal comparison of the forms.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7287943 (author manuscript; Key Points, abstract, Methods, Results, Tables 1 and 2, Discussion, Limitations, Conclusions, reference list and the author-information panel read as text; Figures 1 to 3 are images, their legends were read and their values not extracted; Supplement 1 (protocol) and Supplement 2 (eMethods, eResults, eTables, eFigures) are PDFs and were not opened)

key_findings.finding: 133 people were enrolled and assessed (64 flower, 69 concentrate); 12 were removed because blood THC after use was below 0.02 µg/mL (study mean 0.24), leaving 121 (55 flower, 66 concentrate); mean age 28.8 and 28.3 years; 42% and 48% women.
key_findings.locator: Results › Descriptive Information, paragraph; Abstract; Table 1
key_findings.note: The Abstract gives 25 women (46%) and 30 women (45%); Table 1 gives 23 (42%) and 31 (48%).

key_findings.finding: Within each form, participants were randomly assigned a labelled strength (flower 16% or 24% THC; concentrate 70% or 90% THC), bought it at one dispensary, used it freely for 5 days, then used it in their preferred way at home during a mobile-laboratory visit; measures were taken before use, about 13 minutes after use (mean 13.3, range 3 to 47) and 1 hour after use.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Baseline Appointment, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Experimental Appointment, paragraph

key_findings.finding: Mean blood THC after use was 0.32 µg/mL in the concentrate group and 0.14 µg/mL in the flower group; 11-OH-THC reached 0.011 and 0.005 µg/mL; both were higher in the concentrate group at every time point, including before use, and THC had fallen to 0.03 and 0.02 µg/mL by 1 hour. No difference by labelled strength within form.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabinoids, paragraph; Table 2; Figure 1
key_findings.note: The Abstract and Results label 0.43 and 0.16 as standard errors; the Discussion gives them as standard deviations.

key_findings.finding: Self-rated intoxication rose to similar levels in both groups (short-term mean 2.40 flower, 2.35 concentrate; form effect P = .11); so did the marijuana effects scale (P = .18). Tension and vigor were lower in the concentrate group at every time point (P < .01 and P < .001). No associations with labelled strength.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective Drug Effects, paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Delayed verbal recall errors rose after use in both groups (linear effect P < .001; flower 0.65, 2.21, 1.88; concentrate 0.90, 1.50, 2.33 before, short-term and 1 hour after); form effect P = .65, form by quadratic time P = .02 (above the .01 threshold). Inhibitory control (flanker) was higher in the flower group at every time point (P < .001); inhibitory control and working memory scores rose over the session, which the authors suggest may reflect practice.
key_findings.locator: Results › Neurobehavioral Performance › Cognition, paragraph; Table 2; Figure 3

key_findings.finding: Eyes-closed sway increased after use and returned to its pre-use level by 1 hour in both groups (quadratic P < .001; form effect P = .85); eyes-open balance showed a trend (P = .05); the eyes-closed head-back condition did not change. The authors describe about 11% more sway and compare it with the effect of moderate alcohol.
key_findings.locator: Results › Neurobehavioral Performance › Balance, paragraph; Table 2; Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: At baseline the concentrate group reported concentrate use on 16.5 of the past 30 days against 3.5, started regular use at 17.7 against 20.0 years, and had baseline THC-COOH 0.087 against 0.044 µg/mL; the amount used at the session was 0.11 g against 0.22 g; the concentrate group used a glass rig or tube (92%) or hash pen (8%); the flower group used a pipe (51%), bong (31%), vaporizer (11%) or joint (7%).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Descriptive Information, paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors give three possible explanations for similar intoxication despite higher blood THC (greater tolerance in the concentrate group; receptor saturation; individual differences in metabolism or sensitivity) and say future research must test them; they read the lack of a blood-level difference by strength within each form as suggesting self-titration.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Stated limits: no random assignment to form (ethical reasons), so pre-existing group differences may partly account for the findings; no placebo control (none on the legal market); federal rules restricted control of dosing and masking to strength; interactions of strength, cannabinoid ratio, mode of use, expectancies and technique were not tested.
key_findings.locator: Limitations, paragraph

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: delayed recall and balance impairment were associated with short-term use even in regular consumers; the concentrate group showed similar or lower subjective intoxication and short-term impairment than the flower group; THC exposure was much higher in the concentrate group, prompting concern about long-term clinical and neurobehavioral implications.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions, paragraph
key_findings.note: Long-term and clinical outcomes were not measured.

reporting_issues.issue: Mean blood THC after use is printed as 0.32 (SE 0.43) and 0.14 (SE 0.16) µg/mL in the Abstract and Results; the Discussion gives the same numbers as standard deviations, and the standard errors in Table 2 are 0.02 to 0.03.
reporting_issues.consequence: 0.43 and 0.16 are standard deviations, not standard errors; the means are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The numbers of women differ between the Abstract (25 of 55 flower, 46%; 30 of 66 concentrate, 45%) and Table 1 and the Results text (23, 42%; 31 of 65, 48%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; Table 1 reports 65 concentrate participants because one had no baseline demographics.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 rows for cannabis use disorder symptoms, AUDIT, Beck Depression and Beck Anxiety totals are headed No. (%) but hold means and SDs, and the superscript letters in the table do not match the footnote list (for example the row for days of flower use carries a letter whose footnote concerns psychiatric medication).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which between-form baseline differences were tested, and at what level, cannot be read from the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The intoxication scale is described with items scored 1 to 5 and 1 to 10 in the Methods, while the Figure 2 legend gives all scales a range of 0 to 4 and Table 2 means run from 0.08 to 2.40.
reporting_issues.consequence: The units of the intoxication scale cannot be checked; group comparisons are not affected.

reporting_issues.issue: Results between .01 and .05 are described inconsistently. The Figure 3 legend says a marginal effect suggested more impairment of delayed recall in the flower group (form by quadratic P = .02), while the Abstract says differing outcomes by product type were not observed (in the context of the memory and balance results) and Table 2 shows more errors in the concentrate group at 1 hour (2.33 against 1.88). Eyes-open balance (P = .05) is called a trend.
reporting_issues.consequence: Near-threshold results should be treated as unresolved; the pre-set threshold was P < .01.

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract percentages for the analysed groups (41.4% flower, 49.6% concentrate) are shares of all 133 people assessed; within each form, 86% of the flower group and 96% of the concentrate group were analysed.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader could take 41.4% and 49.6% as compliance rates; exclusions fell mostly on the flower group.

design_detail: Case-comparator laboratory study. Bronchoalveolar-lavage (BAL) fluid from 51 patients with e-cigarette, or vaping, product use-associated lung injury (EVALI) in 16 US states, collected August to December 2019 during routine clinical care and sent to CDC through state health departments, compared with BAL fluid from 99 healthy participants of an unrelated Ohio State University study (52 who neither vaped nor smoked, 18 who vaped nicotine only, 29 who smoked cigarettes only; sampled 2016 to 2019, 90 before 2019). CDC measured by isotope-dilution mass spectrometry a list of priority substances chosen in advance: vitamin E acetate, plant oils (long-chain triglycerides), medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) oil, coconut oil, petroleum distillates and diluent terpenes including limonene; also THC, nicotine and their metabolites, and a lung-surfactant marker (DPPC) to confirm that each sample held lung lining fluid. Results are counts and percentages; no statistical tests or intervals are given. Version read: the author manuscript of the New England Journal of Medicine article.
can_establish: In a convenience sample of 51 patients with EVALI and 99 healthy volunteers, how often vitamin E acetate and a list of other suspected additives were found in lung lavage fluid: vitamin E acetate in 48 of 51 patients and in none of the volunteers, and each other additive in at most one patient.
cannot_establish: Whether vitamin E acetate caused the injury (no dose, timing or experiment; the comparison group contained no one who vaped THC products and was not ill, so the finding could reflect the 2019 supply of THC cartridges rather than the injury); anything about substances not on the chosen list (the analysis was targeted); what product a patient used or where it came from (lavage does not show it); how typical the 51 are of the more than 2,400 patients hospitalized (lavage was done by clinicians' choice, without a standard protocol); and how long after the last use the fluid was taken.

sample.recruitment: Patients: BAL fluid obtained by hospital clinical teams for patient care on a case-by-case basis, sent to CDC by state health departments in 16 states (Arizona 2, Arkansas 2, California 4, Connecticut 1, Hawaii 1, Illinois 12, Indiana 1, Maryland 4, Michigan 2, Minnesota 5, Missouri 1, North Carolina 2, Texas 2, Utah 3, West Virginia 1, Wisconsin 8); accepted if the health department classified the person as a confirmed or probable case; no other criteria. Comparators: recruited through local media and participant registries for a tobacco-product study at Ohio State University, aged 21 to 45, with no major clinical illness or increased risk from bronchoscopy (Methods › Biospecimen collection).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cases met the CDC EVALI case definitions as judged by state or local health officials: use of an e-cigarette or dabbing in the 90 days before symptom onset, a lung infiltrate or ground-glass opacity on imaging, and exclusion of infection and other plausible diagnoses (confirmed), or infection present but judged not the sole cause or testing incomplete (probable) (Table 1).
sample.demographics: Patients: median age 23 (range 16 to 67), 35 of 51 (69%) male. Of 43 with information on product use, 7 (16%) reported nicotine products only, 11 (26%) THC products only and 22 (51%) both (the three others are not accounted for). Comparators: median age 26 (range 21 to 44); 53 of 99 (54%) male; none reported vaping THC products (Table 2).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Lung-fluid volumes were small in some samples, so analytes were prioritized (vitamin E acetate first) and results for the others are not available for all; denominators run from 12 (petroleum distillates) to 51 (Table 3). Product-use information was available for 43 of 51 patients.
sample.selection_effects: The 51 are about 2% of the more than 2,400 patients hospitalized by 12 December 2019 and were sampled when a clinical team judged BAL useful; they are called a convenience sample by the authors. The comparators are healthy volunteers from one Ohio study with different eligibility, sampled mostly before 2019, and include nobody who vaped THC (Methods; Results, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Laboratory: isotope-dilution mass spectrometry in BAL fluid, with limits of detection estimated from repeated measures at zero concentration; results above the limit are positive. Methods were validated by CDC for accuracy, precision, sensitivity and specificity (details in Supplementary Table S1, a PDF that was not opened). Self-reported vaping in the 90 days before illness comes from interviews, available for 43 of 51 patients.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured: concentrations in the fluid are not reported, only presence or absence; time from last vaping to bronchoscopy was unavailable; no product testing in this study.
exposure.polysubstance: Patients commonly used multiple tobacco and cannabis products. THC or its metabolites were found in BAL fluid from 40 of 47 patients (85%) and nicotine or its metabolites in 30 of 47 (64%). Of 11 patients who reported no THC product use in the 90 days before illness, 9 had THC or its metabolites in BAL fluid. 47 of 50 (94%) had THC in BAL fluid or reported vaping THC products.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable for patients (time since last vaping unknown). Comparators' non-smoking status was confirmed by urine anatabine.

comparison.controls: 99 healthy volunteers from an unrelated study at Ohio State University (52 who neither vaped nor smoked; 18 who vaped nicotine only; 29 who smoked cigarettes only), sampled 2016 to 2019 with 90 of the 99 samples taken before 2019, processed by that study's laboratory within 30 minutes of collection.
comparison.matching: None. Patients: median age 23, 69% male, from 16 states; comparators: median age 26, 54% male, from one Ohio study.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Time between last vaping and the lavage; treatment before the lavage; underlying lung disease; what products patients used, from where, and in what amount; no comparison group of people who vaped THC (including cartridges) without injury.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Urine THC biomarkers were positive in 21 of 82 tested comparators (26%), and BAL THC biomarkers in 5.1% of comparators (5 of 99); nicotine or metabolites were found in 52% of comparators' BAL fluid. No comparator reported vaping THC.

outcomes.instruments: Isotope-dilution mass spectrometry for each priority substance in Table 3: vitamin E acetate, MCT oil, coconut oil, plant oil, squalane, squalene, alpha-pinene, beta-pinene, 3-carene, limonene, petroleum distillates; also THC, nicotine and metabolites and the surfactant lipid DPPC, which was detectable in every sample and used as the adequacy marker. EVALI case status was assigned by state or local health officials.
outcomes.validity_norms: Methods met or exceeded US clinical laboratory quality criteria, according to the authors. The authors note that vitamin E acetate and other oils may be missed if BAL fluid was not well mixed, which they could not check, and that samples were collected under each hospital's own routine and not standardized.
outcomes.operationalization: Positive means above the limit of detection; no quantities are reported. Case status is the health department's classification under a definition the authors call intentionally sensitive; EVALI is a diagnosis of exclusion with no confirmatory test.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; no statistical tests are reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Vitamin E acetate in BAL fluid: 48 of 51 patients (94%), 0 of 52 comparators who neither vaped nor smoked, 0 of 18 who vaped nicotine, 0 of 29 who smoked cigarettes, 0 of 99 in all. Editors' calculation, exact binomial 95% intervals: patients 83.8% to 98.8%; comparators 0% to 3.7%. All three patients without vitamin E acetate were probable cases, so all 25 confirmed cases were positive (editors' deduction; 25 of 25, interval 86.3% to 100%) and 23 of 26 probable cases. Other priority substances in patients: coconut oil 1 of 48, limonene 1 of 39, MCT oil 0 of 49, plant oil 0 of 49, squalane 0 of 38, squalene 0 of 38, alpha-pinene 0 of 39, beta-pinene 0 of 39, 3-carene 0 of 39, petroleum distillates 0 of 12; none in comparators (denominators 17 to 98 per substance). THC or metabolites in BAL fluid of patients: 40 of 47 (85%); nicotine or metabolites 30 of 47 (64%).
analysis.covariates: None; unadjusted counts.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a public health response activity: CDC determined this information collection did not meet the regulatory definition of research. The comparators' study is registered (NCT02596685, cited in the reference list; not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: All priority substances on the pre-set list are shown in Table 3, the three vitamin E acetate-negative patients are described in Table 4, and the limitations are stated. Results for substances other than vitamin E acetate were not available for every sample because of small volumes.
analysis.power: Not applicable (descriptive; no hypothesis test).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Vitamin E acetate was found in the lung lavage fluid of 48 of 51 patients with EVALI from 16 states and in none of 99 healthy volunteers, none of whom vaped THC products; nearly none of the other pre-listed additives were found in patients; the three patients without it were all probable cases with other plausible diagnoses recorded; THC or its metabolites were found in 85% of patients, including 9 of 11 who said they had not used THC products.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that vitamin E acetate was associated with EVALI in a convenience sample of 51 patients; the Discussion says it may play a role and lists four supports (high detection in 16 states, absence in healthy comparators, absence of other priority substances, a plausible mechanism and timing with the illicit market). It states that the absence of the other listed substances is evidence against their being a primary cause. Gaps: (1) the healthy comparators included no one who vaped THC, so the contrast cannot separate vitamin E acetate from vaping of THC products in 2019 in general; (2) the absence of other substances is for a targeted list, with 12 to 49 samples for some; (3) the mechanism (loss of surfactant function; heated vitamin E acetate forming ketene) and the supply timing (Minnesota seizures, trade websites, FDA product testing) are from other sources, not tested here; (4) the authors themselves say vitamin E acetate may be a marker for another toxicant and that animal studies are needed to show cause. The paper's wording is cautious ('associated', 'may play a role').

timeline.event: New York State Department of Health (press release, 5 September 2019) reported vitamin E acetate in THC-containing products used by 34 persons with lung illness; the FDA and Minnesota seizure testing are cited as finding it in product fluids (49% of case-associated THC product samples; 20 of 20 THC products seized in September 2019 against 0 of 10 in 2018). Second-hand here: cited, not read.

CDC's earlier report of 29 patients in 10 states, all with vitamin E acetate in BAL fluid (MMWR, cited in this paper's references); this study extends that work and presumably includes those patients, so the two are not independent.
Analysis of illicit THC vaping cartridges recovered from patients in New York State

replication.where_it_stands: The lung-fluid finding comes from one laboratory (CDC) and overlapping patients; the product-level findings come from several laboratories but are cited second-hand in this paper. Whether vitamin E acetate alone causes the injury is stated by the authors to need animal studies.

funding.funder: National Cancer Institute grant P50CA180908; FDA Center for Tobacco Products grant P30CA016058; Ohio State University Pelotonia Intramural Research (Acknowledgments). The paper states that the content is solely the authors' responsibility and does not necessarily represent the views of the National Institutes of Health, CDC or FDA.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported in the text read: the authors' disclosure forms are on the publisher's site and were not opened.
funding.affiliations_note: Most authors work in CDC laboratory and response units, the agency that led the outbreak investigation and gave the public advice discussed; one author is affiliated with the FDA and several with Ohio State University. A government health agency, not the cannabis or tobacco industry.

what_would_settle_it: A study that tests lung fluid or breath from people who vape THC cartridges with and without injury, matched for time and source, with product contents measured, quantities reported and a wide untargeted chemical screen; plus controlled animal and human-tissue exposure to the aerosol of vitamin E acetate with and without THC, at realistic temperatures.

domains.note: Patients (hospitalized across 16 states in 2019) and comparators (healthy volunteers in Ohio, mostly sampled before 2019) differ in age, sex, setting, collection protocol and time, and none of the comparators vaped THC; nothing is adjusted. The contrast cannot separate vitamin E acetate from THC cartridge use in 2019 or from the illness itself.

Validated mass spectrometry with limits of detection and an adequacy marker in every sample, but patients' samples were collected without a standard protocol, at an unknown interval after last use and after treatment, and the authors could not check that fluid was mixed well; only the vitamin E acetate result is available for all, and others have denominators of 12 to 49.

51 patients, about 2% of those hospitalized, whose clinicians chose to do a lavage; comparators from an unrelated study with its own eligibility, 21 to 45 years, no major illness; nobody who vaped THC and was well.

Treatments given before the lavage (for example antibiotics or glucocorticoids, which Table 4 lists for three patients) and their timing are not reported; the interval from last use to lavage is unknown.

Small volumes limited the analytes measured per sample (12 to 49 patients for substances other than vitamin E acetate); product-use history is missing for 8 of 51; time since last use is not available.

Case status was assigned by health departments under a definition the authors call intentionally sensitive, for a diagnosis of exclusion; 26 of 51 are probable cases and the three without vitamin E acetate are all probable cases with other plausible diagnoses in Table 4.
A descriptive report in which every pre-listed substance and the three negative patients are shown; no protocol, but no sign of selective reporting.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E overall is no milder than the worst domain; confounding and selection are high because the two groups come from different populations and times and the comparators do not include people who vaped THC without injury. The laboratory method is validated, the target substance was measured in every sample, the counts are plain and the limitations are stated by the authors. It may be cited for the finding that vitamin E acetate was present in the lung fluid of 48 of 51 patients from 16 states and in none of 99 healthy volunteers, that all 25 confirmed cases were positive, and that the other listed additives were almost never found. It may not be cited as proof of cause, for lung fluid in people who vape THC products without injury, for substances not on the list, for the national proportion, or for any product or source.

key_findings.finding: BAL fluid was obtained from 51 patients with EVALI in 16 states (August to December 2019) and from 99 healthy participants of an unrelated Ohio State University study (52 neither vaping nor smoking, 18 vaping nicotine only, 29 smoking cigarettes only; sampled 2016 to 2019, 90 before 2019). Case status was confirmed for 25 and probable for 26 patients; median age 23 (range 16 to 67), 69% male; BAL fluid came from 3 patients who later died.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 2
key_findings.note: Author manuscript version of the NEJM article.

key_findings.finding: Vitamin E acetate was found in BAL fluid from 48 of 51 patients (94%) and from none of the 99 healthy participants (0 of 52, 0 of 18, 0 of 29). Editors' calculation, exact 95% interval for patients 83.8% to 98.8%, for comparators 0% to 3.7%.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 3 (vitamin E acetate row)

key_findings.finding: Other priority substances in patients' BAL fluid: coconut oil 1 of 48 and limonene 1 of 39 (the limonene patient had no vitamin E acetate or THC and reported daily flavoured nicotine products); MCT oil, plant oil, squalane, squalene, pinenes, 3-carene 0 of 38 to 49; petroleum distillates 0 of 12. None of these was found in any comparator.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 3; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The three patients without detectable vitamin E acetate were all probable cases. Table 4 lists for them unintentional multidrug overdose with benzodiazepines and oxycodone and suspected vaping lung injury (patient 1), acute eosinophilic pneumonia later revised to coccidioidomycosis with or without EVALI (patient 2), and acute hypoxic respiratory failure with Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia attributed to vaping lung injury (patient 3). The two interviewed denied vaping THC products. All 25 confirmed cases were therefore positive (editors' deduction).
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 4; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: THC or its metabolites were found in BAL fluid of 40 of 47 patients (85%); 9 of 11 patients who reported no THC product use in the 90 days before illness had THC or metabolites in BAL fluid; 47 of 50 (94%) had THC in BAL fluid or reported vaping THC products. Nicotine or metabolites were found in 30 of 47 (64%). Self-reported (43 patients): nicotine products only 7 (16%), THC products only 11 (26%), both 22 (51%).
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Results, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Among healthy comparators, urine THC biomarkers were positive in 25.6% (21 of 82) and BAL THC biomarkers in 5.1%; nicotine or metabolites in 52% of BAL fluids. No comparator reported vaping THC. All comparators' BAL fluid was negative for every priority substance.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Context quoted from other sources (second-hand): as of 12 December 2019, more than 2,400 hospitalized patients across all 50 states, Washington DC and two territories and 52 deaths in 25 states and Washington DC (CDC web page); 78% under 35; symptoms over days to weeks, respiratory 95%, constitutional 85%, gastrointestinal 77%; nearly half (47%) needed intensive care for respiratory failure (Siegel et al., not read). New York State laboratory testing of THC-containing products used by 34 persons with lung illness found vitamin E acetate in at least one product for each; FDA testing found it in 49% of case-associated THC product samples, on average 50% by weight (range 23% to 88%), and in none of 197 case-associated nicotine products; in Minnesota, 0 of 10 products seized in 2018 contained it against 20 of 20 THC products seized in September 2019.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs
key_findings.note: These figures are the authors' citations of a CDC web page, a New York State press release, FDA web pages and an MMWR report; none was read for this card.

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: vitamin E acetate may be a marker of another toxicant (which would have to correlate with it, be widespread in the US and have entered THC product fluids in 2019); aerosol products from heating vitamin E acetate (for example ketene) are not examined; sample collection was not standardized; timing and burden of exposure relative to the sample could not be assessed; case and comparator samples come from independent studies at single time points, so unknown confounding remains. Animal studies are needed to show whether vitamin E acetate alone causes the injury.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th and 9th paragraphs; Discussion, 7th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Case definitions as printed in the paper (Table 1): confirmed and probable cases both need vaping or dabbing in the 90 days before symptom onset, a lung infiltrate on chest X-ray or CT, and no evidence in the medical record of an alternative plausible diagnosis (for example cardiac, rheumatologic or neoplastic). Confirmed cases also need negative respiratory viral and influenza tests and negative results on all other clinically indicated infectious-disease tests; probable cases may have an infection identified, or incomplete testing, if the clinical team judges that the infection is not the sole cause of the lung injury. State and local health departments assigned case status.
