design_detail: Cross-sectional survey (STROBE) in 2553 young adults, the 2018 to 2019 wave (June 2018 to October 2019, one year after high-school graduation) of the Happiness and Health Study, a cohort first recruited in Southern California high schools. Self-reported nicotine vaping and cannabis vaping, each in five levels of recency and frequency, against three self-reported respiratory outcomes (bronchitic symptoms, wheeze, shortness of breath), analysed by logistic regression with sociodemographic adjustment and then with full adjustment for the other vaping, cigarette smoking and combustible cannabis use. The cannabis vaping variable combines electronic devices for THC or hash oil with vaping concentrated cannabis (dabs).
can_establish: In one regional cohort of young adults surveyed in 2018 to 2019, whether people who reported vaping THC or hash oil (or dabs) also reported more bronchitic symptoms, wheeze or shortness of breath than people who reported never doing so, and whether that survived adjustment for nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking and smoked cannabis.
cannot_establish: Which came first, vaping or the symptoms (one time point); what product, device, additive or amount was vaped (none recorded); lung function (symptoms were self-reported, with no spirometry); whether the link is the same for older adults, other regions or people not in school; absolute risk in each vaping group (Table 2 gives shares of cases, not symptom rates by group); and whether residual confounding by other exposures, such as tobacco in joints or blunts, accounts for it.

sample.recruitment: Participants of the Happiness and Health Study, originally recruited from high schools throughout Southern California and surveyed in this wave one year after graduation (June 2018 to October 2019); 2553 provided vaping data (75% participation rate). Of these, 2389 (94%) had complete data on shortness of breath, 2396 (94%) on wheeze and 2194 (86%) on chronic bronchitis (Methods › Analytic Sample).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Provision of data on lifetime, past 6-month and past 30-day vaping. People who gave no respiratory data stay in the vaping sample but drop out of the outcome models.
sample.demographics: Mean age 19.3 years (SD 0.79); 1477 women (57.9%) and 1076 men; 1188 Hispanic (47.3%), 454 non-Hispanic Asian (18.1%), 413 non-Hispanic white (16.5%), 166 multiracial (6.6%), 120 Black (4.8%), 109 Pacific Islander (4.3%), 60 other (2.4%), 43 not given; mean body mass index 24.97 (SD 6.51); 1081 of 2392 who answered (45.2%) lived comfortably; 161 gave no financial status (Table 1).
sample.attrition: 75% of the original sample took part in this wave. Per the Methods, people without any respiratory data were less likely to report never having vaped nicotine or smoked cigarettes (eTable 1, in the Supplement, not opened). Outcome data were missing for 359 people (bronchitic symptoms), 157 (wheeze) and 164 (shortness of breath); 110 had no cannabis vaping data and 2 no nicotine vaping data (Table 2 footnotes).
sample.selection_effects: A school-based Southern California cohort that is not nationally representative, ethnically diverse, all aged about 19, a year after leaving high school; the authors say findings may not apply to other regions or to people who did not attend or finish high school. Those who did not take part, or gave no respiratory data, differed in vaping and smoking, so a selected group may be analysed.

exposure.measurement: Self-report questionnaire. For each substance, people answered whether they had ever used it, and whether in the last 6 months; those with use in the last 6 months gave days of use in the past month. Items covered e-cigarettes with nicotine, JUUL or similar, other electronic vaping devices, an electronic device to vape THC or hash oil or dabs (wax, shatter, budder, butane hash oil), cigarettes, smoking marijuana, and blunts. Two five-level variables were built (nicotine vaping; cannabis vaping): never; lifetime but not in the past 6 months; past 6 months but not the past 30 days; 1 or 2 days in the past 30; 3 or more days in the past 30. Combustible cannabis (marijuana cigarettes, joints, blunts) and cigarettes were coded the same way (Methods › Measures).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Recency and days of use in the past month only. No information on the product (cartridge, dry-herb, concentrate), device, source, additives, amounts per session, puffing or time since first use. The cannabis vaping variable lumps vaping THC or hash oil in electronic devices with vaping concentrated cannabis (dabs), so cartridge use and dabbing cannot be separated.
exposure.polysubstance: Large overlap between nicotine vaping, cigarettes, smoked cannabis and cannabis vaping (eTable 2, in the Supplement, not opened). The full model adjusts for the other three exposures at five levels each, so the cannabis vaping estimates are mutually adjusted for nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking and combustible cannabis use. Combustible cannabis includes blunts; whether tobacco was involved in joints or blunts is not recorded. Alcohol, other drugs and secondhand smoke exposure are not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (survey). Exposure categories are by recency, not verified by biomarker.

comparison.controls: Young adults who reported never vaping cannabis (1504 of the 2443 with cannabis vaping data, 61.6%). This group includes people who smoked cannabis or cigarettes or vaped nicotine; those exposures are adjusted for in the full model, not excluded. For nicotine vaping the comparison group is people who reported never vaping nicotine (1456 of 2553).
comparison.matching: None. Logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, personal financial status and body mass index (sociodemographic model); the full model adds the other vaping variable, cigarette smoking and combustible cannabis use, each in five levels.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Asthma and allergy history (the authors used wheeze rather than a diagnosis because most asthma starts early), secondhand smoke, air quality including wildfire smoke, housing, respiratory infections, mental health and symptom-reporting style, other inhaled substances, and any symptom that came before the first vaping. Not measured or not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Reference group contains people who used the other substances; handled by statistical adjustment with coarse five-level frequency bands (the top band is 3 or more days in the past 30, which hides daily use).

outcomes.instruments: Three self-reported outcomes, each analysed separately. Bronchitic symptoms: any of daily morning cough for 3 months in a row, daily cough at other times of day for 3 months in a row, congestion or phlegm other than with a cold, and bronchitis in the past 12 months. Wheeze or whistling in the chest in the past 12 months (yes or no). Shortness of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill (yes or no). The authors base the definitions on earlier reports (references 6 and 9: a 2019 review by Gotts and colleagues and a 2017 adolescent cohort study by McConnell and colleagues; not read).
outcomes.validity_norms: No spirometry or clinical examination; symptoms are self-reported by people who also self-reported their vaping. Whether the 12-month window applies to all four bronchitic items is unclear: the abstract states it for the composite, the Methods only for the bronchitis item. Shortness of breath has no time frame.
outcomes.operationalization: Having the outcome means answering yes to any bronchitic item, or yes to wheeze, or yes to breathlessness; no symptom severity, duration of vaping before symptoms or clinical diagnosis.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: The Methods state that Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted P values were used to correct for multiple tests, but no adjusted P value appears in the Results or Table 3; the printed intervals are unadjusted. There are 48 odds ratios in Table 3 (3 outcomes, 2 exposures, 4 levels, 2 models), several with a lower bound close to 1 (1.01, 1.02, 1.04).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-completed survey). Exposure and outcome were reported by the same person at the same time, which allows correlated reporting.

analysis.effect_sizes: Adjusted odds ratios (95% CI) against never, for lifetime but not past 6 months, past 6 months but not past 30 days, 1 to 2 days in the past 30, and 3 or more days in the past 30 (sociodemographic model; full model). CANNABIS VAPING, bronchitic symptoms: sociodemographic 1.47 (0.97 to 2.23), 1.44 (1.07 to 1.94), 2.95 (1.75 to 4.98), 2.51 (1.63 to 3.84); full 1.73 (1.01 to 2.96), 1.63 (1.04 to 2.56), 2.79 (1.42 to 5.47), 2.19 (1.18 to 4.06). Wheeze: sociodemographic 1.06 (0.65 to 1.73), 1.47 (1.08 to 2.00), 1.76 (0.96 to 3.13), 2.13 (1.35 to 3.36); full 1.12 (0.61 to 2.03), 1.47 (0.92 to 2.35), 1.84 (0.88 to 3.86), 2.27 (1.17 to 4.37). Shortness of breath: sociodemographic 0.95 (0.63 to 1.44), 1.35 (1.04 to 1.75), 1.67 (0.98 to 2.86), 1.67 (1.09 to 2.53); full 0.90 (0.57 to 1.40), 1.25 (0.86 to 1.84), 1.55 (0.81 to 2.96), 1.41 (0.80 to 2.48). NICOTINE VAPING, bronchitic symptoms: sociodemographic 1.35 (0.92 to 1.97), 1.18 (0.79 to 1.78), 1.48 (0.97 to 2.21), 1.78 (1.32 to 2.41); full 1.21 (0.76 to 1.93), 0.82 (0.50 to 1.32), 1.13 (0.71 to 1.81), 0.96 (0.63 to 1.46). Wheeze: sociodemographic 1.13 (0.74 to 1.71), 1.55 (1.04 to 2.32), 1.27 (0.81 to 1.99), 1.41 (1.01 to 1.96); full 0.96 (0.58 to 1.59), 1.06 (0.66 to 1.71), 0.99 (0.59 to 1.65), 0.85 (0.54 to 1.35). Shortness of breath: sociodemographic 1.20 (0.85 to 1.71), 1.41 (0.99 to 2.00), 1.64 (1.14 to 2.36), 1.45 (1.08 to 1.96); full 1.03 (0.68 to 1.57), 1.10 (0.73 to 1.67), 1.31 (0.86 to 1.99), 0.96 (0.64 to 1.42). Overall 17.5% (384 of 2194) reported bronchitic symptoms, 13.0% (312 of 2396) wheeze and 20.4% (488 of 2389) shortness of breath. Among the 384 with bronchitic symptoms, 185 (48.2%) had never vaped cannabis, against 61.6% of the 2443 with cannabis vaping data (Table 2 and Results). Editors' rough calculation, not in the paper: if people with missing outcome data were spread evenly across vaping groups, unadjusted bronchitic-symptom rates would be about 14% in people who never vaped cannabis and about 27% to 31% in those who vaped it in the past 30 days; the paper says missing respiratory data were commoner in people who vaped nicotine or smoked, so the true gap may be larger. Odds ratios overstate rate ratios when the outcome is this common (13% to 20%).
analysis.covariates: Age, sex, race/ethnicity, personal financial status, body mass index; the full model adds the other vaping variable, cigarette smoking and combustible cannabis use. No adjustment for asthma, secondhand smoke, air quality or tobacco co-use in cannabis. The number of people in each model is not given: Table 3 headings show 2194, 2396 and 2389, the counts with outcome data, but the full models also need cannabis vaping, financial status and body mass index.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All three outcomes and both exposures are shown in Table 3, with sociodemographic and full models. The abstract's adjusted odds ratios for bronchitic symptoms differ from Table 3 and the Results text (reporting issue 1). The stated multiple-testing correction is not shown. The headline emphasises the cannabis vaping results in the full model; the nicotine vaping associations seen in the sociodemographic model, which became null on full adjustment, are reported.
analysis.power: No power calculation. The nicotine and cannabis vaping top bands are small (400 and 155 people), and the cannabis vaping intervals at 1 to 2 and 3 or more days are wide (1.42 to 5.47; 1.18 to 4.06).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 2553 young adults in one Southern California school-based cohort, people who reported ever vaping THC or hash oil or dabs had higher odds than people who never had of reporting bronchitic symptoms in the past year at every level of recency and frequency (full-model adjusted odds ratios 1.6 to 2.8, adjusting for nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking and smoked cannabis), higher odds of wheeze only in the top band (3 or more days in the past 30, 2.27, 1.17 to 4.37), and no reliable difference in shortness of breath. Nicotine vaping on 3 or more days in the past 30 was associated with bronchitic symptoms, wheeze and shortness of breath after sociodemographic adjustment only (1.45 to 1.78), and with none of them after full adjustment (0.85 to 0.96).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusions say cannabis vaping is associated with increased risk of bronchitic symptoms and wheeze, independent of nicotine vaping and smoking combustible products, and that nicotine and cannabis vaping warrant consideration in patient care and public health policy. Key Points say cannabis vaping may be associated with bronchitic symptoms beyond the consequences of other drug use. Gaps: (1) risk language comes from one cross-sectional survey, with no information on what came first; (2) independence rests on adjustment with coarse five-level bands for the other exposures, and combustible cannabis includes blunts with unrecorded tobacco, so residual confounding is plausible; (3) odds of bronchitic symptoms were raised even in people who had last vaped cannabis more than 6 months earlier (1.73), about as raised as in those vaping in the past 30 days (2.19 to 2.79), which does not fit an effect of recent vaping alone and is not discussed; (4) the Discussion's mechanisms (vitamin E acetate, higher exposure from deeper puffs and concentrates) were not measured, and the statement that vitamin E acetate vaping has virtually disappeared is made without a source; (5) the abstract's adjusted odds ratios for bronchitic symptoms differ from Table 3; (6) symptoms are self-reported and unconfirmed. The Limitations section does state the cross-sectional design, the single region and the need for longitudinal work.

timeline.event: McConnell et al. (cited, not read) linked nicotine vaping to respiratory symptoms in adolescents; Wills et al. (2019) did the same in adults, per the authors' introduction (Introduction, 2nd paragraph).

This survey, which the authors describe as new evidence for an independent association of cannabis vaping with bronchitic symptoms, with nicotine vaping and smoking adjusted at the same time; they note longitudinal work on cannabis vaping and symptoms is lacking (Discussion, 1st paragraph; Limitations).

replication.where_it_stands: A single cross-sectional survey from one cohort. No second study of cannabis vaping and respiratory symptoms was read for this card, and the authors say longitudinal research on this question is lacking. Evidence on smoked cannabis and symptoms, cited by the authors, is not read here.

funding.funder: National Cancer Institute, National Institutes of Health: grants U54CA180905 (all authors; principal investigator Leventhal), R01CA229617-01 (Barrington-Trimis, Leventhal) and K24DA048160 (Leventhal). The paper states the funders had no role in design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit.
funding.declared_conflicts: None reported.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of young adults with repeated symptom reports and lung function tests before and after people start vaping cannabis, recording product type (cartridge, dry-herb, concentrate), source, device and puffing, tobacco co-use, and biomarker confirmation of use, with separate groups who only vape cannabis, only smoke it, do both, or neither, and a registered analysis plan with the multiple-testing correction shown.

domains.note: One time point, so reverse causation and shared causes cannot be separated. Adjustment is for sociodemographics and for the other exposures in five coarse bands; tobacco in joints or blunts, secondhand smoke, air quality, asthma and allergy are not measured. Raised odds in people who last vaped cannabis more than 6 months before the survey (1.73) point to residual confounding or to an exposure measure that captures more than recent vaping.

Self-reported recency and days of use, not verified; the cannabis vaping variable merges THC or hash oil devices with dabs, and no product, device or amount is recorded. Misclassification is probably not related to symptoms, which would bias towards no association.

A school-based Southern California cohort, 75% participation in this wave; people without respiratory data were more likely to have vaped nicotine or smoked cigarettes; not representative of other regions or of people who left school.
Not an issue for a single-time survey of exposure and symptoms.

Outcome data missing for 14% (bronchitic symptoms) and 6% (wheeze, shortness of breath), with missingness related to vaping and smoking; 110 people have no cannabis vaping data; handling is not described and the number analysed in each model is not given.

Self-reported symptoms from questions used in earlier cohort studies, with no spirometry or clinician; the bronchitic composite counts any of four broad items; the same person reported exposure and outcome.

No protocol or registration; the stated Benjamini-Hochberg correction is not shown; the abstract's adjusted odds ratios for bronchitic symptoms differ from Table 3; all outcomes and both models are shown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E overall is no milder than the worst domain; confounding is judged high because a single cross-sectional survey with coarse adjustment cannot separate cannabis vaping from other exposures and from reverse causation, and the pattern of raised odds in people who last vaped long before the survey suggests residual confounding. The study is sizeable for a vaping survey, adjusts at once for nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking and smoked cannabis, reports both an unadjusted-to-sociodemographic and a fully adjusted model, and shows its null results. It may be cited for the association between self-reported vaping of THC or hash oil or dabs and self-reported bronchitic symptoms (and, in the top band, wheeze) in these young adults, and for the loss of the nicotine vaping association on full adjustment. It may not be cited for causation, for the effect of any particular product, for lung function, for absolute risk in a vaping group, or for older people.

key_findings.finding: 2553 young adults (mean age 19.3, SD 0.79; 57.9% women; 47.3% Hispanic) from a Southern California school-based cohort answered a survey between June 2018 and October 2019, a year after high-school graduation (75% participation). Outcome data were available for 2194 (bronchitic symptoms), 2396 (wheeze) and 2389 (shortness of breath).
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Methods › Analytic Sample, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Of the 2553, 1095 (42.9%) reported ever vaping nicotine. Of the 2443 with cannabis vaping data, 939 (38.4%) reported ever vaping THC or hash oil or dabs: 204 (8.4%) only in their lifetime, 490 (20.1%) in the past 6 months but not the past 30 days, 90 (3.7%) on 1 or 2 days and 155 (6.3%) on 3 or more days in the past 30; 110 people had no cannabis vaping data. Smoked cannabis on 3 or more days in the past 30: 517 (20.3%); cigarettes on 3 or more days: 98 (3.8%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Respiratory Health Outcomes and Levels of Nicotine and Cannabis Vaping, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1; Table 2 footnote f

key_findings.finding: Overall, 384 of 2194 (17.5%) reported bronchitic symptoms, 312 of 2396 (13.0%) wheeze in the past year, and 488 of 2389 (20.4%) shortness of breath. Among the 384 with bronchitic symptoms, 185 (48.2%) had never vaped cannabis. Table 2's percentages are shares of people with each outcome, not rates within each vaping group.
key_findings.locator: Results › Respiratory Health Outcomes and Levels of Nicotine and Cannabis Vaping, 1st paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: Table 2's heading calls these prevalence, but footnote a says column percentages.

key_findings.finding: Bronchitic symptoms and cannabis vaping, full model (adjusted for nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking, smoked cannabis, age, sex, race/ethnicity, financial status, body mass index), adjusted odds ratios against never vaping cannabis: lifetime but not past 6 months 1.73 (95% CI 1.01 to 2.96); past 6 months but not past 30 days 1.63 (1.04 to 2.56); 1 or 2 days in the past 30 2.79 (1.42 to 5.47); 3 or more days 2.19 (1.18 to 4.06). Sociodemographic model only: 1.47 (0.97 to 2.23), 1.44 (1.07 to 1.94), 2.95 (1.75 to 4.98), 2.51 (1.63 to 3.84).

key_findings.note: The abstract prints 1.83 (1.08 to 3.10), 1.58 (1.02 to 2.46), 2.83 (1.46 to 5.50) and 2.14 (1.16 to 3.92) for the same four; use Table 3.

Sociodemographic model: 2.13 (1.35 to 3.36) in the top band and 1.47 (1.08 to 2.00) for past 6 months but not past 30 days.

Full model: 0.96 (0.63 to 1.46), 0.85 (0.54 to 1.35), 0.96 (0.64 to 1.42); no nicotine vaping level was reliably associated with any outcome. key_findings.finding: Limits and explanations given by the authors: cross-sectional design (temporality unknown); school-based Southern California sample with 75% participation, not nationally representative; the cannabis vaping measure includes dabs; longitudinal research on cannabis vaping and symptoms lacking; possible reasons for a difference from nicotine vaping include the chemicals in THC e-liquids, device and heating differences, tampering with products, and deeper or longer puffs. None of these was measured.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's fully adjusted odds ratios for bronchitic symptoms with cannabis vaping (1.83, 1.08 to 3.10; 1.58, 1.02 to 2.46; 2.83, 1.46 to 5.50; 2.14, 1.16 to 3.92) differ from Table 3 and the Results text (1.73, 1.01 to 2.96; 1.63, 1.04 to 2.56; 2.79, 1.42 to 5.47; 2.19, 1.18 to 4.06). The wheeze value (2.27, 1.17 to 4.37) is the same in both.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract appears to quote an earlier version of the model. Table 3 is used for every figure; the direction and the conclusion are unchanged, but the abstract values must not be quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives 204 of 2553 (8.4%) for lifetime-only cannabis vaping and 939 of 2553 (38.4%) for any, but 8.4% and 38.4% are shares of the 2443 people with cannabis vaping data (204 of 2553 is 8.0%, as in Table 2; 939 of 2553 is 36.8%). The abstract also says lifetime but not in the past '60 months'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Mixed denominators and a typing error (6 months); the 110 people with no cannabis vaping data are the difference.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results sentence on nicotine vaping and bronchitic symptoms in the fully adjusted model gives 'aORs range from 1.63-2.79 [95% CI, 1.01-5.47]', which are the cannabis vaping figures. Table 3 gives 0.82 to 1.21 for nicotine vaping.
reporting_issues.consequence: A copy error; the table shows no reliable nicotine vaping association with bronchitic symptoms on full adjustment, consistent with the sentence's claim of no significant association.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 is headed 'Prevalence of each respiratory outcome', but the percentages are column percentages (the share of people with each outcome who fell in each vaping group), not symptom rates within each vaping group.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper never gives the percentage of each vaping group with symptoms; do not read the 48.2% of cases who never vaped cannabis as the rate in that group.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 headings give n = 2194, 2396 and 2389 (people with outcome data), but the fully adjusted models also need cannabis vaping (110 missing), financial status (161 missing), body mass index and the smoking variables. The Methods also say 2553 provided complete data on lifetime, 6-month and 30-day vaping while 110 have no cannabis vaping data.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 3 headings; Methods › Analytic Sample; Table 2 footnote f
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of people in each model is not stated; complete-case loss may be larger than 14%.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted P values corrected for multiple tests; no adjusted P value or adjusted interval is shown. Several fully adjusted lower bounds are close to 1 (1.01 for lifetime-only cannabis vaping and bronchitic symptoms; 1.04 and 1.02 elsewhere).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the weaker associations survive the stated correction cannot be told.

reporting_issues.issue: The pattern of odds in Table 3 is not discussed: people whose last cannabis vaping was more than 6 months before the survey had raised odds of bronchitic symptoms in the past 12 months (1.73, 1.01 to 2.96), similar to those vaping in the past 30 days (2.19 to 2.79).
reporting_issues.consequence: The data do not show a clear gradient with recency, which argues for caution about an effect of current vaping and for residual confounding.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7756238 (all sections, Tables 1 to 3 and author notes read as text; the Supplement, with eTable 1, eTable 2 and the questionnaire, is a PDF and was not opened)

design_detail: Descriptive laboratory analysis of product samples, with no comparison group. The Wadsworth Center (the New York State Department of Health public health laboratory) analysed 38 samples of residual fluid from vaporizer cartridges recovered from the first 10 New York State patients with e-cigarette, or vaping, product use-associated lung injury (EVALI) for whom cartridges were obtained (the laboratory began receiving cartridges in August 2019), and six commercial products sold online as cannabis-oil diluents or thickeners. Untargeted screening by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and high-resolution liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-HRMS/MS), then targeted measurement of 11 natural cannabinoids (HPLC with photodiode array), five mycotoxins, vitamin E acetate (VEA; GC-MS), the fungicide myclobutanil and the pesticide synergist piperonyl butoxide (PBO; LC-MS/MS), a screen of 884 pesticides and metabolites, and a screen for synthetic cannabinoids and 150 synthetic opioid compounds; nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) for the commercial products. Results are counts and percentages by mass; no statistical tests or intervals are given. Version read: the PMC full text of the Toxics article (2020;8(1):8).
can_establish: What was in the residual fluid of vaporizer cartridges recovered from 10 New York patients with EVALI in 2019: of 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids, 23 (64%) contained VEA, at 16 to 58% by mass; 14 or 15 contained medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) oil; most also held pesticide residues; some had unusually high delta-8-THC; none had synthetic cannabinoids, opioids or mycotoxins above the stated limits. It also shows that three of six commercial products sold online as cannabis-oil diluents or thickeners were essentially pure VEA, so VEA was on sale for this use.
cannot_establish: That VEA, or any other substance in the fluid, caused the lung injury: there are no fluids from people who vaped without injury, no dose or timing data and no result per patient. It cannot show what share of the 10 patients had a VEA-containing cartridge (13 of the 36 fluids had none), how common VEA was in cartridges in general in 2019, what the patients inhaled other than the residue left in the cartridge, or how these cartridges differ from legally sold ones (that contrast rests on the laboratory's earlier work with New York medical products, not on data shown here). The aerosol was not analysed; products formed when VEA is heated are mentioned from initial experiments that are not shown.

sample.recruitment: Cartridges and devices were obtained through New York Poison Control Centers and health care providers. Medical staff of the Department of Health's Center for Environmental Health reviewed each reported case's medical record for consistency with the CDC clinical description of EVALI; when case-associated cartridges were available they were sent to the Wadsworth Center (Methods 2.1). The six commercial products were bought on the internet by the Department of Health (Results 3.4).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Fluids from the first 10 New York EVALI cases for which cartridges were obtained. Cartridges with little fluid were centrifuged to recover it and run at adjusted dilution; sample 38 had too little material for the PBO test (Table 2). Whether any cartridge was excluded is not stated. How each cartridge was judged to be illicit is not described: the Methods call them case-associated and say that packing and markings were noted, but report neither.
sample.demographics: Not reported for the 10 patients (no age, sex, dates or hospital course). The only patient information is that, of the first 10 cases who provided product-use histories (the number who provided one is not stated), all reported using cannabinoid-containing vaping products and 80% reported using both cannabinoid- and nicotine-containing products (Discussion 4.3, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Thirty-eight samples are analysed from 10 patients, about 3.8 per patient on average; the number per patient is not given.
sample.selection_effects: Only cartridges that patients, families or clinicians handed over, from 10 patients in one state, are analysed; who handed over cartridges and who did not is not described. The fluid is what was left in the cartridge at recovery, which may differ from what was inhaled earlier. No sample of cartridges from the wider market was taken, so the shares apply to these cartridges, not to cartridges in general.

exposure.measurement: Laboratory analysis of residual fluid, about 10 mg weighed into acetonitrile. VEA: GC-MS with a deuterated internal standard, calibration 0.039 to 2.5 micrograms per mL, analytical range 1 to 100% by mass; identity confirmed against an analytical standard by retention time, library mass spectrum and accurate mass (Results 3.1). Cannabinoids: HPLC with photodiode array, the method the laboratory has used for New York medical marijuana products since December 2015. MCT oil was estimated roughly (3 to 24% by mass) by comparing four peak areas with a commercial MCT oil, because standards for the individual components are not available. Pesticides: myclobutanil and PBO by LC-MS/MS; a wider screen with a cut-off of 1 microgram per gram. Synthetic cannabinoids and opioids: detection to 0.05% by mass.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured. The paper gives no information on how much each patient vaped, for how long, which cartridge they used when, or how the cartridges were obtained. The statement that vaping heats fluids to 250 to 350 degrees Celsius is made without a source.
exposure.polysubstance: Two of the 38 fluids held nicotine and no cannabinoids (samples 4 and 16); 36 held cannabinoids. Of the first 10 cases who provided product-use histories, 80% reported using both cannabinoid- and nicotine-containing vaping products.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (product analysis).

comparison.controls: None within the study. The authors contrast the fluids with vaporizer products of New York State's medical marijuana program that the same laboratory has tested ('thousands of samples'): free of additives and 80 to 90% total cannabinoids (Discussion 4.1, 2nd paragraph). No data from those products are shown here. No fluids from people who vaped without injury, and none from legal retail in 2019, are analysed.
comparison.matching: None.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Which cartridge each patient used and when; how many cartridges each of the 10 patients contributed; where and how each was obtained; whether patients whose cartridges held no VEA (13 of 36 fluids) also used a cartridge that did.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: GC-MS and LC-HRMS/MS untargeted screens; HPLC with photodiode array for 11 natural cannabinoids; LC-MS/MS for five mycotoxins (aflatoxins B1, B2, G1, G2 and ochratoxin A), myclobutanil and PBO; GC-MS for VEA; Q-Orbitrap screen of 884 pesticides and metabolites; NMR, GC-MS and LC-HRMS/MS for the six commercial products.
outcomes.validity_norms: The cannabinoid, mycotoxin, myclobutanil and PBO methods are ones the New York laboratory has validated and had certified or accredited for medical marijuana products; they were adapted here (a scaled-down mycotoxin extraction because of small samples; cannabinoid samples run without the usual surrogate spike). The VEA method was developed for this work. Whether the methods perform the same in illicit fluids was not tested in the text read. Figures S1 to S6 and Table S1 (supplement) were not opened.
outcomes.operationalization: VEA 'found' means measured at 1% by mass or more; lower values are printed as below 1.0. A fluid is cannabinoid-containing if any of the 11 natural cannabinoids was quantified. The paper's 64% is 23 of 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids, not 23 of 38 fluids and not a share of patients.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no hypothesis tests).

analysis.effect_sizes: Cannabinoid-containing fluids (36): VEA in 23 (64%), 16.4 to 57.6% by mass, median 38.4% among the 23 (editors' calculation from Table 1); no detectable VEA in 13, of which 12 held MCT oil. MCT oil: 15 in the text, 14 marked in Table 1 (editors' count); both VEA and MCT in 2 fluids (samples 7 and 14); neither in 1 (sample 27). Delta-9-THC 3.1 to 66.3% by mass, median 29.6%; sum of quantified cannabinoids 23 to 73%, under 50% in 27 of 36 (editors' calculation; the paper gives no totals). Delta-8-THC quantified in 8, higher than delta-9-THC in 6 of them (editors' count). At least one pesticide (myclobutanil in 22, PBO in 18, other pesticides above 1 microgram per gram in 26 fluids) in 31 of the 36 (editors' count from Table 2); none in the other 5. Mycotoxins below 4.8 ng/g and synthetic cannabinoids and opioids below 0.05% by mass in all 38. Commercial products: three of six (two diluents, one thickener) essentially pure VEA, two squalane-based, one alpha-bisabolol-based. Update to 12 December 2019 given in the Conclusions without methods: 206 fluids from 61 New York cases, 147 containing THC and 59 nicotine; 101 of the 147 (69%) contained VEA. Editors' calculation, exact binomial 95% intervals, treating fluids as independent (they come from 10 and 61 patients, so these are too narrow): 23 of 36, 46% to 79%; 101 of 147, 61% to 76%.
analysis.covariates: None; unadjusted counts.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not registered; a public health laboratory response analysed as samples arrived. The paper says the laboratory had no prior expectation of what the cartridges held (Results 3.1).
analysis.selective_reporting: All 38 samples are shown in Tables 1 and 2 and the six commercial products in Table 3. The untargeted screens are reported only for the additives and contaminants the authors discuss; other compounds seen are not tabulated in the text read. The extended series (206 fluids) and the heating experiments are reported as statements with no data.
analysis.power: Not applicable (descriptive).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids recovered from 10 New York patients with EVALI, 23 (64%) held VEA at 16 to 58% by mass, 13 held none, 14 or 15 held MCT oil, 31 held at least one pesticide, and no synthetic cannabinoids, opioids or mycotoxins were found; cannabinoid content was mostly under 50% by mass; three of six commercial diluent and thickener products were essentially pure VEA.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title names VEA as a major diluent, and the abstract says the cause of EVALI is unknown. The Discussion says it is possible that VEA is causative or contributes, offers lipoid pneumonia and heating products as mechanisms, and states that there is no evidence that vaping large amounts of VEA, squalane or other diluents is safe. The Conclusions add that there is additional evidence of a strong association of VEA with EVALI (101 of 147 fluids and 28 of 28 lung-fluid samples in a CDC report) and that in vitro and in vivo studies will be required to establish cause. Gaps: (1) this paper has no comparison fluids, so the association is not tested within it; (2) 13 of 36 fluids held no VEA; (3) the contrast with legal products rests on unpublished laboratory experience; (4) the market timeline for VEA diluents (introduced in 2018, sales up in spring 2019) is sourced to trade-press articles on a cannabis-industry website, not peer-reviewed work; (5) heating products of VEA and the claim that pesticide contamination is 'intermittent and random' are inferences without data shown.

timeline.event: The laboratory shared its VEA findings with CDC, FDA and state health officials on 19 August and the New York State Department of Health announced them on 5 September (the authors' account; the announcement was not read).

The authors cite the FDA, Utah and Minnesota as later finding VEA in case-associated fluids; Blount et al. quote FDA testing that found it in 49% of case-associated THC product samples. These reports were not read; the proportions differ from this study's 64% and from the New York update's 69%.
CDC reported vitamin E acetate in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients with EVALI and in none of 99 healthy volunteers (the New York laboratory cites an earlier CDC report of 28 of 28).
CDC update on the outbreak: 2,668 hospitalized patients by 14 January 2020, most who reported product use having used THC-containing products.

replication.where_it_stands: Several agencies are cited as finding VEA in case-associated products or lung fluid, and the New York figures overlap one another, so they are not independent replications. The proportions differ between reports. Whether VEA alone causes the injury is stated by the authors to need laboratory and animal studies.

funding.funder: This research received no external funding (Funding section).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no financial or other conflicts of interest (Conflicts of Interest section).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors work at the Wadsworth Center and the Center for Environmental Health of the New York State Department of Health, the University at Albany School of Public Health and Albany Medical Center. The Wadsworth laboratory also tests the state's medical marijuana products, which the paper uses as the comparison for the illicit fluids. A government health laboratory, not the cannabis or tobacco industry; no industry tie is declared.

what_would_settle_it: Testing every cartridge each patient used, by laboratories blind to case status, alongside cartridges from people of similar age and product use who vaped without injury and from legal retail in the same months, with the number of cartridges per patient and their source reported; plus experiments on the aerosol of VEA, with and without THC, at realistic temperatures.

domains.domain: Selection and provenance of the samples
domains.note: Cartridges from 10 patients in one state, handed over for analysis; the number per patient, the dates, the source of each cartridge and the basis for calling them illicit are not reported.

Mass-spectrometric identification confirmed against standards, validated or certified methods for most analytes, and detection limits stated. MCT oil is only roughly estimated, the VEA method is new, performance in this fluid type was not tested in the text read, and the supplement was not opened.

No fluids from people who vaped without injury or from legal retail; the contrast with New York medical products is the laboratory's experience and is not shown. The share with VEA cannot be read as higher or lower than other cartridges.

domains.domain: Link between the analysed product and the patient's illness
domains.note: Results are not given per patient; 13 of 36 fluids held no VEA; the residue in a recovered cartridge may not be what a patient inhaled earlier.

domains.domain: Separation of findings from inference about cause
domains.note: The findings are described as findings and cause is called unknown, but the Discussion's mechanisms, the safety statement about large amounts, the market timeline from trade press and the 'strong association' wording go beyond the data shown.

The text counts 15 fluids with MCT oil where Table 1 marks 14; the VEA ceiling is 57% in the Results, 57.6% in Table 1 and 58% in the Discussion; the extended series of 206 fluids has no methods or table; no per-sample MCT amounts are given.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a laboratory analysis of case-associated products (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used, with domains chosen for product analysis. The overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. The chemistry is careful and the findings are clearly tabulated, and the authors keep the cause open. The paper may be cited for what was in the fluid of 38 cartridges recovered from 10 New York patients, for the VEA content of three commercial diluent and thickener products, and for the absence of the named synthetic compounds and mycotoxins. It may not be cited for the cause of EVALI, for how common VEA was in cartridges in general, for a difference from legal products, or for what any patient inhaled.

key_findings.finding: Thirty-eight samples of fluid from vaporizer cartridges recovered from the first 10 New York State patients with EVALI for whom cartridges were obtained were analysed; two held nicotine and no cannabinoids (samples 4 and 16) and 36 held cannabinoids. The laboratory began receiving cartridges in August 2019 and chose untargeted analysis because it had no prior information on what they held.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Introduction, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Results 3.2, 3rd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: VEA was found in 23 of the 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids (64%), at 16 to 57% by mass (Table 1 maximum 57.6%; the Discussion says as much as 58%); 13 held none above 1% by mass. Editors' calculation: exact 95% interval 46% to 79%, treating the 36 fluids as independent, which they are not.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.2, 3rd paragraph; Table 1 (VEA column); Discussion 4.1, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: MCT oil was estimated at 3 to 24% by mass in the 15 fluids the text says held it (Table 1 marks 14 with a plus sign, by the editors' count); 12 of the 13 fluids without VEA held MCT oil and 2 held both. MCT was estimated roughly because standards for its components are not available.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.2, 4th paragraph; Table 1 (MCT column)

key_findings.finding: Cannabinoid content was lower than the laboratory's usual medical products: delta-9-THC 3.1 to 66.3% by mass (median 29.6%, editors' calculation) in the 36; the authors say illicit fluids are usually under 50% cannabinoids against 80 to 90% in New York's medical program products (27 of 36 under 50% by the editors' sum of the quantified cannabinoids). Delta-8-THC was quantified in 8 fluids and exceeded delta-9-THC in 6 of them (editors' count).
key_findings.locator: Results 3.2, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1; Discussion 4.1, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The medical-program comparison is the laboratory's account; no data are shown. Table 1 units are not printed in the text read; per cent by mass is taken from the surrounding text.

key_findings.finding: Pesticides: myclobutanil was quantified in 22 fluids (up to 28.3 micrograms per gram), PBO in 18 (up to 24.1), and several other fungicides, insecticides and acaricides above 1 microgram per gram in 26; 31 of the 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids held at least one (editors' count). The authors judge the pattern intermittent and say EVALI is not due to a single pesticide. No mycotoxins (below 4.8 ng/g) and no synthetic cannabinoids or opioids (below 0.05% by mass) in any fluid.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.1, 5th paragraph; Results 3.3; Table 2; Discussion 4.1, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of six commercial products bought online as cannabis-oil diluents or thickeners, two diluents and one thickener were essentially pure VEA, one diluent was mostly squalane with MCT and triethyl citrate, one thickener was squalane, and one thickener was alpha-bisabolol with a little isophytol. The sellers did not list ingredients on label or website.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.4; Table 3; Discussion 4.2, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of the first 10 New York cases who provided product-use histories (number not stated), all reported using cannabinoid-containing vaping products and 80% reported using both cannabinoid- and nicotine-containing vaping products. The two nicotine-containing fluids held no unusual compounds of concern.
key_findings.locator: Discussion 4.3, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Update to 12 December 2019 (Conclusions, no methods or table): 206 fluids from 61 New York cases, 147 with THC and 59 with nicotine; 101 of 147 THC-containing fluids (69%) held VEA. Editors' calculation, exact 95% interval 61% to 76%, treating fluids as independent. The authors also cite 28 of 28 lung-fluid samples with VEA in an early CDC report, and CDC counts of 2,409 hospitalized cases and 52 deaths as of 12 December 2019, and 205 New York cases including 2 deaths as of 10 December.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions
key_findings.note: National and lung-fluid figures are the authors' citations of a CDC web page and an MMWR report, not read here.

key_findings.finding: The authors' timeline for the diluents rests on articles from a cannabis-industry news site: VEA-based diluents appeared on the market in 2018, sales greatly increased in spring 2019, and they were touted as tasteless, odourless and miscible with cannabis oil in all proportions. The authors also say cutting product with cheaper material the customer cannot detect is long-standing practice in illegal drug markets.
key_findings.locator: Discussion 4.2, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; references 20 to 22
key_findings.note: Trade-press sources, not peer-reviewed; not read.

key_findings.finding: Limits and inferences stated by the authors: the cause or causes of EVALI are unknown; VEA is high-molecular-mass, lipophilic and similar to oils known to cause lipoid pneumonia, so it is possible that it is causative or contributes; initial experiments (not shown) indicate compounds including duroquinone form when VEA is vaped; extensive in vitro and in vivo studies are required to establish cause.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Discussion 4.3, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Conclusions

key_findings.finding: Funding: none external. Declared conflicts: none. Authors are employees of the New York State Department of Health Wadsworth Center and Center for Environmental Health, with academic affiliations at the University at Albany and Albany Medical Center.
key_findings.locator: Funding; Conflicts of Interest; author affiliations

reporting_issues.issue: The text says MCT oil was detected in 15 fluids; Table 1 marks 14 fluids with a plus sign (samples 3, 7, 14, 15, 18, 24, 26, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33 and 34).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which fluid is the fifteenth is not clear, and the 3 to 24% range cannot be checked because per-sample MCT amounts are not tabulated.

reporting_issues.issue: The basis for calling the cartridges illicit is not stated. The title, abstract and Discussion say illicit or street products; the Methods say only that case-associated cartridges were collected and that packaging and markings were noted.
reporting_issues.consequence: The label may be an inference from the contents, the cartridges' look or the patients' accounts; the shares cannot be applied to 'illicit' cartridges as a class.

reporting_issues.issue: The extended series (206 fluids from 61 cases; 101 of 147 with VEA) appears only in the Conclusions, with no methods, no table and no statement of whether the first 38 are included.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 69% cannot be checked and overlaps the 64% from the first 10 cases; the two should not be counted as independent.

reporting_issues.issue: The upper VEA value is given as 57% in the Results, 57.6% in Table 1 and 58% in the Discussion; Table 1 units are not printed in the text read.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results 3.2, 3rd paragraph; Table 1; Discussion 4.1
reporting_issues.consequence: Rounding only; the units are inferred from the surrounding text.

reporting_issues.issue: Results are not given per patient: the 38 fluids are listed by sample number only.
reporting_issues.consequence: It cannot be seen how many of the 10 patients had a VEA-containing cartridge, or whether the 13 fluids without VEA came from patients who also had one that did.

reporting_issues.issue: Claims that the lab's medical-program products are 80 to 90% cannabinoids and free of additives, that heating VEA forms compounds including duroquinone, and that the extended series found more VEA are given without data.
reporting_issues.consequence: These statements are the authors' account and are not checkable from the paper.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7151740 (all sections, Tables 1 to 3, figure captions, funding and conflict statements, author affiliations and reference list read as text; Figures 1 to 5 were not viewed as images; the supplementary PDF with Figures S1 to S6 and Table S1 was not opened)

design_detail: National passive surveillance report (CDC Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, 24 January 2020, with state and local health departments and the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists) on e-cigarette, or vaping, product use-associated lung injury (EVALI) as of 14 January 2020. States and jurisdictions voluntarily reported confirmed and probable hospitalized or deceased patients to CDC each week using CDC case definitions and a national case report form (linked documents, not read). The report describes 2,668 hospitalized patients (age, sex, race and ethnicity, case status), the substances they reported using in vaping products in the 3 months before symptom onset (limited to people who reported vaping or dabbing at least one substance), weekly hospital admissions, and trends in possible EVALI-related emergency department visits from the National Syndromic Surveillance Program (a query on vaping products in the stated reason for the visit; about 70% of emergency visits nationwide). No product or patient samples are tested in this report, and there is no comparison group.
can_establish: How many people had been reported to CDC as hospitalized with this lung injury by 14 January 2020, who they were, what they said they had vaped, and when weekly admissions and related emergency visits rose and fell between August 2019 and January 2020.
cannot_establish: What caused the injury (nothing was tested in this report; it relies on other work for vitamin E acetate); how many people were affected out of all who vape, or out of all who vape cannabis (no denominator); how severe the illnesses were or how many people died (not reported here); whether what patients said they vaped was what was in the device; whether every reported case was EVALI (the authors say the case definition favored sensitivity over specificity); and the full size of the outbreak (voluntary reporting; product information missing for a quarter of patients).

sample.recruitment: Not a sample: all cases reported by the 50 states, the District of Columbia, the US Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico as of 14 January 2020, by voluntary weekly reporting using CDC case definitions (main text, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Confirmed and probable hospitalized or deceased EVALI patients meeting the CDC surveillance case definition (not reproduced in the report). Substance-use percentages are limited to people who reported vaping or dabbing at least one substance in the 3 months before symptom onset (Table footnotes).
sample.demographics: Median age 24 years (range 13 to 85); age groups 13 to 17 years 404 (15%), 18 to 24 979 (37%), 25 to 34 631 (24%), 35 to 44 335 (13%), 45 to 64 223 (9%), 65 and over 47 (2%) of 2,619 with age; 1,731 of 2,606 with sex (66%) male; of 1,856 with race and ethnicity, 1,360 (73%) non-Hispanic white, 64 (3%) Black, 12 (1%) American Indian or Alaska Native, 38 (2%) Asian, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, 97 (5%) other, and 285 (15%) Hispanic.
sample.attrition: Product-use information was missing for 24% of patients (646 of 2,668; editors' count), and many patients were not interviewed because of loss to follow-up, refusal, or lack of resources (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Race and ethnicity were missing for about 30% (812 of 2,668; editors' count). The admissions figure shows 2,398 patients, so 270 reported patients are not in it (editors' count; the report gives no reason).
sample.selection_effects: Cases are those clinicians recognized, hospitals admitted, health departments classified and states chose to report; about half (47%) are 'probable' rather than 'confirmed'. The authors say the high sensitivity of the case definition likely lowered specificity, so some patients may not have had EVALI (Discussion, 2nd paragraph). People with milder illness who were not hospitalized are outside the report.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported by patients (interview or case report form; who interviewed and how is not described) as substances used in e-cigarette, or vaping, products in the 3 months before symptom onset: any THC-containing product, any nicotine-containing product, both, exclusive THC, exclusive nicotine, neither. No laboratory confirmation of the products or of the patients' exposures in this report.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported: no product type (cartridge or other), brand, source, amount, frequency or duration. The report says vaping or dabbing and that CDC advises against products from informal sources, but gives no numbers on sources.
exposure.polysubstance: Nicotine and THC product use were recorded together as categories: both 834 (41%), exclusive THC 669 (33%), exclusive nicotine 274 (14%), neither reported 44 (2%) among the 2,022 with information. Other substances, additives and contaminants cannot be captured by self-report; the authors say patients may not know the content of what they vaped.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None in this report. For context, the report notes a low but long-standing background rate of emergency visits related to vaping products before the outbreak, which could reflect chemicals of concern in nicotine products or sporadic cases from the same substances that later spread (Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: There is no denominator of people who vape THC or nicotine products, no comparison with people who vape and were not ill, no information on source, device, additive or amount, and no testing in this report, so the share of patients who used THC products says nothing about the risk to a person who does.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: CDC surveillance case definitions (confirmed, probable; not reproduced); weekly count of hospital admissions by week of admission (Figure 1, an image); National Syndromic Surveillance Program rate of possible EVALI-related emergency visits per million (Figure 2, an image), using a query on vaping products in the stated reason for the visit, excluding injuries such as device explosions and accidental ingestion of e-liquid but not acute THC intoxication or nicotine poisoning.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors say the exposure query in the emergency data may have been affected by public and clinical awareness of the outbreak, and that coverage of the system is uneven across and within states and changes over time (Discussion, 5th paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Severity beyond hospitalization (intensive care, ventilation, death) is not reported in this update; the report speaks of hospitalized or deceased patients but gives no count of deaths.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive report).

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive. 2,668 hospitalized patients; among 2,022 with substance information (76% of cases), any THC-containing product 1,650 (82%), any nicotine-containing product 1,162 (57%), both 834 (41%), exclusive THC 669 (33%), exclusive nicotine 274 (14%), neither 44 (2%). Editors' calculation: 1,650 of all 2,668 patients (62%) is the least that reported any THC-containing product, if none of the 646 with no information had. Weekly hospital admissions peaked at 215 in the week of 15 September 2019 and have declined steadily since. Possible EVALI-related emergency visits rose by a mean of 26 per million per week (95% CI 18 to 33) between 11 August and 8 September 2019, peaked at 116 per million in the week of 8 September, fell by about 4 per million per week (95% CI 4 to 5) to 35 per million in the week of 5 January 2020, which is still above 23 per million in the week of 18 August 2019.
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable; surveillance report.
analysis.selective_reporting: The report is a descriptive update that cites earlier CDC updates (October and November 2019, and a January 2020 product and demographic update) for other characteristics; deaths, intensive care use and product sources are not given here.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: By 14 January 2020, 2,668 people in every US state, Washington DC and two territories had been reported as hospitalized with this lung injury; they were young (median 24, three quarters under 35), two thirds male and mostly non-Hispanic white. Among the 76% with substance information, 82% said they had used a THC-containing vaping product (33% only THC products) and 57% a nicotine-containing product (14% only nicotine products). Weekly admissions and related emergency visits peaked in September 2019 and fell steadily afterwards.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The report concludes that vitamin E acetate is strongly linked to the outbreak (a conclusion drawn from another paper, not shown here), that the evidence is not sufficient to rule out other chemicals of concern in THC or non-THC products in some cases, and that the decline might be multifactorial (public awareness, removal of vitamin E acetate from products, enforcement). CDC's recommendation to avoid THC vaping products, especially from informal sources, and its advice to adults who vape instead of smoking are statements of advice, not findings of this report. Gaps: (1) the abstract's and the Summary box's percentages are of patients with information, stated as 'of EVALI patients', without the 24% with no information; (2) the exclusive categories do not add up with the 'any' categories (reporting issue 1); (3) the reasons offered for the decline are not tested, and the suggestion that vitamin E acetate was removed from products cites two news articles; (4) no number is given for deaths or for how people obtained products. The report is open about its limits and about the unexplained 14% who reported only nicotine products.

timeline.event: Earlier CDC updates in October and November 2019 (Moritz et al.; Chatham-Stephens et al.; cited in this report's reference list, not read) described patients in the same outbreak.
Laboratory analysis of lung fluid from patients, cited here for the link with vitamin E acetate
This update: 2,668 hospitalized patients and the decline in cases after September 2019.

replication.where_it_stands: A cumulative surveillance snapshot, not a study that can be replicated. Its counts are firmer than its product-use shares, which are self-reported and missing for a quarter of patients. Deaths and the later course of the outbreak are not covered by this update.

funding.funder: Not stated as a grant. Authors are staff of CDC centers (injury, immunization and respiratory diseases, chronic disease, surveillance, birth defects, minority health, environmental health, toxic substances) and the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists, with a task force of state health department staff; the report is a CDC publication.
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors completed the ICMJE disclosure form and no potential conflicts of interest were disclosed.
funding.affiliations_note: The authors are the agency that ran the investigation and issued the public recommendations discussed; the report describes its own surveillance. A government health agency, not the cannabis or tobacco industry.

what_would_settle_it: A case-control or cohort study of people with and without lung injury, interviewed with the devices in hand, with products tested for contents and source, with the denominator of people who vape and which products they used, and with outcomes (intensive care, ventilation, death, recovery) followed for months.

domains.note: Voluntary reporting by states; 47% of cases are 'probable'; the authors say the sensitive definition lowered specificity and may include people without EVALI. Counts of hospitalized patients are probably an undercount of all lung injury and may include some other illnesses.
Missing for 24% of patients (646 of 2,668); many were not interviewed; the 2,022 with data may differ from those without. Race and ethnicity are missing for about 30%.

Patients may not know or may not report what was in a device, and the authors say so; no sample was tested in this report; the 14% who reported only nicotine products are explained by misreporting, misclassification or true exclusive nicotine use without telling which.

domains.domain: Separation of surveillance findings from inference about cause
domains.note: The report states that its evidence is not sufficient to rule out other chemicals and that reasons for the decline might be multifactorial, but the vitamin E acetate link and the effects of awareness, product removal and enforcement are not tested here; advice is mixed with findings.
The exclusive and any product categories do not reconcile; the abstract's shares are of patients with data; the under-35 share is 76% in the text and 76.9% from the table counts.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a national surveillance case series (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used, with domains chosen for surveillance counts. The report is a clear description of who was reported as hospitalized and when, by an agency with access to the case reports, and the counts of patients and their age and sex are reasonably firm descriptions of reported cases. Its product-use shares are self-reported and incomplete and cannot show what was in any product. It may be cited for the number and characteristics of hospitalized patients reported to CDC by 14 January 2020, the share who said they had used THC-containing or nicotine-containing products among those asked, and the timing of the September 2019 peak. It may not be cited for the cause of EVALI, for the risk to any person who vapes, for the proportion of patients who used illicit or informally sourced products, for deaths, or for what the decline was due to.

key_findings.finding: As of 14 January 2020, all 50 states, the District of Columbia, the US Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico had reported 2,668 hospitalized EVALI patients to CDC: 1,401 (53%) confirmed and 1,267 (47%) probable cases.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Case status row)

key_findings.finding: Median age 24 years (range 13 to 85); 404 (15%) aged 13 to 17, 979 (37%) 18 to 24, 631 (24%) 25 to 34, 335 (13%) 35 to 44, 223 (9%) 45 to 64, 47 (2%) 65 and over, of 2,619 with age; 1,731 of 2,606 (66%) male; of 1,856 with race and ethnicity, 73% non-Hispanic white and 15% Hispanic. The text says 76% were under 35 (404 + 979 + 631 = 2,014 of 2,619 is 76.9%, editors' calculation).
key_findings.locator: Main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Sex, Median age, Age group, Race/Ethnicity rows)

key_findings.finding: Among 2,022 patients with information on substances used (76% of 2,668): any THC-containing product 1,650 (82%); any nicotine-containing product 1,162 (57%); both 834 (41%); exclusive THC 669 (33%); exclusive nicotine 274 (14%); neither 44 (2%). Limited to people who reported vaping or dabbing at least one substance in the 3 months before symptom onset.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Substances used rows and footnotes)
key_findings.note: The four exclusive categories add to 1,821, not 2,022, and 1,650 minus 834 is 816, not 669 (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: Weekly hospital admissions for EVALI peaked at 215 in the week of 15 September 2019 and have declined steadily since (Figure 1 is titled N = 2,398 patients, 270 fewer than the 2,668 reported, with no reason given; values not extracted from the image).
key_findings.locator: Main text before the Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1 title

key_findings.finding: Possible EVALI-related emergency visits (National Syndromic Surveillance Program) rose by a mean of 26 per million per week (95% CI 18 to 33) from 11 August to 8 September 2019, peaked at 116 per million in the week of 8 September, and fell by about 4 per million per week (95% CI 4 to 5) to 35 per million in the week of 5 January 2020, still above 23 per million in the week of 18 August 2019.
key_findings.locator: Main text before the Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Figure 2 title

key_findings.finding: The authors state that vitamin E acetate is strongly linked to THC-containing products used by patients (citing the lung fluid study), that a minority of patients consistently report only nicotine-containing products (possible reasons: patients may not report or know the content of what they vaped, some cases may be misclassified because the case definition was sensitive rather than specific, or the reports may be accurate), and that evidence is not sufficient to rule out other chemicals of concern in THC or non-THC products in some cases.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: The abstract and Discussion state the vitamin E acetate link; the data behind it are in the cited paper, not in this report.

key_findings.finding: Possible reasons for the decline after mid-September 2019 given by the authors (not tested): public awareness and actions by people who vape, removal of vitamin E acetate from THC products after the link was identified (supported by two news articles in footnotes), and enforcement affecting supply from informal sources. Also noted: it is not known whether additives other than vitamin E acetate could cause similar injury, and long-term consequences need long-term follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; footnotes ¶ and **

key_findings.finding: Limits given by the authors: product-use data missing for 24% of patients and many not interviewed; the emergency visit query may have been affected by awareness of the outbreak; coverage of the surveillance system is uneven and changes over time.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The Table's mutually exclusive categories (exclusive THC 669, exclusive nicotine 274, both 834, neither 44) add to 1,821 of the 2,022 patients with information; and 'any THC' (1,650) minus 'both' (834) is 816, not 669, while 'any nicotine' (1,162) minus 'both' is 328, not 274.
reporting_issues.consequence: About 201 patients (10%) are in none of the four categories; the report does not say who they are (for example, THC use reported but nicotine unknown). The 'exclusive' shares should not be summed with 'both' to get 'any'.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that 82% of EVALI patients used any THC-containing product and 57% any nicotine-containing product, but these are shares of the 2,022 with information (76%), not of the 2,668 reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: A share 'of EVALI patients' overstates what is known; the least that is known is 62% (1,650 of 2,668) for THC (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 76% of patients were under 35, while the table counts give 2,014 of 2,619 (76.9%); the 76% is the sum of the rounded table percentages (15 + 37 + 24).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Age group)
reporting_issues.consequence: A rounding artefact of 1 percentage point; no effect on interpretation.

reporting_issues.issue: The suggestion that vitamin E acetate was removed from THC products and so contributed to the decline is supported by two news articles (footnotes ¶ and **), a state recall report and FDA statements; no data on product contents after the outbreak are presented.
reporting_issues.consequence: Treat the explanations for the decline as the authors' conjecture.

reporting_issues.issue: Race and ethnicity are available for 1,856 of 2,668 patients (70%), sex for 2,606, age for 2,619, and the figure for 2,398; percentages use these differing denominators.
reporting_issues.consequence: The race composition rests on 70% of cases and may differ for the rest.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7367698 (all sections, the Table, figure titles, footnotes and reference list read as text; Figures 1 and 2 are images and their values were not extracted; the linked CDC case definition and case report form were not opened)

design_detail: Retrospective chart review of emergency department (ED) visits at one academic hospital in Colorado (University of Colorado Hospital: urban, about 100,000 visits a year, more than 97% adults), 1 January 2012 to 31 December 2016. The unit is the visit, not the person. Visits carrying a cannabis-related ICD-9-CM or ICD-10-CM code were read by trained research assistants, who judged whether the visit was at least partly attributable to cannabis, the route (edible or inhaled), the dose when written down, and the symptoms. Edible-attributed and inhaled-attributed visits were then compared for symptoms, who attended and what happened to them. A second analysis set the share of attributable visits that involved edibles against the share of THC sold as edibles in Colorado in 2014 to 2016, using state sales data and assumed THC contents. There is no group of people who used cannabis and did not come to hospital, and none of people who do not use cannabis.
can_establish: What clinicians at this one emergency department recorded as the reasons for visits they linked to cannabis, and how the mix of recorded reasons differed between visits recorded as edible and visits recorded as inhaled (or, where no route was written down, presumed inhaled), with differences in percentage points and 95% confidence intervals (Table 2). That serious cardiovascular events (myocardial infarction, ventricular dysrhythmia) occurred in both groups, although the paper gives no counts (Results › Comparison of Visits Attributable to Inhalable Versus Edible Cannabis, 2nd paragraph). A rough size of the gap between edibles’ share of attributable visits and their share of THC sold, under stated assumptions about product strength.
cannot_establish: How often a visit follows each form, per person or per occasion: only people who reached this department are counted, with no count of people who took each form and did not attend, so the percentages are shares among visits, not risks. Whether the form itself caused the different mix of reasons: the two groups differed (more women and more people living outside Colorado among edible-attributed visits), the amount taken was written down in 130 of 2,567 visits (5.1%), product strength was not measured, route was presumed inhaled when not documented (135 visits), and the paper reports no adjustment for age, sex, residence, previous experience, alcohol, tobacco or other drugs. What happens in other hospitals or states, to people treated elsewhere or to people who did not seek care. The sales comparison rests on assumed THC content (20% of flower weight, 10 mg per edible unit), leaves out home-grown and illicit supply, and sets one hospital against statewide sales, so it cannot show how much more likely an edible is to lead to a visit than the same amount of THC taken another way. The edible group (238 visits) is small beside the inhaled group (2,329).

sample.recruitment: No one was recruited. All ED visits at the hospital in the five years were eligible (449,031). Visits with a cannabis-related ICD code (9,973) were abstracted by hand, and 2,567 (25.7%) were classed as at least partly attributable to cannabis if the ED provider named cannabis as likely precipitating or contributing, or the inpatient provider did after admission, or the urine drug screen was positive with a documented link within about 24 hours and a condition known to be associated with cannabis (Methods › Study Participants and Coding). Attribution is a clinician judgment recorded in the chart.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: adults with an ED visit carrying a cannabis-related ICD-9-CM or ICD-10-CM code (Appendix Table lists the codes), and within them the attributable visits as defined above. Visits without such a code were not abstracted, so visits in which cannabis mattered but was not coded would be missed: a check of 4,800 randomly chosen records found 26 with a mention of cannabis that the code search had not captured (all in 2015 to 2016, the ICD-10 period; medical shorthand in consultants’ notes, polypharmacy ingestions), none judged attributable (Results › Chart Review Sensitivity and Interrater Reliability).
sample.demographics: Attributable visits (n = 2,567): median age 30 (interquartile range 24 to 41); 65.2% male; 43.4% White, 36.6% Black, 17.8% Hispanic; 90.2% Colorado residents and 9.8% (252) from other states; 31.6% admitted, 62.5% discharged, 2.1% transferred to a psychiatric facility, no deaths (Table 1). Pregnant: 46 patients (under 2%). Edible-attributed against inhaled-attributed visits: women 51.3% vs 33.1%, living outside Colorado 40.8% vs 6.6%, admitted 18.9% vs 32.9% (each P < 0.001); median length of stay 2 hours (range 1 to 54) vs 3 hours (range 0 to 121); age said to be similar, no figures (Results › Comparison…, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable to a chart review. Route was recorded in 2,432 of 2,567 attributable visits (94.7%); for the 135 visits with insufficient documentation, inhalation was assumed. A dose was recorded in 130 (5.1%).
sample.selection_effects: Strong. Only people who came to this hospital’s ED, were coded with a cannabis-related diagnosis and were judged by a clinician to be affected by cannabis are in the data; people who took cannabis without harm, or were harmed and did not attend, are absent, so the paper cannot say who tends to choose which form or how many came to no harm. Attribution depends on what patients said and what clinicians asked and wrote down. The authors note that this department has the second-highest number of visits a year in the state and sits in an area of high cannabis availability, which they say likely raises its rates of attributable visits (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Visitors from outside Colorado are 9.8% of attributable visits and 40.8% of edible-attributed visits (Results › Comparison…, 1st paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Route and dose as written in the chart: the drug-use section of the standard nursing assessment questionnaire and the medical providers’ notes (Methods › Study Participants and Coding). Self-report, not verified; no blood levels. Route was assumed to be inhalation when not documented, because that is the most common route in Colorado (Methods › Measurements, 1st paragraph); the authors say this could have biased the comparison toward greater toxicity in the inhaled group (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Product strength and content were not measured. The paper reports two groups only, edible and inhaled; no breakdown of the inhaled group by product (for example flower, vaporized oil or concentrates) appears in the text or tables.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Route: edible or inhaled (inhaled includes anything documented as smoked or inhaled and every undocumented route). A dose was written down in 130 of 2,567 visits; among edible-attributed visits it was written down in 80, and in 19 of those it was 50 mg of THC or more (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Frequency and duration of use before the visit are not reported. Time between exposure and the visit is not reported, apart from the 24-hour link used in one attribution criterion.
exposure.polysubstance: Not examined. The paper does not describe alcohol, tobacco or other drugs taken at the same time, and no comparison accounts for them. One attribution criterion rests on a positive urine screen plus a documented link within about 24 hours and a condition known to be associated with cannabis; the screen does not show which form was taken. Tobacco mixed into joints is not recorded.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (emergency presentation).

comparison.controls: No group of people who do not use cannabis, and none of people who used cannabis and did not come to hospital. The comparison is inside the attributable visits: edible-attributed (238) against inhaled-attributed (2,329, of which 135 presumed). The sales analysis sets the edible share of attributable visits (10.7%, 2014 to 2016) against the edible share of THC sold by weight (0.32%).
comparison.matching: None. Crude percentages, chi-square tests and absolute differences in percentage points with 95% confidence intervals; no adjustment (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not measured: previous experience with cannabis (the authors suggest inexperience among visitors as one explanation, without testing it: Discussion, 7th paragraph), usual frequency and amount of use, tolerance, mental-health and heart history (only partly seen in the reasons ‘acute exacerbation of underlying chronic disease’ and ‘chronic psychiatric condition’), other substances, and which product was taken.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not described.

outcomes.instruments: Manual chart abstraction by four trained research assistants who were blinded to the study hypothesis, after an ICD code search; no clinical scales. Variables: attribution to cannabis, route, dose when available, clinical and presenting symptoms (not mutually exclusive), length of stay, disposition. A medical toxicologist abstracted a random 10% for reliability and arbitrated questionable attributions; 1,111 visits were abstracted twice (Methods › Measurements, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Inter-rater agreement kappa 0.79 (95% CI 0.75 to 0.83), described as good (Results › Chart Review Sensitivity and Interrater Reliability). The symptom groups in Table 2 are the authors’ own groupings; the Appendix Table gives the codes used to find visits, not definitions of the symptom groups.
outcomes.operationalization: ‘Attributable to cannabis’: the ED provider, or the inpatient provider after admission, named cannabis as likely precipitating or contributing, or a positive urine screen plus a documented link within about 24 hours plus a condition known to be associated with cannabis. ‘Edible’ or ‘inhalable’: the route as documented, with inhalation presumed when not documented.
