Cannabis, tobacco and alcohol use were self-reported once, at conscription, in non-anonymous questionnaires; lung cancer was taken from national registers by record linkage (inpatient Patient Register to the end of 2009, Cause-of-Death Register to the end of 2006). Cox regression of time to lung cancer by lifetime cannabis use (ever against never; never, once, 2–4, 5–10, 11–50 and more than 50 times), crude, tobacco-adjusted and fully adjusted. Exposure was recorded before the outcome, but the study is a historical record-linkage analysis of data collected for conscription.
can_establish: Whether men who reported more cannabis use by age 18 to 20 were diagnosed with lung cancer more often over the next 40 years than men who reported none, after adjustment for tobacco, alcohol, respiratory illness and occupation as recorded at that time.
cannot_establish: That smoking cannabis causes lung cancer, or the risk in men who never smoked tobacco (too few to analyse), in women, above about age 60 or with later patterns of use and products: use after conscription, how cannabis was smoked, how much and whether tobacco was mixed in were never recorded, and the number of cancers in each cannabis group is not given in the text or tables.

sample.recruitment: Registry/conscription: all men conscripted for compulsory Swedish military service in 1969–70 (born 1949–51), which the authors say covered more than 97% of Swedish men of that age, 2–3% being excused for disqualifying mental or physical conditions (p. 2 of the online-first PDF).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Men conscripted in 1969–70 at age 18 to 20. The models are complete-case analyses: men without cannabis answers (3,768 for ever use, 3,800 for frequency) or with other missing predictors were left out, and 10 of the 189 lung cancers were excluded for missing predictor information.
sample.demographics: Men only, aged 18 to 20 at baseline. At conscription 41.4% did not smoke tobacco, 11.2% smoked 1–5 cigarettes a day, 20.7% 6–10, 23.1% 11–20 and 3.6% more than 20; 10.5% had ever used cannabis and 1.7% more than 50 times; physician-diagnosed respiratory conditions about 2% in every cannabis group; occupation from the 1970 census, about half manual skilled or unskilled (Table 1).
sample.attrition: During follow-up 2,958 men (6.0%) died of causes other than lung cancer and 930 (1.9%) emigrated, both censored; 44,257 to 44,285 men entered the adjusted models (about 90% of the cohort).
sample.selection_effects: Population-based and nearly complete for Swedish men of that age, so selection into the cohort is not the concern. Limits to generalising: men only, Swedish cannabis and tobacco use of 1969–70, and follow-up ending at about age 60. The men who did not answer the cannabis questions (about 7.6%) had a lower lung cancer risk than men who reported never using cannabis (fully adjusted HR 0.41, 0.17 to 0.99), so non-responders differed in some way the paper does not explain.

exposure.measurement: Non-anonymous self-report at conscription: ever against never use of cannabis, and lifetime frequency in six bands (never, once, 2–4, 5–10, 11–50, more than 50 times); the bands follow an earlier analysis of the same cohort, and this paper calls more than 50 times 'heavy' use. No biological verification; the authors cite a validation study of self-reported drug use in this cohort as showing reasonable accuracy.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Lifetime number of uses by age 18 to 20 only. No quantity, potency, duration, method of smoking (joint or pipe) or tobacco mixed in, and no measure of cannabis use at any time after conscription over the 40 years; smoking is assumed as the route.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco (cigarettes a day at conscription, five answers collapsed into three bands: none, 1–10, more than 10) and alcohol (grams a week from five questions, four levels) were adjusted for, each measured once. Of the 831 men reporting more than 50 cannabis uses, 756 (91.0%) also smoked tobacco and 514 (61.8%) more than 10 cigarettes a day, against 54.7% and 23.2% of the men who reported never using cannabis (editors' arithmetic from Table 1). Other drug use was collected at conscription but not used in the analysis. Whether tobacco was mixed into cannabis is unknown.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (registry outcomes decades later).

comparison.controls: Men who reported never using cannabis at conscription (40,397; 44.8% did not smoke tobacco, 31.5% smoked 1–10 cigarettes a day and 23.2% more than 10).
comparison.matching: None. Cox models adjusted for tobacco (three bands), alcohol (four levels), respiratory conditions diagnosed at conscription (chronic bronchitis, emphysema, pneumonia or asthma) and socioeconomic status (occupation in the 1970 census).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Tobacco and cannabis use after conscription; how much tobacco was smoked within the coarse bands (the top band runs from 11 to more than 20 a day); occupational and environmental exposures, diet and family history of lung cancer; use of other drugs. None was adjusted for.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported; 54.7% of the men who reported never using cannabis smoked tobacco (editors' arithmetic from Table 1).

outcomes.instruments: Lung cancer coded ICD-8/9 162 or ICD-10 C33–C34 in any diagnostic position in the Swedish Patient Register (inpatient care) from conscription to the end of 2009, or as the underlying cause in the National Cause-of-Death Register to the end of 2006; emigration from the Total Population Register. The Swedish Cancer Register was not used.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors cite 78% to 99% concordance between lung cancer records in the Patient Register and the Cause-of-Death or Cancer Registers, and sensitivities of about 80% to 95% for administrative lung cancer codes in studies elsewhere. Of the 189 cases, 95 were in both registers, 88 in the Patient Register only and 6 in the death register only.
outcomes.operationalization: Time to a first lung cancer record, censored at death from other causes, emigration or 31 December 2009; person-time from 1 January 1970 (1 October 1969 for two men who died in 1969), about 1.9 million person-years per line of analysis. Proportional hazards checked with log survival plots.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: one outcome, but ever use and five frequency bands were each tested in three models, with p < 0.05 as the threshold.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Outcomes came from national registers, independent of the conscription questionnaire.

analysis.effect_sizes: Hazard ratios with 95% CIs (Tables 2–4). Lifetime frequency against never (crude; tobacco-adjusted; fully adjusted): once 2.07 (1.06–4.06); 1.48 (0.75–2.91); 1.52 (0.77–3.01). 2–4 times 0.95 (0.39–2.33); 0.65 (0.26–1.58); 0.66 (0.27–1.62). 5–10 times 1.02 (0.32–3.20); 0.66 (0.21–2.09); 0.68 (0.21–2.16). 11–50 times 2.69 (1.26–5.74); 1.68 (0.78–3.62); 1.68 (0.77–3.66). More than 50 times 3.72 (1.96–7.06); 2.24 (1.17–4.29); 2.12 (1.08–4.14). Ever against never: 1.90 (1.30–2.75); 1.25 (0.85–1.83); 1.25 (0.84–1.87). Tobacco against none, fully adjusted: 1–10 a day 2.34 (1.47–3.70), more than 10 a day 5.03 (3.23–7.81). Missing cannabis answers against never, fully adjusted: 0.41 (0.17–0.99) and 0.40 (0.16–0.98). No absolute risks by group are given; editors' calculation of the base rate: 189 of 49,321 men (0.38%, about 4 in 1,000) had a lung cancer record by the end of 2009, about 9 per 100,000 person-years in the analysed cohort (179 cases over about 1.9 million person-years).
analysis.covariates: Tobacco (three bands), alcohol (four levels), respiratory conditions at conscription and socioeconomic status (occupation, 1970 census), all measured once at baseline.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned. The frequency bands, including 'more than 50 times', follow an earlier analysis of the same cohort (Zammit et al., 2002, cited for consistency); the label heavy is this paper's.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract reports only the more-than-50 band, the one band significant after adjustment, and omits the null ever-use result after tobacco adjustment, the lack of a gradient across bands and the crude and tobacco-only estimates (all in the Results and tables). Tobacco-stratified analyses are in Supplemental Tables 1 and 2, described as unstable or inestimable; the supplement was not available to this reader.
analysis.power: 179 cases in the models; the number among the 831 men in the heaviest band is not given in the text or tables (Figure 1, a stacked bar chart by year, was not extracted); too few men used cannabis without tobacco for stratified analyses.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Men who reported more than 50 lifetime uses at age 18 to 20 had about twice the hazard of a lung cancer record by about age 60 (fully adjusted 2.12, 1.08 to 4.14), with an interval reaching close to 1; the estimate fell from 3.72 unadjusted to 2.24 with a three-band tobacco adjustment, ever use was not associated after tobacco adjustment (1.25, 0.84 to 1.87), and the lower bands showed no gradient. Of the heaviest band 91% also smoked tobacco, and no estimate could be made for men who did not.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports 'more than a twofold risk' for heavy use 'even after statistical adjustment for baseline tobacco use' and concludes that the study provides 'initial longitudinal evidence that cannabis use might elevate the risk of lung cancer' (p. 1 of the online-first PDF); the conclusion adds that the finding requires further replication (p. 8). The Discussion proposes that the findings be integrated into drug-prevention programmes as initial evidence of the risks of marijuana smoking for lung cancer (p. 7), and argues that unmeasured changes in use after conscription would bias the estimate toward the null (p. 8). Gaps: the label 'heavy' for more than 50 lifetime uses by age 20; an abstract silent on the null ever-use result, the missing gradient and the near-1 lower limit; and a one-sided bias argument, since later tobacco smoking, more common in men who used cannabis, could bias the estimate away from the null, which the authors cover only as residual confounding by tobacco. The conclusion itself is hedged ('might', 'requiring further replication') and the limitations are stated candidly.

timeline.event: Sidney et al.: Kaiser Permanente cohort in California, no association between cannabis smoking and lung cancer; this paper notes its members were followed only to a mean age of 42 (as cited).
Hashibe et al.: population-based case-control study in Los Angeles, no association (as cited).
This cohort: HR 2.12 (1.08–4.14) for more than 50 lifetime uses at conscription, no gradient below that band, no association for ever use after tobacco adjustment.

Zhang et al.: pooled analysis of six case-control studies in the International Lung Cancer Consortium, habitual against non-habitual cannabis smoking OR 0.96 (0.66–1.38), known here only through the National Academies committee's account.

National Academies committee: 'moderate evidence of no statistical association' between cannabis smoking and lung cancer, naming this cohort as a study outside the pooled analysis that points to an increased risk.
Muheriwa-Matemba et al., systematic review by route: the reviews it included did not conclusively link cannabis smoking and lung cancer.

replication.where_it_stands: The only cohort with follow-up of decades among the sources read. Its raised estimate in the heaviest band stands against the null pooled case-control analysis and has not been repeated in another cohort in the sources read; it rests on one baseline report of cannabis and tobacco use, with 91% tobacco co-use in that band, and on follow-up that ends before the ages at which most lung cancers are diagnosed.

funding.funder: Supported indirectly by an institutional grant from the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care to the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (salary support for R. C. Callaghan), and by a research grant from the Swedish Council for Working Life and Social Research (FAS 2009-1611 to P. Allebeck; salary support for A. Sidorchuk). The paper states that the funders had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, manuscript preparation or approval to publish, and that the views are not necessarily the Ministry's.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that they have no conflict of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: University of Northern British Columbia, University of Toronto and CAMH (Callaghan); Karolinska Institutet (Allebeck, Sidorchuk); North-Western State Medical University, Saint Petersburg (Sidorchuk). No cannabis- or tobacco-industry ties are declared.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort, or pooled cohorts, that records cannabis and tobacco use repeatedly through adult life (including how cannabis is smoked, how much and whether tobacco is mixed in), includes enough people who smoke cannabis but never tobacco, follows them with cancer-register outcomes into the ages at which most lung cancers occur, and reports absolute risks by group.

domains.note: Tobacco, the main confounder, was measured once at age 18 to 20 in three coarse bands; 91% of the heaviest cannabis band smoked tobacco and 61.8% more than 10 a day, against 23.2% of the never group. Adjustment for these bands alone cut the ever-use estimate from 1.90 to 1.25 and the heaviest band from 3.72 to 2.24, so residual confounding by tobacco amount within bands and by smoking after conscription is plausible and would run away from the null. Occupational exposures, diet, family history and other drugs were not adjusted for, and estimates among men who did not smoke tobacco could not be made.

A single non-anonymous self-report of lifetime frequency at age 18 to 20 stands for 40 years of exposure: no use after conscription, no method, amount, potency or tobacco mixing. The authors expect under-reporting from non-anonymity and report anecdotal over-reporting to avoid military training; with several bands and a confounded exposure, the direction of the resulting bias is not certain.
Population-based cohort covering more than 97% of Swedish men of that age, followed through national registers from baseline; only 1.9% emigrated.
No intervention after exposure is described that would differ by cannabis use.

About 7.6% lacked cannabis answers and 10 of 189 cancers were dropped for missing predictors (complete-case analysis). The men without cannabis answers had a lower lung cancer risk than the never group (fully adjusted 0.41, 0.17 to 0.99), so missingness was related to the outcome; the effect on the heavy-against-never contrast is unclear.

Register-based lung cancer records, independent of the exposure report; cited concordance between registers 78% to 99%. Inpatient and death records rather than the cancer register, and death records only to 2006, may miss some cases, but not in a way linked to cannabis answers given decades earlier.

No registered protocol; the frequency bands were taken from an earlier paper on this cohort, which limits the choice of cut-off, but ever use and five bands were each tested in three models without correction, and the abstract reports only the one significant band.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High because confounding by tobacco and the single baseline measure of exposure could each change the estimate materially, and the remaining tobacco confounding most plausibly biases away from the null. The design's strengths are real: a near-complete national cohort, outcomes from registers and 40 years of follow-up. The study may be cited for the adjusted association between reporting more than 50 lifetime cannabis uses at age 18 to 20 and a lung cancer record by about age 60, with its crude and tobacco-adjusted versions, the null ever-use result and the absent gradient; not for an effect of smoking cannabis, for people who never smoked tobacco, for women, for later or current patterns of use and products, or for risk at older ages.

key_findings.finding: 49,321 men aged 18 to 20 conscripted for compulsory Swedish military service in 1969–1970 (more than 97% of Swedish men of that age; 2–3% were excused for disqualifying conditions), linked to the Patient Register, the National Cause-of-Death Register and the Total Population Register.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Methods); Materials and methods › Data sources; Swedish male conscripts' files

key_findings.finding: Cannabis use was self-reported once, at conscription, in a non-anonymous questionnaire: ever against never, and lifetime frequency (never, once, 2–4, 5–10, 11–50 and more than 50 times); the bands follow an earlier analysis of the cohort, and this paper labels more than 50 times heavy use. 10.5% (5,156) reported lifetime use and 1.7% (831) more than 50 uses.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Materials and methods › Measurement of cannabis use

key_findings.finding: Tobacco was measured once, at conscription, by cigarettes smoked a day (none 41.4%, 1–5 11.2%, 6–10 20.7%, 11–20 23.1%, more than 20 3.6%), collapsed into three bands for the models: none, 1–10 and more than 10 a day. Confounders adjusted: tobacco, alcohol, respiratory conditions diagnosed at conscription (chronic bronchitis, emphysema, pneumonia or asthma) and socioeconomic status from occupation in the 1970 census.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Measurement of tobacco use; Potential confounders

key_findings.finding: Table 1: of the 831 men reporting more than 50 cannabis uses, 60 (7.2%) did not smoke tobacco, 242 (29.1%) smoked 1–10 a day, 514 (61.8%) more than 10 and 15 (1.8%) had no tobacco answer; of the 40,397 men reporting never using cannabis, 18,100 (44.8%) did not smoke tobacco, 12,725 (31.5%) smoked 1–10 a day and 9,364 (23.2%) more than 10. Alcohol above 250 g a week: 192 (23.1%) against 918 (2.3%). Respiratory conditions: 18 (2.2%) against 747 (1.9%). The Results say about 91% of the heaviest band reported some tobacco use.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (never and more-than-50 columns)
key_findings.note: 756 of 831 is 91.0% (92.6% of the 816 with a tobacco answer); editors' arithmetic.

key_findings.finding: Follow-up from 1 January 1970 (1 October 1969 for two men) to lung cancer, death from other causes, emigration or 31 December 2009, about 1.9 million person-years in each line of analysis. Lung cancer (ICD-8/9 162; ICD-10 C33–C34) came from the Patient Register in any diagnostic position to the end of 2009 and from the Cause-of-Death Register as underlying cause to the end of 2006; cited concordance between registers 78% to 99%, and sensitivity of administrative codes about 80% to 95% elsewhere.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Study outcome; Validity of lung cancer outcome codes; Statistical analyses

key_findings.finding: 189 incident lung cancers (95 in both registers, 88 in the Patient Register only, 6 in the death register only); 2,958 men (6.0%) died of other causes and 930 (1.9%) emigrated; ten cases were excluded for missing predictor information, leaving 179 in the analyses. Cases by cannabis group are shown only in Figure 1, a stacked bar chart by year.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1 legend; Tables 2-4 (n = 179 in the titles)
key_findings.note: Figure 1's values were not extracted, so no absolute risk by cannabis group is given; editors' calculation of the base rate: 189 of 49,321 (0.38%, about 4 in 1,000) by the end of 2009.

key_findings.finding: More than 50 lifetime uses against never (Table 4, 44,257 men, 179 cancers): crude HR 3.72 (95% CI 1.96 to 7.06), tobacco-adjusted 2.24 (1.17 to 4.29), fully adjusted 2.12 (1.08 to 4.14), described by the authors as more than a twofold risk even after adjustment for tobacco, alcohol, respiratory conditions and socioeconomic status.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 4 (more than 50 times row; footnotes a and b)

key_findings.finding: Ever against never use (Table 3, 44,285 men, 179 cancers): crude 1.90 (1.30 to 2.75), tobacco-adjusted 1.25 (0.85 to 1.83), fully adjusted 1.25 (0.84 to 1.87); the authors say tobacco adjustment greatly attenuated the risk and further adjustment did not change it.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Lower frequency bands, fully adjusted against never: once 1.52 (0.77 to 3.01), 2–4 times 0.66 (0.27 to 1.62), 5–10 times 0.68 (0.21 to 2.16), 11–50 times 1.68 (0.77 to 3.66); crude, once 2.07 (1.06 to 4.06) and 11–50 times 2.69 (1.26 to 5.74). The authors state that the results did not show a clear dose–response relationship.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 4

key_findings.finding: Tobacco against none, with cannabis and the other covariates in the model: 1–10 cigarettes a day 2.34 (1.48 to 3.71) and more than 10 a day 5.06 (3.25 to 7.86) with ever use; 2.34 (1.47 to 3.70) and 5.03 (3.23 to 7.81) with cannabis frequency; crude 2.29 (1.48 to 3.57) and 5.16 (3.45 to 7.73). The authors call this a strong dose–response relation.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Men without cannabis answers (3,768 on ever use, 7.64%; 3,800 on frequency, 7.70%) were not more likely to develop lung cancer than men reporting never using cannabis: ever-use item crude 0.52 (0.24 to 1.10), tobacco-adjusted 0.47 (0.21 to 1.07), fully adjusted 0.41 (0.17 to 0.99); frequency item 0.51 (0.24 to 1.09), 0.47 (0.21 to 1.06), 0.40 (0.16 to 0.98).
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Missing data; Results, 5th paragraph and its continuation after Table 4

key_findings.finding: Analyses stratified by tobacco (Supplemental Tables 1 and 2, not available to this reader) did not give compelling results: there were too few people who used cannabis but not tobacco and too few lung cancers, even when men smoking 5 or fewer cigarettes a day were grouped with those who did not smoke.
key_findings.locator: Results, last paragraph (continued on p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: no detailed information on use before conscription and none on tobacco or cannabis use after it; residual confounding by tobacco possible, since more than 91% of the men in the heavy band also reported tobacco smoking at conscription; participants may have mixed tobacco into cannabis cigarettes, which would inflate the cannabis-related risk, and whether this was common in Sweden in 1969–1970 is unclear; non-anonymous reports may have led to under-reporting, while some men may have inflated their use to be exempted from military training. They argue that changes in use after conscription would bias the estimates toward the null.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors note that the only earlier cohort ended at a mean age of 42 and that the median age at a first lung cancer diagnosis is about 70; their cohort was followed for 40 years from age 18 to 20.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: men born in 1949 to 1951 were 58 to 60 at the end of 2009.

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: the authors call their primary finding initial longitudinal evidence, requiring further replication, that cannabis use might raise the risk of lung cancer; the Discussion proposes that the findings be used in drug-prevention programmes.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Conclusions

key_findings.finding: Funding as printed: an institutional grant from the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care to the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (salary support for the first author) and a research grant from the Swedish Council for Working Life and Social Research (FAS 2009-1611; salary support for the third author); the funders had no role in the study or the decision to publish. No conflicts of interest declared.
key_findings.locator: Acknowledgments; Conflict of interest

reporting_issues.issue: Heavy use is defined as more than 50 lifetime uses in the Methods, Results and Table 4, but as at least 50 uses in the first paragraph of the Discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the analysis uses the more-than-50 band (Table 4), which is the definition to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives n = 44,284 for the Cox analyses that produced HR 2.12, but Table 3 (ever use) gives 44,285 and Tables 2 and 4 (frequency, the source of 2.12) give 44,257.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite 44,257 with the heavy-use estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say approximately 91% and the Discussion more than 91% of the heaviest band reported tobacco use; Table 1 gives 756 of 831 (91.0%), or 92.6% of the 816 with a tobacco answer (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; about 91% is the figure to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of lung cancers in each cannabis group is given only in Figure 1, a stacked bar chart by year, and not in the text or tables.
reporting_issues.consequence: No absolute risk can be stated for the heavy-use group from the text or tables; only the cohort's overall base rate (189 of 49,321) is available.

verification.source_read: PDF, online-first version (published online 12 July 2013) without printed page numbers, 10 pages (PDFs/Cannabis/Callaghan_2013_LungCancerCohort.pdf); text extracted once with pdftotext -layout: all text, Tables 1 to 4 with footnotes, the Figure 1 legend (the stacked bar chart, viewed on a rendered page, was not extracted), acknowledgments (funding), conflict statement and reference list. The electronic supplementary material (Supplemental Tables 1 and 2) was not available and was not read. The printed article (reference record) is pp. 1811–1820; page references here are to the PDF's own pages 1 to 10.

design_detail: Research letter (JAMA 2015;313(24):2491-2493) reporting a laboratory analysis of commercial products, not of people or cells (the schema has no design for a laboratory analysis of products; 'in-vitro' is the nearest, as for sc_mallock_2024). Purchasers holding a physician's letter, with no history of buying edibles, bought labelled edible cannabis products (baked goods, beverages, candy or chocolate) at nine medical-cannabis dispensaries, three each in San Francisco and Los Angeles (California) and Seattle (Washington), between August and October 2014, within $400 per city: 75 products of 47 brands. Each whole package was homogenized and two samples were tested by high-performance liquid chromatography; measured delta-9-THC and CBD were compared with the label, within 10% counting as accurately labelled. Read together with the correction notice (JAMA 2015;314(2):188, 'Incorrect Labels in Text and in Table 1 Column Headings'), which rewrites two sentences of the Results and gives the column headings of Table 1; where the saved PDF and the correction differ, this card follows the correction.
can_establish: How often the measured THC content of 75 labelled edible products, bought at nine medical-cannabis dispensaries in three US cities in August to October 2014, was within 10% of the label, more than 10% above it or more than 10% below it, and by how much, by city and by product type; how many contained CBD and how often a printed CBD content matched; and the measured content of six cannabinoids per package.
cannot_establish: How accurate edible labels are in other cities or years, in adult-use shops, or under later testing and labelling rules (a non-random sample from 2014 markets that the authors call unregulated, not weighted by sales); how evenly THC was spread between the pieces or servings of a package (whole packages were mixed before testing); whether batches of the same product differ (the number of packages per product is not stated); why products deviated (manufacture, loss in storage, or measurement); and what happens to people who eat these products: no one was given a product, and the Discussion's statements about missing medical benefit and adverse effects are inferences, not measurements.

sample.recruitment: Products, not people. From an Internet directory of dispensaries that listed each one's menu, dispensaries in each city were selected at random until three were found that offered at least one edible product in each of three categories (baked goods, beverages, candy or chocolate) with a label giving at least a specific delta-9-THC content. Between August and October 2014, purchasers with a physician's letter (in line with state law) and no history of buying edibles were sent to these dispensaries to buy as wide a variety of products (type and labelled content) as possible within $400 per city. Purchasers knew the products would be tested, dispensary staff did not, and neither knew the details of the analyses (Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, p. 2491).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Dispensaries: at least one labelled product in each of the three categories, with a specific THC content on the label. Products: chosen by the purchasers for variety within the budget; the number per city reflects what $400 could buy (Table 1, footnote e, p. 2492). Products without a THC label are not described; the Discussion notes that many products carry no cannabinoid content on the label.
sample.demographics: Not applicable (products). The number of purchasers is not stated.
sample.attrition: None reported: all 75 products appear in Table 1.
sample.selection_effects: Not a random sample of products, as the authors state (no source lists all dispensaries, and many products carry no cannabinoid label); medical dispensaries only; three cities; purchases aimed at variety, not at what is most bought; 20 to 32 products per city. Whether the same brand was bought in more than one dispensary or city is not reported. The authors describe these 2014 markets as unregulated.

exposure.measurement: Whole package homogenized (crushed or mixed); two samples (1.5 g of a solid, 25 g of a liquid) tested by high-performance liquid chromatography, averaged and scaled to the total product weight. When the two samples differed by more than 10%, which the paper calls cannabinoid heterogeneity, the entire product was analysed (37 of 75); five randomly chosen products whose duplicates agreed within 10% were also analysed in full and confirmed the duplicate method (Methods, 4th and 5th paragraphs, p. 2491). Six cannabinoids were measured (THC, THCA, CBD, CBDA, CBG, CBN; Table 2, p. 2493). No validation data are given (recovery from chocolate, baked goods or drinks, calibration, limits of quantification), the laboratory that ran the tests is not named, and whether the analysts knew the labels is not stated.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Measured product content, not a dose. Per package (Table 2, p. 2493; median, interquartile range as printed, range): THC 54 mg (99), under 1 to 1,236 mg; THCA 2 (15), under 1 to 173; CBD 2 (3), under 1 to 51; CBDA 1 (5), under 1 to 20; CBG 3 (3), under 1 to 43; CBN 2 (2), under 1 to 20. Labelled THC ranged from 2 to 1,000 mg per package (Table 1, p. 2492). No one consumed the products in the study.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (products). Only six cannabinoids were measured and the results focus on THC and CBD (Methods, 3rd paragraph, p. 2491); other contents (for example solvents, pesticides, microbes or added drugs) were not measured.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (products).

comparison.controls: The content printed on each package is the comparator. No reference product, no second laboratory and no comparison with flower or other forms were included.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a product analysis. Not measured or not described: batch-to-batch variation; how long and how products had been stored; whether labels stated content per package or per serving and how per-serving labels were converted; and whether labelled THC was compared with delta-9-THC alone or with THC plus THCA (THCA is reported separately in Table 2, up to 173 mg in one product).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: High-performance liquid chromatography (instrument, standards and conditions not given); labels read by the investigators.
outcomes.validity_norms: The 10% limit is described as a basic label-accuracy standard for pharmaceuticals, with no source given. Method validation is limited to the full analysis of five products as a check of the duplicate method.
outcomes.operationalization: As corrected: accurately labelled, measured THC (or CBD) within 10% of the label; underlabelled, more than 10% above the label (the product holds more than it says); overlabelled, more than 10% below the label (it holds less than it says). Deviation is the actual against the labelled amount, in percent (Methods, 5th paragraph, p. 2491; Table 1 footnotes a to d, p. 2492).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not needed: the only test is one chi-squared test of city against the three accuracy categories for THC.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Dispensary staff did not know the products would be tested; the purchasers did. Whether the analysts knew the labels is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: No intervals are given. THC: 13 of 75 (17%) within 10% of the label, 17 (23%) more than 10% above it, 45 (60%) more than 10% below it. Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% intervals): 10.4% to 27.4%, 14.7% to 33.3% and 48.7% to 70.3%; 62 of 75 (82.7%; 72.6% to 89.6%) outside 10%. Mean deviation (SD): within 10%, -3% (4), largest 9%; above, +28% (13), largest +55%; below, -47% (29), largest -99% (Table 1). City: chi-squared 12.94, P = .01; the degrees of freedom are not printed (4 by design); the editors' recomputation from Table 1 gives 12.94 and P = 0.012, with 3 of the 9 expected counts below 5.
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned (a research letter).
analysis.selective_reporting: Other cannabinoids were analysed but the results focus on THC and CBD (Table 2 gives their content); accuracy by product type is shown only as counts, without a test; results for single products are not listed.
analysis.power: Not addressed; 20 to 32 products per city and 13 to 40 per product type.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 75 labelled edibles bought at nine medical dispensaries in three US cities in 2014, about one in six held THC within 10% of its label, about one in four held more and about three in five held less, some almost none. The pattern differed by city (as corrected: products holding more THC than labelled were commonest in Los Angeles, products holding less in Seattle). Only 13 products printed a CBD content, and none of them was within 10%.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Discussion says the products failed basic label-accuracy standards for pharmaceuticals (the 10% limit is not sourced) and calls the shortfalls significantly less content, meaning beyond the 10% limit, not a statistical test. Its statements that products with less THC may not give the desired medical benefit and that products with more put patients at risk of adverse effects are inferences resting on two citations (a report of two cases of psychosis after oral cannabis and a viewpoint), not on measurements in people. The authors state the limits plainly (few cities, dispensaries and products; no true random sample; results may not generalize). The main reporting problem is the reversed labels in the text, fixed by the correction: anyone citing the uncorrected text has the city and CBD findings the wrong way round.

timeline.event: Products bought, August to October, at nine medical-cannabis dispensaries in San Francisco, Los Angeles and Seattle.

This research letter (JAMA, 23/30 June 2015). A correction notice (JAMA, 14 July 2015, p. 188) rewrote the Results' sentence on which city had which kind of mislabelling and the sentence on CBD, and gave the column headings of Table 1. The saved PDF carries a note that the article was corrected online on 23 June 2015 to fix labels, yet still prints those two sentences in the form the July correction replaces.

RTI Press overview of edibles cites this letter second-hand: 83 percent of edibles more than 10 percent from the labelled THC, more than half with significantly less and nearly a quarter with more. This agrees with the corrected figures (62 of 75 outside 10%, 82.7%, editors' arithmetic), although the overview calls the measure total THC, a term the letter does not use.

replication.where_it_stands: A single, small, non-random sample of products from 2014. No one has re-tested these products, and later label tests in other markets were not read for this card, so the figures describe what could be bought at these dispensaries then, not edible products in general.

funding.funder: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, except the cost of the analytical testing, which Werc Shop Laboratories covered. The paper states that neither Johns Hopkins University nor Werc Shop Laboratories had any role in the design or conduct of the study, the data, the manuscript or the decision to submit (Funding/Support and Role of the Funder/Sponsor, p. 2493).
funding.declared_conflicts: Dr Bonn-Miller reported receiving personal fees and nonfinancial support from Tilray (Division of Privateer Holdings) and travel reimbursement from Americans for Safe Access; no other disclosures were reported (p. 2493).
funding.affiliations_note: Four of the six authors are at Werc Shop Laboratory (Pasadena, California: J. C. Raber and M. E. Raber; Bellevue, Washington: Douglass and Miller); Vandrey is at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and Bonn-Miller at the University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine (p. 2491). The author contributions credit two Werc Shop authors (J. Raber and Douglass) with the study's concept and design and with its supervision (p. 2493), which sits uneasily with the statement that Werc Shop Laboratories had no role in the design or conduct. The paper does not describe what Werc Shop Laboratories or Tilray do, and the editors have not added that from other sources.

what_would_settle_it: Repeated, sales-weighted mystery-shopper sampling of edible products in several markets and years, with several packages and batches per product and separate tests of single servings, analysed blind to the label by an independent laboratory that reports its recovery for each food type, would show how often labels match and how evenly THC is spread within a package.

domains.note: Dispensaries chosen at random from a directory, but only those with labelled products in all three categories; products bought for variety within $400 per city, not by sales; medical dispensaries in three cities in 2014. Staff did not know the products would be tested (a strength). Describes what was on offer at these nine dispensaries, not the market.

Duplicate chromatography of the homogenized whole package, with full analysis when duplicates disagreed (37 of 75) and a five-product check of the duplicate method; but no recovery, calibration or quantification-limit data for the food matrices, no named or independent laboratory, and no statement on blinding to the labels. Incomplete extraction from chocolate or baked goods, if present, would push results towards 'less than labelled'; the letter gives no data to judge it.

A clear 10% rule applied to THC and CBD; but whether labels gave content per package or per serving, and how per-serving labels were converted, is not described, nor whether labelled THC was compared with delta-9-THC alone or with THC plus THCA. The text first used the two mislabelling terms the wrong way round in two places (corrected).

Shares reported without intervals; one chi-squared test whose degrees of freedom are not printed and in which 3 of 9 expected counts are below 5 (editors' calculation); products treated as independent although 75 products came from 47 brands and nine dispensaries.

Two Results sentences had the city and CBD findings reversed and were corrected; the saved PDF still prints them reversed. The overall mean shortfall in Table 1 for products below their label (-47%) does not match the city rows (n-weighted -52.5%, editors' arithmetic). The Discussion's inferences about benefit and adverse effects go beyond what was measured but are worded as possibilities.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated risk-of-bias instrument exists for a laboratory analysis of commercial products (METHODS 5.3), so the editors' checklist is used with domains adapted to this design, as for sc_mallock_2024; the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. Once the correction is applied, the THC counts are simple and agree with the table, and buying through unannounced purchasers protects against staff picking products. The concerns are representativeness (nine dispensaries, 2014), unreported method validation, unstated label conventions and the correction history; a second reader may judge measurement validation more severely. Citable for how often the THC and CBD content of these 75 products matched their labels, by city and type; not for the label accuracy of edibles in general or today, for how evenly THC was spread within a package, or for effects in people.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 75 products of 47 brands, bought August to October 2014 at three randomly selected medical-cannabis dispensaries in each of San Francisco (32 products), Los Angeles (20) and Seattle (23), within $400 per city, by purchasers with a physician's letter and no history of buying edibles; dispensary staff did not know the products would be tested. Product types (editors' sums of Table 1): 22 baked goods, 13 beverages, 40 candy or chocolate.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 2491); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 2491); Table 1, products tested and type rows, footnote e (p. 2492)

key_findings.finding: THC against the label, all three cities: 13 of 75 (17%) within 10% (mean deviation -3%, SD 4; largest 9%); 17 (23%) more than 10% above the label (mean +28%, SD 13; largest +55%; measured 34 to 1,236 mg against labelled 20 to 1,000 mg); 45 (60%) more than 10% below (mean -47%, SD 29; largest -99%; measured under 1 to 267 mg against labelled 2 to 325 mg). By type (within / above / below): baked goods 2 / 7 / 13; beverages 3 / 2 / 8; candy or chocolate 8 / 8 / 24.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph, 1st sentence (p. 2491, unchanged by the correction); Table 1, Overall (3 Cities) rows (p. 2492)
key_findings.note: The overall mean for products below their label (-47%) does not match the city rows (-44%, -55% and -61% for 20, 7 and 18 products), whose n-weighted mean is -52.5% (editors' arithmetic); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: By city, within 10% / more than 10% above / more than 10% below: San Francisco 8 (25%) / 4 (13%) / 20 (62%) of 32; Los Angeles 4 (20%) / 9 (45%) / 7 (35%) of 20; Seattle 1 (4%) / 4 (17%) / 18 (78%) of 23; chi-squared 12.94, P = .01. As corrected, products holding more THC than labelled were likeliest in Los Angeles and products holding less in Seattle.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, city rows (p. 2492); Results, 1st paragraph, 2nd sentence as corrected (JAMA 2015;314(2):188)

key_findings.finding: CBD: 44 of 75 products (59%) had detectable CBD but only 13 printed a CBD content; as corrected, 4 held more than 10% more CBD than labelled and 9 more than 10% less, so none of the 13 was within 10% (editors' arithmetic: 4 + 9 = 13). Median THC:CBD ratio among products with detectable CBD 36:1; 7 had ratios below 10:1 and 1 a 1:1 ratio. Content of cannabinoids other than THC was generally low.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (3rd sentence as corrected, JAMA 2015;314(2):188); Table 2 (p. 2493)

key_findings.finding: Measured content per product (measured product content, not doses), mg, median (interquartile range as printed) and range: THC 54 (99), under 1 to 1,236; THCA 2 (15), under 1 to 173; CBD 2 (3), under 1 to 51; CBDA 1 (5), under 1 to 20; CBG 3 (3), under 1 to 43; CBN 2 (2), under 1 to 20.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 and its footnote a
key_findings.note: The interquartile range is printed as a single number, apparently its width; medians are given because the values were not normally distributed.

key_findings.finding: Testing: whole packages homogenized, two samples tested by high-performance liquid chromatography, averaged and scaled to the product's total weight; duplicates differed by more than 10% (called cannabinoid heterogeneity) in 37 products, which were then analysed in full; five randomly chosen products whose duplicates agreed were also analysed in full and confirmed the duplicate method. Rule: within 10% of the label, accurate; more than 10% above, underlabelled; more than 10% below, overlabelled. Location effect tested by chi-squared, P < .05 two-sided.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 4th, 5th and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Authors' reading: products from three large cities, though unregulated, failed basic label-accuracy standards for pharmaceuticals; more than half held significantly less cannabinoid than labelled, some negligible THC, and may not give the desired medical benefit; others held significantly more THC than labelled, putting patients at risk of adverse effects (two citations); regulation and quality assurance are needed. Limits stated: few cities, dispensaries and products; no source lists all dispensaries and many products lack a cannabinoid label, so a true random sample was not possible and the results may not generalize.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Correction notice: the Results should read that underlabelled products were likeliest in Los Angeles and overlabelled products in Seattle (chi-squared 12.94, P = .01), and that 4 products were underlabelled and 9 overlabelled for CBD; the third column of Table 1 is headed Underlabelled (footnote b) and the fourth Overlabelled (footnote c). The overall shares (17%, 23%, 60%) are as in the saved PDF.
key_findings.locator: JAMA 2015;314(2):188, Correction, 'Incorrect Labels in Text and in Table 1 Column Headings' (right column)

key_findings.finding: Funding and ties as printed: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine funded the project except the cost of analytical testing, covered by Werc Shop Laboratories; neither had a role in the design, conduct, data, manuscript or decision to submit. Four of six authors at Werc Shop Laboratory; concept and design credited to Vandrey, J. Raber, Douglass and Bonn-Miller, supervision to Vandrey, J. Raber and Douglass. Bonn-Miller: personal fees and nonfinancial support from Tilray (Division of Privateer Holdings), travel reimbursement from Americans for Safe Access.
key_findings.locator: Author Affiliations (p. 2491); Author Contributions, Conflict of Interest Disclosures, Funding/Support, Role of the Funder/Sponsor (p. 2493)

reporting_issues.issue: The saved PDF (downloaded 23 June 2015, with a note that the article was corrected on 23 June 2015 to fix labels in the text and in Table 1) still says overlabelled products were likeliest in Los Angeles and underlabelled in Seattle, which contradicts its own Table 1 (Los Angeles 45% above the label; Seattle 78% below). The July 2015 correction reverses the sentence to match the table.
reporting_issues.consequence: Follow the correction, which agrees with Table 1. Any source repeating the uncorrected sentence has the city finding the wrong way round.

reporting_issues.issue: The CBD sentence in the saved PDF says 4 products were overlabelled and 9 underlabelled; the correction says 4 underlabelled and 9 overlabelled.
reporting_issues.consequence: Under the corrected wording, 9 of the 13 products with a CBD label held less CBD than stated and 4 held more; none was within 10%.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1, the overall mean deviation for products below their label is -47% (SD 29), but the city rows (-44%, n = 20; -55%, n = 7; -61%, n = 18) give an n-weighted mean of -52.5% (editors' arithmetic). The same check reproduces the overall means for accurate (-2.8%, printed -3%) and above-label products (+27.7%, printed +28%). The correction does not mention it.
reporting_issues.consequence: The typical shortfall is about half of the labelled THC either way; cite the overall -47% with a note that the city rows imply about -53%.

reporting_issues.issue: The chi-squared test is printed without its degrees of freedom; 3 of the 9 expected counts are below 5 (editors' calculation from Table 1), and products are treated as independent although they came from 47 brands and nine dispensaries.
reporting_issues.consequence: The city difference is suggestive rather than firm; the P value is approximate.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion's 'significantly less' and 'significantly more' content means beyond the 10% limit; no per-product test or measurement uncertainty is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Products close to the 10% limit may be misclassified by measurement error; the large deviations are not affected.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter does not say whether labels gave content per package or per serving, or whether labelled THC was compared with delta-9-THC alone or with THC plus THCA; the 2016 overview citing it calls the measure total THC.
reporting_issues.consequence: What counts as accurate rests on conventions the letter does not spell out; this matters most for products with a per-serving label or with much THCA.

verification.source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Vandrey_2015_EdibleLabelAccuracy.pdf (all three printed pages, pp. 2491-2493: text, Tables 1 and 2, affiliations, contributions, disclosures and funding; Table 1 and page 2491 also checked on rendered page images) and the correction notice PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Vandrey_2015_EdibleLabelAccuracy_Erratum.pdf (JAMA 2015;314(2):188, the Vandrey correction in the right column; the rest of that page is unrelated letters and corrections). Text extracted once with pdftotext -layout.

design_detail: Narrative review comparing cannabis flower, concentrates and edibles on prevalence of use (mainly US samples), methods of consumption and cannabis use disorder (CUD) outcomes. PubMed keyword searches screened for relevance by title and abstract, plus backward and forward citation searches; 27 articles included (Figure 1), 72 references listed. No eligibility criteria beyond relevance, no search dates, no appraisal of the included studies; the authors scored their own review 12 of 12 on SANRA, a scale for the quality of narrative reviews. Published online 26 October 2024; issue dated 2026.
can_establish: What a 2024 narrative reading of mostly US survey studies says about which forms of cannabis people use and about CUD by form, and which comparisons the authors found missing (form-specific longitudinal data, CUD with edibles, flower by mode of use).
cannot_establish: Whether concentrates, flower or edibles differ in CUD risk, or by how much: there is no systematic search, no appraisal and no pooling, and the CUD evidence it cites is cross-sectional.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). PubMed searches combining 'cannabis' with a form, a method of consumption or CUD terms; studies kept if the title or abstract mentioned both the form and the outcome or method; further studies from reference lists and PubMed's Cited By feature (Methods, 1st paragraph, p. 4; Figure 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Relevance to a form of cannabis and its prevalence, method of consumption or CUD outcomes; 3,861 articles excluded on title or abstract and 196 at relevance review (Figure 1). No dates, languages, designs or quality thresholds are stated, and who screened is not stated.
sample.demographics: Not applicable. The cited samples are mostly from the US: national adult surveys, college students, high-school students in Colorado and Los Angeles, web-based and Twitter-based samples of people who use concentrates, and medical cannabis patients.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: One database and no stated search dates. The reference list does not include the 2022 systematic review of potency and mental ill health and addiction (Petrilli et al., 2022) or the UK and multinational survey studies of potency and dependence that it covers (editors' check of the 72 references). The prevalence part is restricted to US samples by design; the CUD part draws on US college, high-school, web and national samples.

exposure.measurement: As in the cited studies: self-reported form and frequency of use in surveys; no measured THC.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Forms as the authors define them: flower (raw plant material), concentrates (material extracted from the plant to increase potency; typically about three times the THC content of flower or more, as cited), and edibles (products for oral ingestion). Product content as cited only.
exposure.polysubstance: Blunts (cannabis rolled in a tobacco wrap) are flagged as a confounder of flower findings because they add tobacco; otherwise not addressed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Comparisons across forms within the cited surveys (frequent concentrate use against frequent flower use or no concentrate use; one form against several; inhaled forms against edibles); none with people who do not use cannabis.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not discussed. The authors note that people who frequently use concentrates may also use higher-potency cannabis when not using concentrates, and that frequency of use is the most reliable predictor of CUD across forms, both of which bear on any comparison by form.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed except tobacco in blunts.

outcomes.instruments: As in the cited studies (CUD symptom counts and severity, problematic use, tolerance and withdrawal, worry about one's use); the review does not name the instruments.
outcomes.validity_norms: No appraisal of the cited studies; the SANRA score is the authors' own rating of their review.
outcomes.operationalization: CUD outcomes are described as types such as symptom count, severity and problematic use (Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 5).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (narrative review).

analysis.effect_sizes: None for CUD comparisons. Prevalence percentages are reported as cited, for example US adults in 2017 (n = 9,003): past-year flower smoking 12.9%, vaporizing 4.7%, concentrates 1.9% and edibles 6%.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol; a narrative review.
analysis.selective_reporting: Null findings on concentrates and CUD reported elsewhere (a US sample of 156 in the 2022 systematic review) are not cited; the cited survey of 191 people is described as showing heightened CUD symptoms with frequent concentrate use, a difference the 2022 systematic review reports as not statistically significant.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The CUD evidence by form that the review cites is a handful of cross-sectional US surveys: one of 191 people comparing frequent concentrate with frequent flower use (Bidwell et al., 2018), surveys of dab or butane hash oil use in web and college samples (Sagar et al., 2018; Meier, 2017), surveys linking more frequent use of the inhaled forms but not edibles to problematic use (Steeger et al., 2021) and high-frequency use of all three forms to more CUD than high-frequency flower-only use (Gunn et al., 2020), a college survey linking flower potency to CUD symptom count (Piercey et al., 2024), and a US study linking average potency to a first CUD symptom (Arterberry et al., 2019). For edibles it finds no CUD data and argues by analogy from studies of slower-acting formulations of other drugs. It finds no form-specific longitudinal data.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Results state that concentrate use has consistently been associated with increased CUD risk compared with other forms, and the Highlights state as a fact that concentrate use "is associated with more severe cannabis use disorder outcomes"; the Abstract says only that it may be. Gaps: (1) 'consistently' rests mainly on one cross-sectional survey of 191 people, which the 2022 systematic review reports as showing no significant difference between frequent concentrate and frequent herbal use (editors' comparison; the primary paper was not read), plus surveys that compare people by how often they use concentrates rather than by form; (2) the Discussion's own conclusions, that frequency of use is the most reliable predictor across forms and that causal roles of quantity and potency are not established, are not carried into the Highlights; (3) case reports of paranoia and psychosis-like symptoms after concentrate use are called alarming; (4) the 12 of 12 SANRA score, including for the literature search, is self-assigned. Against this, the Abstract and Conclusion say plainly that comparisons across forms are scarce and form-specific longitudinal data are lacking, and the edibles section says the CUD risk is unknown.

timeline.event: Bidwell et al. (2018), a US cross-sectional study of 191 people buying concentrates and flower on the legal market (doi 10.1016/j.abrep.2018.08.004), the main source of this review's statement on concentrates and CUD; not read here.
Meta-analysis of the prevalence of cannabis use disorder among people who use cannabis (not cited by this review)
Systematic review of potency and mental ill health and addiction, which reports the same 191-person study as showing no significant difference (not cited by this review)
This narrative review, online 26 October 2024 (issue 2026).

replication.where_it_stands: A narrative review that adds no new evidence on CUD by form. Its statement on concentrates traces mainly to one cross-sectional survey that the 2022 systematic review describes differently, and it omits that review. It is useful for the gaps it names (edibles, form-specific longitudinal data, mode of flower use) and for US prevalence figures as cited; claims should trace any CUD figure to the primary studies.

funding.funder: No funding associated with the preparation of the review (Funding, p. 10).
funding.declared_conflicts: No potential conflict of interest reported by the authors (Disclosure statement, p. 10).
funding.affiliations_note: Oregon State University (Department of Integrative Biology; School of Psychological Science). No study by the authors is among the cited sources for the CUD findings (editors' check of the reference list). No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry ties are printed.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts of people who use cannabis that record each form used, its labelled or tested THC content, and how much and how often it is used, and that measure DSM-5 cannabis use disorder by interview over years, analysed with frequency and amount as possible confounders or mediators and including enough people who mainly use edibles.

domains.note: PubMed only, no dates, no eligibility criteria beyond relevance, screening by unstated reviewers; the main systematic review on potency and addiction (2022) and the survey studies it covers are missing from the 72 references.
No appraisal. Designs are sometimes named (survey, case reports), but no study's limits are weighed, and 'consistently' rests on one cross-sectional study.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: No study by the authors is cited for the review's findings (editors' check of the reference list).

Hedged in the Abstract and Conclusions ('may', 'suggest'), but the Highlights state the concentrate association without a hedge, and the edibles argument by analogy from formulations of other drugs sits beside the data.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a higher CUD risk with concentrates (evidence of no difference under-represented)
domains.note: A null comparison of concentrates with herbal cannabis (US sample of 156) is not cited, and the cited 191-person survey's non-significant difference is presented as heightened symptoms; the review does note that frequency predicts CUD across forms and that potency's causal role is not established.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The selection is unsystematic and misses the main systematic review, the cited studies are not appraised, and the concentrate statement in the Results and Highlights is stronger than its main cross-sectional source; on the other hand the review is explicit that comparisons by form and longitudinal data are lacking. It may be cited for what it says, for the gaps it names and for US prevalence figures as cited; its statement on concentrates and CUD should be traced to the primary studies, and it is not evidence of a CUD difference by form.

key_findings.finding: Methods: PubMed keyword searches screened for relevance by title and abstract; 4,077 articles found, 3,861 excluded, 216 reviewed for relevance, 196 excluded, 20 included, 7 added from reference lists and citing articles, 27 in the review. The authors rated their own review on SANRA and scored it 2 of 2 in all six areas (12 of 12).
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 4-5); Figure 1 (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Flower: among US adults (n = 9,003), 12.9% reported past-year flower smoking, more than edibles and concentrates combined; 94.6% of college-age people who used cannabis in the past year (n = 1,390) had ever used flower; among Colorado high-school students who currently used cannabis (n = 4,637), 76.1% had used flower in the past 30 days and 53.1% named it their usual form. Flower potency is cited as having risen from about 4% THC in 1995 to over 12% in 2014 and commonly 20% or more by 2020, with dispensary flower testing at 13% to 36%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabis flower, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Concentrates: among US adults in 2017 (n = 9,003), 4.7% reported vaporizing cannabis, 1.9% concentrates and 6% edibles in the past year; 44.2% of the college-age sample had ever used concentrates; among the Colorado high-school students, 47.1% had used concentrates in the past 30 days and 17.4% named them their usual form (edibles 9.5%); in web-based studies with over 600 participants each, 13% of people who used concentrates did so daily or near daily. Concentrates are described as typically about three times the THC of flower or more, from 50-60% to over 90% THC, as cited. The authors note a lack of recent nationally representative data on concentrate use.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabis concentrates, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 6-7)

key_findings.finding: Edibles: 6% of US adults reported past-year edible use; among Los Angeles high-school students (n = 2,163), 17.5% had ever used edibles against 25.8% flower; among the Colorado high-school students, 34.3% had used edibles in the past 30 days and 9.5% named them their usual form.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabis edibles, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Flower and CUD: a cross-sectional survey of Colorado college students (n = 617; ref. 36) found flower potency positively associated with CUD symptom count and severity; bong use (refs 18, 20-22) and blunt frequency (refs 26-28) are cited as associated with more frequent use, problematic symptoms, tolerance or CUD. The authors say the literature lacks CUD data for flower compared with other forms.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabis flower › Methods of consumption, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 5); Results › Cannabis flower › CUD outcomes, paragraph (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Concentrates and CUD: the review states that concentrate use has consistently been associated with higher CUD risk than other forms; that people who frequently use concentrates show more CUD symptoms than people who do not use them but may also use higher-potency cannabis when not using concentrates, and report fewer positive effects from concentrates (ref. 40, Bidwell et al., 2018); that people who use concentrates chronically may show more tolerance and withdrawal (ref. 37, a 2021 review); that people who regularly use concentrates more often feel worried about their use than people who have tried them (ref. 42, a national web survey of dab use); and that among college students more frequent use of butane hash oil went with more physical symptoms such as tolerance after adjustment for demographic, substance-use and personality covariates (ref. 43). Longitudinal studies of long-term concentrate use are called for. No effect sizes are given.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabis concentrates › CUD outcomes, paragraph; references 37, 40, 42 and 43 (p. 12)

key_findings.finding: Edibles and CUD: there is limited information specific to the CUD potential of edibles. The review argues from studies of other drugs (refs 50 and 51, on formulations of hydrocodone and methylphenidate) that a slower onset of action goes with a lower potential to contribute to a substance use disorder, and cites one source (ref. 44, titled as a study of medical cannabis patients with chronic pain) for people who use cannabis medically preferring oral use and for people new to non-medical use or using it infrequently more often naming edibles as their primary form. The section concludes that the CUD outcomes of edibles have not been sufficiently characterised.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabis edibles › CUD outcomes, paragraph; Results › Cannabis edibles › Conclusion, paragraph

key_findings.finding: Across forms, the Discussion describes the literature on problematic use as small and incomplete and mostly about flower. It cites a positive association between product potency and CUD risk (ref. 52), more CUD symptoms with frequent concentrate use than with frequent flower use (ref. 40), more problematic use with more frequent use of the two inhaled forms but not edibles (ref. 39), and more CUD with high-frequency use of all three forms than with high-frequency flower-only use (ref. 15); it states, without a citation, that inhalation is generally associated with a higher CUD risk than ingestion. It concludes that frequency of use remains the most reliable predictor of CUD risk across all forms and that further causal factors, such as quantity and THC potency, have yet to be firmly established.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › CUD outcomes, paragraph

key_findings.finding: Other harms, as cited: smoking flower linked to asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease but not reported as a significant contributor to lung cancer or irreversible airway changes (refs 54-58); case reports of paranoia and psychosis-like symptoms after concentrate use (refs 62-64); edibles commonly associated with hospital visits for accidental ingestion or over-intoxication (ref. 65), while in a survey of 172 people who had an uncomfortable experience with edibles, 95.2% reported no medical problem from it (ref. 66).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Other acute and chronic health complications, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Abstract and Highlights: concentrate use may be associated with a greater CUD risk (Abstract); concentrate use is associated with more severe CUD outcomes, and edible CUD risk is unclear (Highlights). Conclusion: few single studies report all three forms, and form-specific long-term data are lacking.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Highlights (p. 3); Conclusion, paragraph (p. 10)

key_findings.finding: No funding; no potential conflict of interest reported.
key_findings.locator: Disclosure statement; Funding

reporting_issues.issue: A sentence on dry herb vaping is garbled as printed: after lower plasma carbon monoxide, the next sentence reads as a fragment comparing respiratory toxicity with flower smoke at comparable plasma THC, so what ref. 30 found cannot be told from the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The basis of the review's suggestion that dry herb vaping may be a safer alternative for people who use cannabis chronically cannot be checked from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Ref. 44, titled as a cross-sectional study of medical cannabis patients with chronic pain, is cited for statements about non-medical use (people new to it or using it infrequently naming edibles as their main form; flower and concentrates being more popular among people who use cannabis non-medically) and for vaporization having risen to a prevalence comparable to smoking.
reporting_issues.consequence: These statements may not rest on samples of non-medical use; the primary paper was not read.

reporting_issues.issue: The review says 44.2% of the college-age sample had ever used concentrates, which is only 20% less than the number who had ever used edibles, without giving the edible figure for that sample.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the gap is relative or in percentage points cannot be told.

reporting_issues.issue: The same 191-person survey (Bidwell et al., 2018) is described here as showing heightened CUD symptoms in people who frequently use concentrates, while the 2022 systematic review reports no significant difference (means 2.1 and 1.3).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's main source for concentrates and CUD is reported differently by two reviews; the primary paper (doi 10.1016/j.abrep.2018.08.004) should be read before either description is used.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 3-13 (PDFs/Cannabis/Inman_2026_FlowerConcentratesEdiblesCUD.pdf; version of record, online 26 October 2024): all text, Figure 1 (read from the page image), the 72 references, disclosure and funding statements; no supplementary material

design_detail: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of proportions (PROSPERO CRD42019133166) estimating the prevalence and risk of cannabis use disorder (CUD), cannabis abuse (CA) and cannabis dependence (CD), by DSM or ICD criteria from structured interviews, among people in general-population samples who had used cannabis. Cohorts were sought in PubMed and cross-sectional surveys in the Global Burden of Disease data input sources (studies published from January 2009; searched February 2019, updated April 2020); 21 studies gave 153 data points. Subgroups by design and by recall period of use (lifetime, past year or month, weekly or daily); meta-regression on year of data collection, tool and country adjusted for age, sex and recall period. Read from the journal pre-proof (accepted manuscript).
can_establish: The average share of people who had used cannabis who met DSM criteria for cannabis use disorder, abuse or dependence in general-population studies from high-income countries published 2009 to 2020, and how it differed by design and by how often people had used.
cannot_establish: The risk for any one product, form or strength (no included study estimated risk by potency), the risk outside high-income countries, or a precise lifetime risk of developing a disorder, because lifetime, past-year and past-month measures are pooled together and the included studies were not appraised.

sample.recruitment: PubMed (MeSH 'marijuana abuse' AND 'cohort studies', with title and abstract synonyms) for longitudinal studies and the Global Burden of Disease data input sources for cross-sectional studies, searched in February 2019 for papers from January 2009; supplemented by reference lists, key population surveys, drug monitoring agency publications, references forwarded by experts, the authors' collection and a search for new publications in April 2020 (Method › Search strategy, p. 6).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Observational general-population studies reporting DSM or ICD cannabis use disorder, abuse or dependence ascertained by structured clinical interviews; high-risk or sub-populations such as prisoners or ethnic minorities excluded, as were unvalidated scales, self-reported problems and studies published before 2009 (Method › Selection criteria; Search strategy, pp. 5-6). Full texts excluded: 9 not observational general-population studies, 48 without data on the disorders, 31 without estimates among people who had used cannabis, 21 duplicating data in another included study (Results › Study selection, p. 8).
sample.demographics: Samples from the US (over half of the studies), the Netherlands, Germany, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland and France; 11 studies sampled adolescents or young adults, one older adults and the rest broad age ranges such as 12 or older or 18 or older (Results › Study characteristics and narrative summary, 1st paragraph, p. 8; Discussion, 12th paragraph, p. 15). Table 1 gives no sample size for any study.
sample.attrition: Not reported for the included cohorts.
sample.selection_effects: General-population surveys from high-income countries only. Definitions of a person who uses cannabis range from having tried it once to daily use: nine studies counted people who had ever tried cannabis, three required more than a few occasions, nine past-year use and four weekly or daily use (Results › Study characteristics and narrative summary, 2nd paragraph, p. 8). Excluding studies published before 2009 leaves out the early-1990s survey behind the widely cited one-in-ten dependence figure, which the review discusses separately (Introduction, p. 4).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported cannabis use in each survey, recorded as ever used, number of times used, past-year, past-month, or weekly or daily use (Method › Data extraction, p. 7).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Frequency only through these recall categories; no data on potency, form or route. The authors found no population study that estimated cannabis use disorder risk by the potency of products used (Discussion, 11th paragraph, p. 15).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed; other substance use disorders are named only as a topic for future research (Discussion, 14th paragraph, p. 16).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None; proportions among people who had used cannabis.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a pooled prevalence; age and sex differences and age of first use are summarised from the studies that reported them.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Structured diagnostic interviews: CIDI and M-CIDI, AUDADIS-IV and AUDADIS-5, SCID and DIGS, and DSM-IV criteria-based tools in the US National Survey on Drug Use and Health (Table 1). One study used DSM-III-R and one DSM-5; the rest used DSM-IV, in which cannabis use disorder means abuse or dependence (Discussion, 13th paragraph, p. 16).
outcomes.validity_norms: No appraisal of the included studies is reported. A Canadian study using the Severity of Dependence Scale was excluded for not using a structured interview; it classed 10.5% of adolescents who used cannabis in the past year as dependent (p. 16).
outcomes.operationalization: Prevalence over the lifetime, the past 3 years, the past year or the past month, or incidence at follow-up, of cannabis use disorder, abuse or dependence among people who had used cannabis as each study defined use; several data points per study by sex, age, survey year or recall period (Method › Data extraction, p. 7; Table 1 footnote).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable; three outcome pools, each with subgroups and a meta-regression.

analysis.effect_sizes: Pooled proportions with 95% CI (Table 2, p. 28). Cannabis use disorder: overall 0.22 (0.18 to 0.26); longitudinal, lifetime use 0.27 (0.25 to 0.28), recent use 0.22 (0.20 to 0.24); cross-sectional, lifetime 0.28 (0.10 to 0.48), recent 0.17 (0.12 to 0.23), regular (weekly or daily) 0.22 (0.17 to 0.28). Abuse: overall 0.13 (0.08 to 0.18); longitudinal recent 0.17 (0.14 to 0.20); cross-sectional lifetime 0.20 (0.14 to 0.26), recent 0.10 (0.03 to 0.19), regular 0.08 (0.02 to 0.16). Dependence: overall 0.13 (0.10 to 0.15); longitudinal lifetime 0.12 (0.07 to 0.18), recent 0.09 (0.01 to 0.19), regular 0.33 (0.22 to 0.44); cross-sectional lifetime 0.11 (0.07 to 0.15), recent 0.08 (0.06 to 0.10), regular 0.18 (0.12 to 0.24). Q, I2 and the studies in each pool are in S4 (not read). Meta-regression: year of data collection moderated cannabis use disorder (B = -0.01, p = 0.049) and abuse (B = -0.01, p = 0.017), not dependence (B = 0.00, p = 0.270); age, sex, recall period, assessment tool and country did not (p. 12).
analysis.covariates: Meta-regression adjusted for study-level age, sex and recall period.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42019133166, described as an a priori protocol; PRISMA checklist in S1 (p. 5). Separate analyses for each DSM version were planned (Method › Selection criteria, 2nd paragraph, p. 6) but are not reported, and the main pools combine DSM-III-R, DSM-IV and DSM-5 estimates. The registry record was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: Heterogeneity statistics, forest plots and the studies in each pool are only in the supplement; Table 1 gives no sample sizes; the abstract and conclusions report the overall pools and the cohort figure for regular use, not the lower cross-sectional figure for daily use.
analysis.power: The authors state they had limited power to detect moderators other than year of data collection (Discussion, 7th paragraph, p. 14).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 21 general-population studies from high-income countries (153 data points), the pooled share of people who had used cannabis who met criteria was 22% (18 to 26) for cannabis use disorder, 13% (8 to 18) for abuse and 13% (10 to 15) for dependence. Single-study estimates of use disorder ranged from 4.5% (US adults aged 50 or more) to 41.1% (Australian 21-year-olds), and of dependence from 3.5% (young adults in Ireland) to 40.9% (daily use in an Australian adolescent cohort). Dependence was 33% (22 to 44) in two longitudinal studies of young people who used weekly or daily, and 18% (12 to 24) in cross-sectional studies of daily or near-daily use. No study estimated risk by potency.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions present the pooled shares as risks (1 in 5 for use disorder, 1 in 8 for abuse or dependence) and extend the cohort figure to people who use cannabis weekly or more often (1 in 3); the Discussion says closer to 1 in 8 people who have used cannabis will develop dependence and that clinicians "can have confidence in using this updated figure". Gaps: (1) the pools mix lifetime, past-3-year, past-year and past-month prevalence with incidence, so they are not a lifetime risk of developing a disorder, as the authors themselves caution (Discussion, 9th paragraph); (2) the 1 in 3 figure comes from two cohorts of young people in Australia and the Netherlands, while cross-sectional studies of daily or near-daily use gave 18%; (3) confidence is claimed without heterogeneity statistics in the main text and without any appraisal of the pooled studies; (4) the abstract's message on early initiation does not mention that two of four studies found no association with dependence; (5) the Introduction and Conclusions point to more potent products, but no study in the review measured potency. Against this, the Discussion names the heterogeneity, the reliance on cross-sectional surveys, the different recall periods, the high-income samples and the lack of potency data.
