domains.note: The main text gives, for each study, the outcome, comparison, number of exposed cases and often follow-up and cohort; effect estimates, characteristics of the snus groups and confounder adjustments are in Table S2 (not read); the text does not describe setting and follow-up for every study.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Joanna Briggs Institute checklists for cohort and case-control studies, assessed and discussed by two researchers, covering confounding, selection and exposure and outcome measurement; the checklists do not cover selection of the reported result, and the study-level ratings are in Table S5 (not read). All studies were rated moderate risk of bias.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported in the main text; Table S2, which lists other study details, was not read. The review did screen for industry links and sponsorship at eligibility.

The only pooling is a generic inverse-variance combination of two adjusted hazard ratios for rectal cancer from non-overlapping parts of the same collaboration (the non-construction cohorts and the longer follow-up of the construction cohort); it is appropriate for that purpose, though the model and heterogeneity are not stated.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No meaningful quantitative synthesis: one two-study pooling, with all studies rated the same (moderate) risk of bias.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion (4.2) analyses how single baseline recording of exposure, misclassification of smoking and cohort features could affect estimates and says why smoking was handled by restriction; but the moderate risk of bias did not lead to a GRADE downgrade.

Differences between estimates for the same cancer are examined (time-varying hazard ratios for pancreatic and rectal cancer across follow-up periods, with a shorter and a longer follow-up of the same cohort).
No meaningful quantitative synthesis, so no test is possible; the Discussion does not address publication bias or selective reporting qualitatively.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: The authors declare no conflicts of interest; the funding of the review is not stated in the page text read.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: AMSTAR 2 rates one critical item as 'no' (item 4: an unjustified language restriction and no other sources beyond databases and reference lists), and item 7 is provisional because Table S4 was not read; if that list does not give reasons, the rating becomes critically low. Items 2 and 9 are partly met. The review is registered, uses duplicate screening, a standard bias checklist and GRADE, and writes its uncertainty out, so its estimates are best cited as a transparent, graded summary of a small observational literature that is dominated by one cohort and one sex. It may be cited for the site-by-site estimates and their certainty, the absolute risks in its GRADE table, the shrinking of the pancreatic and rectal estimates with longer follow-up, and the absence of data on women; not for causal statements, for any comparison with smoking beyond what is stated, or for independent replication.

key_findings.finding: 2,450 records screened, 67 read in full, 15 studies included (14 cohort studies, 1 case-control study); all rated moderate risk of bias, mostly for the validity of exposure information. Only one study reported any estimate for women (lymphoma, no cases).
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Results › 3.1 Cancer risk of snus use compared with no tobacco use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Graded estimates, snus only against no tobacco (Table 1): oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma HR 3.5 (1.6 to 7.6) from one cohort study of 142,891 men, 16 against 55 cases per 100,000, moderate certainty; non-cardia stomach cancer HR 1.4 (1.1 to 1.9), 237 against 332 per 100,000, low; rectal cancer HR 1.38 (1.07 to 1.77), 339 against 468 per 100,000, low; pancreatic cancer at 27 years RR 2.1 (1.2 to 3.3 in the table), 72 against 151 per 100,000, moderate; oral cancer HR 0.93 (0.59 to 1.44), very low; cancer-specific mortality HR 1.12 (1.00 to 1.26), 2,141 against 2,395 per 100,000, low.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › 3.1.1 to 3.1.5, 3.1.11

key_findings.finding: Pancreatic cancer in the Construction Workers Cohort varied with the length of follow-up: HR 1.98 (0.97 to 4.03, 4 exposed cases) to 1994, 2.1 (1.2 to 3.6, 18 cases) to 2004, 1.34 (0.90 to 1.99, 31 cases) to 2013; the pooled nine-cohort analysis (36 years, 41 exposed cases) gave HR 1.07 (0.77 to 1.50), graded very low. In that pooled analysis two thirds of participants and 72% of cases or deaths came from the Construction Workers Cohort.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1.4 Cancer of the pancreas, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Figure 2 (values not extracted)

key_findings.finding: Rectal cancer: HR 1.38 (1.07 to 1.77, 73 exposed cases) at 27 years of follow-up in nine pooled cohorts; combining the non-construction cohorts with a 10-years-longer follow-up of the Construction Workers Cohort gave HR 1.10 (0.91 to 1.34), a drop of almost 20% in the point estimate. Colon cancer HR 1.02 to 1.08 and anal cancer 0.61 (0.07 to 5.07, 1 case) showed no clear difference.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1.5 Cancer of the colon, rectum and anus, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 3 (values not extracted)

key_findings.finding: Estimates close to no difference or lower: oral cancer (pooled 9 cohorts HR 0.93, 0.59 to 1.44, 25 exposed cases; a third study of oral and pharyngeal cancers combined HR 2.3, 0.7 to 8.3, 5 cases), lung cancer RR 0.8 (0.4 to 1.3, 15 cases), non-Hodgkin lymphoma IRR 0.77 (0.59 to 1.01), Hodgkin lymphoma IRR 0.88 (0.49 to 1.58), leukaemias and myeloma IRR 0.81 to 1.24, all melanoma IRR 0.65 (0.52 to 0.82); lymphoma, leukaemia and melanoma results were not graded because they were given as incidence rate ratios.

Mortality: pooled Swedish analysis all-cause HR 1.28 (1.20 to 1.35) and cancer-specific HR 1.12 (1.00 to 1.26); a separate cohort not in that analysis, HR 1.23 (1.09 to 1.40) for all-cause and 1.28 (0.96 to 1.69) for cancer death in never-smoking men who had ever used snus. After a cancer diagnosis in construction workers, total mortality HR 1.13 (1.05 to 1.20) and cancer death HR 1.15 (1.05 to 1.26); after prostate cancer, overall HR 1.19 (1.04 to 1.37) and prostate cancer death HR 1.24 (1.03 to 1.49); after colorectal cancer, overall HR 1.16 (0.89 to 1.50), and 1.89 (1.21 to 2.94, 22 deaths) when the construction cohort was left out.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1.11 to 3.1.14

key_findings.finding: The authors' summary: snus probably increases the risk of cancer of the oesophagus and pancreas (moderate certainty), may increase the risk of stomach and rectal cancer (low), and the evidence suggests more cancer deaths and more deaths after a cancer diagnosis (low); they are very uncertain about the other cancers, and do not know the effect in women. They conclude snus entails a cancer hazard whose size may depend on a person's history of use and host susceptibility.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph; Summary of evidence for cancer risk

key_findings.finding: Smoking comparison: where smoking and snus were compared against the same never-tobacco group in the same studies, cancer risk estimates were higher for smoking than for snus at most sites, and all confidence intervals overlapped except for lung cancer; the figure with the estimates (Figure 4) was not read as numbers. The authors say it is not known how much switching from smoking to snus would reduce the benefit expected from quitting all tobacco.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › 4.5 (snus compared with cigarettes), 2nd to 4th paragraphs; Figure 4 (values not extracted)

key_findings.finding: Exposure caveats: a single baseline recording of tobacco habits; about 30% of men using snus only may later stop or switch to smoking (a Swedish study cited); more than 75% of men using snus only were under 30 at entry and few were followed beyond 70; seven of the included studies used construction-worker data from 1971 to 1975, when non-use could not be told from non-response; 13.2% of never-smoking men using snus, against 6.7% of men who never used tobacco, had a repeat record showing smoking, though the authors cite a sensitivity analysis in which 60% of the snus group would have to be smokers to shift one oesophageal result.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › 4.2 Impact of exposure information, 1st to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Tobacco-industry studies were excluded by design; studies reporting only dual use of snus and cigarettes were also excluded; the review states that adjusting for smoking in samples that included smokers distorted snus estimates in one study.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.3 Study eligibility criteria; Discussion › 4.1 Grading the results, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the pancreatic cancer estimate at 27 years is printed as RR 2.1 (1.2 to 3.3); the text prints the same estimate as 2.1 (1.2 to 3.6) twice. The table's absolute risk (151 per 100,000, upper limit 237) matches an upper limit of 3.3 (72 x 3.3 = 238).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 1; Results › 3.1.4, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: The upper limit is uncertain by 0.3. IARC Monograph 100E (sc_iarc_2012) prints the Swedish construction-worker cohort's never-smoker pancreatic estimate as 2.1 (1.2 to 3.6; 18 cases), which agrees with the text of this review; the primary study has not been checked. The industry-linked review in this batch (Lee 2013) prints what appears to be the same study's never-smoker estimate as 2.00 (1.20 to 3.30), so the point estimate also differs (2.0 against 2.1).

reporting_issues.issue: The bracketed numbers in Table 1's absolute-risk column are the confidence limits of the risk with snus (for example oral cancer 53 to 130 per 100,000 around 84), but they are labelled 'fewer' and 'more' as if they were differences from the no-tobacco risk of 90.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader who takes '53 fewer to 130 more' as a difference would be misled; the claim should quote the risks with and without snus, not the bracketed words.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 attributes the oral cancer, 36-year pancreatic cancer and rectal cancer estimates all to 'Araghi et al' with the same reference number (18), while the text cites different reference numbers for these (25 for oral cancer, 23 for pancreatic cancer, 18 for colorectal cancer) and uses both 18 and 23 for the rectal cancer estimate.
reporting_issues.consequence: The three estimates come from different papers by the same group; the reference list must be checked before any is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The oesophageal estimate is rated moderate and footnote b says it was downgraded for very few events, while the review's own rule starts observational evidence at low and upgrades to moderate for an estimate above 2.0; a downgrade after an upgrade would give low.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 1 footnote b; Methods › 2.6, after Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The certainty for oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma may be one level lower than printed; Table S3 (not read) holds the reasoning.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists stomach cancer as one study, the Results describe two (a case-control study and the cohort study), and the Discussion refers to 14 included studies where the Results count 15.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Abstract; Results › 3.1.3; Discussion › 4.2, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor counting inconsistency; the case-control stomach result (OR 0.5, 0.2 to 1.2) is lower than the cohort result and is not part of the graded estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: The cancer-specific mortality row cites 163,412 participants, whereas the source paper analysed 169,103 men; the difference of 5,691 equals the number of men who formerly used snus there.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 1 (cancer-specific mortality row); compare sc_byhamre_2021
reporting_issues.consequence: Explained by counting only the two groups compared; the same estimate and its overlap with the mortality paper must not be counted twice in a claim.

verification.source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ijc.34643 (all sections and Table 1 read as text, author affiliations, conflict-of-interest and author-contribution statements; Figures 1 to 4 are images and their values were not extracted; Supporting Information Tables S1 to S5 and the reference list were not read; the page has no funding statement)

design_detail: Single-session laboratory measurement followed by exposure modelling and toxicological risk assessment. 17 adult volunteers who vaped daily took 5 or 25 puffs on one of three device-and-liquid combinations and exhaled the first breath after each puff onto filters; nicotine, propylene glycol, glycerol, four tobacco-specific nitrosamines (TSNAs), three aldehydes and 13 metals were measured, with each person's own breath before vaping as the control. The amounts were scaled up with an assumed lung-retention fraction (a model first built for cigarette smoking) to air concentrations for two imagined scenarios, a one-hour trip in a small unventilated car with two people vaping and a child as the bystander, and a four-hour day in a ventilated office with one person vaping, and compared with air-quality limit values or margins of exposure. No bystander, room air or cigarette smoke was measured.
can_establish: What was in the first exhaled breath of 17 volunteers who vaped three products in a laboratory, compared with their own breath beforehand, and what air concentrations and margins of exposure follow if the stated scenario assumptions hold.
cannot_establish: What bystanders are actually exposed to or what happens to their health (no room, car or body was measured, and the scenarios are imagined and use worst-case assumptions); how exhaled vapour compares with second-hand tobacco smoke (not measured here); whether the findings hold for other devices, liquids or ways of vaping (three low-powered products with tobacco flavour were tested); or any long-term effect.

sample.recruitment: Online screening (computer-assisted web interviewing) of 44,439 members of a Dutch national panel database run by a market-research agency; volunteers were recruited from the people who met the criteria, with the sex ratio and dual-use status matched to those found in the screening. Ethics approval from the Medical Research Ethics Committee of Wageningen University.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: aged 18 or over; daily e-cigarette use with a nicotine-containing liquid (above 6 mg/mL); no diagnosis of diabetes or lung disease. No smoking or vaping for at least 30 minutes before the session. Age, vaping history and exact exclusions beyond these are not given in the main text.
sample.demographics: 10 men and 7 women; 9 also smoked cigarettes (dual use). Age is not reported in the main text.
sample.attrition: All 17 are listed in Table 2; no withdrawals are mentioned. Each person provided nicotine, propylene glycol and glycerol data (5 puffs) and only one 25-puff analysis (nitrosamines, aldehydes or metals), so the three 25-puff analyses rest on 9, 4 and 3 people.
sample.selection_effects: Small convenience group of volunteers who vape daily, from a national panel. The products were chosen by the researchers rather than the volunteers' own, all were tobacco-flavoured and relatively low-powered by the authors' account (a cig-a-like and a refillable device run at 7.6 W). The 113 potential subjects named in Methods and the 485 named in Results (see reporting issues) leave unclear how many people met the criteria.

exposure.measurement: Exhaled breath captured through a mouthpiece onto a quartz filter pad (and a carbon cartridge for aldehydes) immediately after each puff; filters and devices weighed before and after. Nicotine and TSNAs by liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry; propylene glycol and glycerol by the WHO TobLabNet method; carbonyls by derivatisation and chromatography; metals by ICP-MS. Repeatability below 10% (below 5% for TSNAs) and recoveries 80 to 120% as stated. Only the first exhalation after each puff was sampled; the rest of what is exhaled is estimated by the model.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: 5 puffs for nicotine, propylene glycol and glycerol; 25 puffs for the other analytes; puff length, volume and interval were left to the volunteers (natural vaping). Liquid used per puff 5.6 ± 2.4 mg. Exhaled volume per exhalation 33 to 1528 mL. Products (Table 1): A, a non-refillable cig-a-like, tobacco flavour, 18 mg/mL nicotine, propylene glycol/glycerol 50/50; B, refillable dual-coil device (3.7 V battery), tobacco flavour, 18 mg/mL, 50/50; C, the same refillable device, tobacco flavour, 11 mg/mL, 80/20.
exposure.polysubstance: Nine of 17 volunteers also smoked. Breath collected before the first puff served as each person's control and was subtracted; the control breath contained small amounts of nicotine (up to 0.2 ng per puff) from earlier use or second-hand exposure. Total TSNAs did not differ between people who also smoked and people who only vaped (t-test, p = 0.79), tested in the 9 people analysed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 30 minutes without smoking or vaping before the session; not verified biologically.

comparison.controls: Each volunteer's own exhaled breath before the first puff. No comparison with cigarette smoke, with room air, or with people who do not vape.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (within-person baseline).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to an exposure measurement; what was not measured: air in any room or car, particles, bystanders' blood, urine or saliva, second and later exhalations, changes in the vapour as it ages in air, and deposits on surfaces.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Mass gain of the trapping devices and the chemical analyses above. Risk assessment: modelled air concentrations compared with human limit values, WHO Air Quality Guidelines first, and otherwise a margin of exposure (the ratio between a dose that caused effects and the estimated exposure) against a point of departure; for cancer-causing substances a margin of at least 10,000 was taken as low concern. Limit values and the exhaled-fraction calculation are in two supplements that were not read.
outcomes.validity_norms: Analytical recoveries and repeatability are stated. For the model, 40% (local effects) and 33% (systemic effects) of the amount inhaled were assumed to appear in the first exhalation, using worst-case alveolar retention assumptions from a model developed for cigarette smoking. The four nitrosamines were all treated as equally potent as N-nitrosodimethylamine, which the authors say probably overestimates the risk.
outcomes.operationalization: Health risk to a bystander is the gap between a modelled concentration or dose and a limit value or point of departure, not an observed effect. Highest exhaled amounts among the volunteers were used for each chemical, and the final (highest) air concentration of each scenario was used rather than an average over the period.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: 23 analytes measured, descriptive; only two significance statements (mass gain, and the dual-versus-exclusive TSNA comparison, p = 0.79).

analysis.effect_sizes: Mass gain of the trapping device per exhalation: 4.24 ± 2.54 mg for exhaled vapour against 1.86 ± 1.28 mg for control breath (Table 2), strongly correlated with the water content of the extracts (R = 0.98), so mostly water. Editors' calculation from Table 2: mean paired difference 2.39 mg (95% CI 1.41 to 3.38), paired t = 5.15 with 16 degrees of freedom; 16 of 17 volunteers gained more mass with vapour than with control breath (subject 1 did not). Exhaled in the first breath after one puff (Table 3, range across volunteers and median): nicotine below the limit of quantification to 2140 ng, median 108 ng (detected in all samples but one); propylene glycol below the limit to 127 µg, median below the limit (seen in 4 of 17); glycerol below the limit in all 17; TSNAs in 9 people: NNN up to 111 pg (median 29), NNK up to 71 pg (15), NAT up to 40 pg (14), NAB up to 8 pg (2), total as N-nitrosodimethylamine equivalent up to 77 pg (median 28); formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acrolein below the limit in all 4 people; 12 of 13 metals below the limit in 3 people, copper up to 2.92 ng (median below the limit). Modelled concentrations (Table 5; car / office): propylene glycol 9.5 / 2.16 mg/m3; nicotine 0.16 / 0.036 mg/m3; TSNAs as NDMA equivalent 5.8 / 1.31 ng/m3; copper 219 / 50 ng/m3. Editors' calculation: these Table 5 values are reproduced from the Table 3 maxima with the section 2.7 formula, the 40% exhaled fraction, the Table 4 scenario settings and, for the office, the 42.5% ventilation factor. Margins of exposure (Table 6; car / office): propylene glycol local 17 / 74 or 81; TSNAs local 521 / 2297; propylene glycol systemic 535 / 1475; nicotine systemic margin to the effect level 2.1 / 6; nicotine local 3 to 14 below the rat no-effect level and about 170 / 750 below a human airway effect level.
analysis.covariates: None. The model uses scenario parameters (people vaping, puffs per minute, minutes, room volume, ventilation) and assumed retention fractions.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All analytes measured are listed in Table 3. The limit values, points of departure and the exhaled-fraction calculation are in Supplementary Materials 1 and 2, which were not read. Which of the three products produced which result is not reported, and the nitrosamine content of the three liquids is not reported.
analysis.power: Not addressed. 17 volunteers overall and 9, 4 and 3 for the three 25-puff analyses; the authors point to large differences between people (editors' calculation: the highest nicotine value is about 20 times the median) and say that studies of second-hand vaping before theirs used three or fewer people.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 17 volunteers vaping three low-powered products, the first breath after a puff held measurable nicotine (median 108 ng, up to 2140 ng), propylene glycol in 4 people, tobacco-specific nitrosamines in the 9 people tested (total up to 77 pg) and copper in one of three people tested; glycerol, three aldehydes and 12 other metals were below the detection limit in the few people tested for them. Scaling these up with worst-case assumptions gave modelled air concentrations; against limit values the margins were thin for propylene glycol irritation in the car scenario (17), for nicotine's effects on heart rate and blood pressure (2.1 in the car, 6 in the office) and for nitrosamine cancer risk (521 and 2297 against a threshold of 10,000). The authors themselves call the effects relatively mild even in the extreme scenario. Nothing was measured in a room, a car or a bystander, and no cigarette was measured.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions say bystanders may experience irritation of the respiratory tract from propylene glycol and glycerol, that systemic effects of nicotine should also be expected, with palpitations and a rise in systolic blood pressure, and that an increased risk of tumours cannot be excluded in the car scenario; the abstract also says e-cigarette use can clearly affect bystanders' health, while the discussion calls the effects relatively mild. Gaps: (1) the effects are model outputs from exhaled-breath measurements and worst-case assumptions, not observations in bystanders; (2) glycerol was below the detection limit in all 17 volunteers and the risk assessment itself says nothing is expected from amounts below that limit, yet glycerol is named as an irritant in the abstract and conclusions; (3) the expectation of nicotine effects rests on estimated exposure lying only 2.1 times below an effect level reported in one human study, with the authors adding variability between people; (4) the cancer statement rests on treating four nitrosamines as equal in potency to N-nitrosodimethylamine, on the highest exhaled amounts, and on nitrosamines whose source in the liquids was not measured; (5) 'increased levels of copper' rests on one of three people; (6) the claim that nitrosamines in exhaled vapour can be avoided is not tested in the paper. In the authors' favour, they state the worst-case assumptions and the opposite-direction limitations (low-powered products, few volunteers, only the first exhalation sampled).

timeline.event: Ballbe et al.: air and biomarker measurements in homes of people who vape, with difficulty excluding exposure to tobacco smoke elsewhere (as described in the introduction; not read).

Hess et al.: systematic review of passive exposure to e-cigarette vapour; the authors say it agrees with their main findings on upper-airway irritation and nicotine effects (as described in the discussion; not read).
National Academies review of the health consequences of e-cigarettes, cited as the first reference of this paper; read separately for the claims on this topic.
This study: the authors state it is the first toxicological risk assessment of e-cigarette vapour to bystanders and that earlier measurements of second-hand vaping used three or fewer volunteers.

replication.where_it_stands: A single small laboratory study with a modelled risk assessment. This card does not cover later measurements in rooms or in bystanders; the reviews read for the claim on vapour near others are named in that claim.

funding.funder: Dutch Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (research and article-processing charge).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: All six authors share affiliation number 1; the PMC text does not name the institution (the task brief names the Dutch national institute RIVM, and reference 9 is an earlier RIVM report with the same first author). A market-research agency helped with recruitment and the experiments, and two people named in the acknowledgments, who are not authors, carried out the risk assessment. No tobacco or vape industry funding is stated.

what_would_settle_it: Measurements in real rooms and cars of nicotine, particles, nitrosamines and other compounds during vaping and, in the same spaces, during smoking, across ventilation and room sizes, with a range of current devices, liquids and puffing patterns; plus nicotine and nitrosamine biomarkers (for example cotinine) in bystanders who are not exposed to tobacco smoke elsewhere, over days and weeks.

domains.note: 17 volunteers and three low-powered tobacco-flavoured products; the 25-puff analyses (nitrosamines, aldehydes, metals) rest on 9, 4 and 3 people; large differences between people.

Validated methods with stated recoveries and repeatability and a within-person baseline; only the first exhalation was sampled and many results were below the limit of quantification; glycerol was measured with lower sensitivity.

domains.domain: Measurement in air and in bystanders
domains.note: Nothing was measured in a room, a car or a bystander; the air concentrations are modelled from imagined scenarios.

Worst-case retention fractions from a cigarette model, highest exhaled amounts, final rather than average concentration, and equal potency of four nitrosamines; some assumptions run toward overestimation, others (low-powered products, few volunteers, no ageing of the aerosol) toward underestimation, as the authors state.
No comparison with second-hand tobacco smoke or with background air in the same rooms; the comparison is with limit values and points of departure from other studies, many in animals.

Glycerol named as an irritant though below the detection limit; 'increased' copper from one of three people; recruitment counts differ between Methods and Results; the three 25-puff analyses cover 16 of 17 people; no test named for the mass-gain difference.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a measurement-plus-modelling risk assessment (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used, with domains adapted to this design. The laboratory measurements are transparent and the authors state their assumptions, but the headline findings are model outputs about imagined scenarios resting on small numbers of people and no measurement in the places or people at issue. Citable for what was in the exhaled breath of 17 volunteers who vaped three products and for the authors' own risk estimates under stated assumptions; not citable for what bystanders are exposed to or for how this compares with second-hand smoke.

key_findings.finding: 17 volunteers took part (10 men, 7 women; 9 also smoked); 4 used product A, 6 used B and 7 used C. Product A was a non-refillable cig-a-like at 18 mg/mL, B and C a refillable dual-coil device at 18 and 11 mg/mL; all tobacco flavour. The volunteers' own breath before the first puff served as control.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.2 Collection and Analysis of Exhaled Vapor, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1; Results › 3.1 and 3.2

key_findings.finding: Mass gain of the trapping devices was higher with exhaled vapour (4.24 ± 2.54 mg per exhalation) than with control breath (1.86 ± 1.28 mg), strongly correlated with the water content of the extracts (R = 0.98); no test statistic is printed.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3 Analysis of Exhaled Vapor, 2nd paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 2: mean paired difference 2.39 mg (95% CI 1.41 to 3.38), paired t = 5.15, 16 degrees of freedom; one volunteer (subject 1) had a lower value with vapour.

key_findings.finding: Nicotine was found in the first exhaled breath of all volunteers but one: range below the limit of quantification to 2140 ng per puff, median 108 ng; exhaled volume per exhalation ranged from 33 to 1528 mL; control breath held up to 0.2 ng and was subtracted.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3, 3rd paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Propylene glycol was seen in 4 of 17 volunteers (maximum 127 µg per puff, median below the limit); glycerol was below the limit of quantification in all 17, and the method was less sensitive for glycerol.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3, 4th paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Tobacco-specific nitrosamines, measured in 9 volunteers: NNN up to 111 pg (median 29), NNK up to 71 pg (15), NAT up to 40 pg (14), NAB up to 8 pg (2); total as NDMA equivalent up to 77 pg (median 28) per puff. Total TSNAs did not differ between people who also smoked and people who only vaped (p = 0.79).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3, 5th paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acrolein were below the limit of quantification in all 4 volunteers analysed (amounts of formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acetone found did not exceed control-breath levels); of 13 metals measured in 3 volunteers only copper was seen (maximum 2.92 ng, median below the limit).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3, 6th paragraph; Table 3; Results › 3.12 and 3.13

key_findings.finding: Scenarios modelled: car, 2 people vaping at 0.5 puffs a minute for 1 hour in a space of 2 m3 with no ventilation, the bystander a child; office, 1 person at 2 puffs a minute for 4 hours in 30 m3 with ventilation of 0.5 per hour (final concentration reduced to 42.5%). The authors say the car scenario approximates the highest levels expected in everyday situations and the office scenario a more typical level.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.4 Bystander Exposure, 1st paragraph; Table 4; Methods › 2.7, last paragraph; Conclusions, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Modelled air concentrations (car / office): propylene glycol 9.5 / 2.16 mg/m3; nicotine 0.16 / 0.036 mg/m3; TSNAs as NDMA equivalent 5.8 / 1.31 ng/m3; copper 219 / 50 ng/m3.
key_findings.locator: Table 5
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: reproduced from the Table 3 maxima, the 40% exhaled fraction and the Table 4 settings (for example nicotine 2.14 µg / 0.4 x 0.5 per min x 60 min x 2 people / 2 m3 = 0.16 mg/m3).

key_findings.finding: Propylene glycol: margin of exposure for upper-airway irritation 17 in the car and 74 or 81 in the office; local effects on the airways and eyes 'cannot be excluded' in the car and are expected to be mild if they occur; no local effects anticipated in the office; no systemic effects expected (margins 535 and 1475).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.7 Propylene Glycol; Table 6

key_findings.finding: Nicotine: local airway effects not expected in either scenario (exposure 3 to 14 times below the no-effect level in a two-year rat inhalation study and about 170 and 750 times below a human airway effect level); systemic effects (higher heart rate and systolic blood pressure) 'should be expected' in the car (margin to the human effect level 2.1) and cannot be excluded in the office (margin 6); the size is compared with the caffeine in 2 or 3 cups of coffee.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.9 and 3.10; Conclusions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Nitrosamines: margins of exposure 521 (car) and 2297 (office) against 10,000 taken as low concern; an increased risk of respiratory-tract tumours cannot be excluded in the car, and for the office a risk assessment cannot be made with sufficient certainty. All four nitrosamines were treated as equal in potency to N-nitrosodimethylamine, which the authors say probably overestimates the risk.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.11; Table 6; Methods › 2.8, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Copper stayed below a tolerable air concentration of 1 µg/m3 in both scenarios; the other metals were below the limit of quantification, with no conclusion possible for chromium (only total chromium, nickel and arsenic were measured).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.12 Copper; 3.13 Other Metals

key_findings.finding: The authors call the effects on bystanders relatively mild even in the extreme scenario, say the nitrosamine risk could be avoided if e-liquids had no detectable nitrosamines and that only a limited number of liquids on the market contain significant amounts, and say the study is the first toxicological risk assessment of e-cigarette vapour to bystanders.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusions › Regulatory Implications

key_findings.finding: Limitations the authors state: only the first exhalation after each puff was sampled and the rest estimated with an assumed retention; the model was originally developed for cigarette smoking; the final, highest concentration was used; the highest emissions seen probably do not represent the worst case with so few volunteers, and low-powered products probably lead to underestimation; changes of the vapour in air, nicotine reacting to form nitrosamines, and deposits on surfaces were not modelled; toxicity data are missing for most flavour compounds.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.7; Results › 3.5; Discussion, 3rd to 7th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: Methods say the national panel screening of 44,439 respondents identified 113 potential test subjects; Results say 485 people who vaped matched the criteria. The screening method is written 'CAWI' in Methods and 'CIWA' in Results. Figure 1, which should explain the numbers, is an image and was not extracted.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pool the 17 volunteers came from is unclear; no effect on the measurements.

reporting_issues.issue: The three 25-puff analyses cover 9 (nitrosamines), 4 (aldehydes) and 3 (metals) volunteers, which add to 16, although 17 volunteers are reported and the methods say each had one such analysis.
reporting_issues.consequence: One volunteer's 25-puff analysis is not accounted for; findings on aldehydes and metals rest on 4 and 3 people at most.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and the conclusions name glycerol, with propylene glycol, as a cause of respiratory irritation for bystanders. Table 3 and section 3.6 report glycerol below the limit of quantification in all 17 volunteers (with a less sensitive method) and say amounts below the limit are not expected to cause effects; only propylene glycol carries a margin of exposure for irritation (Table 6).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Abstract; Conclusions, 1st paragraph; Results › 3.3, 3.6; Table 6)
reporting_issues.consequence: Glycerol should not be cited as a finding of irritation from this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says increased levels of propylene glycol and copper were found in exhaled breath. Table 3 shows propylene glycol above the limit in 4 of 17 people (median below the limit) and copper above the limit in at most one of 3 people (median below the limit).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's list is stronger than the table; the scenario values use the single highest exhaled amount for each chemical.

reporting_issues.issue: The nitrosamine margin of exposure in the office scenario (2297) is below the 10,000 threshold the authors set for low concern, as in the car scenario (521); the abstract and conclusions state the cancer risk 'could not be excluded' only for the car, and the text says only that the office risk cannot be assessed with sufficient certainty.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two scenarios are not as different in this respect as the abstract suggests; neither meets the authors' own threshold.

reporting_issues.issue: The statements that the nitrosamines can be avoided and that only a limited number of liquids on the market contain significant amounts have no citation in the passage, and the nitrosamine content of the three liquids used, and which products produced the nitrosamines found, are not reported.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Discussion, 1st paragraph; Regulatory Implications; Table 3)
reporting_issues.consequence: The source of the nitrosamines in exhaled breath is not shown by this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The mass-gain difference between vapour and control breath is called significant without naming a test; the means and standard deviations in the text match Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: No effect on interpretation (editors' paired test confirms the difference); the gain is mostly water.

reporting_issues.issue: The car scenario names a child as the bystander, but the main text does not give the body weight, breathing rate or child-specific limit values used for the doses and margins; these are described as being in Supplementary Material 2, which was not read.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the margins apply to a child cannot be checked from the main text.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6539638 (all sections, Tables 1 to 6 as text, reference list, funding, conflicts and author contributions; Figure 1 is an image and was not extracted; Supplementary Materials 1 and 2 not read)

design_detail: Prospective cohort analysis of the PATH Study (US national probability cohort), Waves 1 to 4 (September 2013 to January 2018), public-use files. Adults aged 18 or older with no respiratory condition at baseline were classed by baseline self-reported e-cigarette status (never; former, which includes any past use even 1 or 2 puffs; current, every day or some days) and followed for newly self-reported diagnoses of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), emphysema, chronic bronchitis and asthma, singly and as a composite. Poisson regression gave incidence rate ratios, with sequential adjustment and sensitivity analyses.
can_establish: How the rate of newly self-reported respiratory diagnoses over up to about four years compared, after adjustment for demographics, smoking history, other tobacco, other drugs, body mass index and chronic conditions, between US adults who had ever used e-cigarettes at baseline (former or current) and adults who had never used them.
cannot_establish: Whether e-cigarettes cause any respiratory condition (observational; baseline-only exposure; smoking history adjusted by broad categories, so residual confounding is likely), whether the same holds for devices since 2014, how much risk comes from current versus past use, or measured lung function (all outcomes are self-reported diagnoses).

sample.recruitment: PATH Study, a national longitudinal survey begun in 2013 by NIH and FDA, oversampling people who use tobacco, young adults (18 to 24) and African American adults. Wave 1 data were collected from 12 September 2013 to 14 December 2014 and Wave 4 from 1 December 2016 to 3 January 2018. Retention of the Wave 1 cohort was 83.2% at Wave 2, 78.4% at Wave 3 and 73.5% at Wave 4 (Methods › Study Setting). Excluded: a baseline respiratory condition, loss to follow-up by Wave 2, missing e-cigarette data; sample sizes differ by condition (Table 2). The selection flow chart (eFigure 1) was not read.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Adults 18 or older at baseline without COPD, emphysema, chronic bronchitis or asthma; at least one follow-up wave; e-cigarette status known. Youth who aged into the adult sample and Wave 4 replenishment respondents were not included.
sample.demographics: 49.1% men, 65.2% non-Hispanic White, 11.5% Black, 15.5% Hispanic, 7.9% other; weighted age spread even from 18-24 (13.1%) to 65 and over (16.9%); mean baseline pack-years 6.7 (Results › Baseline Characteristics, 1st paragraph; Table 1). People who currently used e-cigarettes were younger (21.9% aged 18-24 against 10.8% of people who had never used them) and much more likely to have smoked cigarettes: 16.0% had never smoked cigarettes against 72.1% of those who had never used e-cigarettes (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Retention fell to 73.5% by Wave 4; people lost after Wave 2 are censored at the wave of loss, and the extent of loss by e-cigarette group is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Baseline-only classification and exclusion of anyone with an existing respiratory condition. At baseline 7,405 (16.8% weighted) had ever used e-cigarettes; 'former' use includes people who had tried them for 1 or 2 puffs. Among people who currently used e-cigarettes, only 401 had never smoked cigarettes, so any analysis in never smokers rests on small numbers (the authors report one in the supplement, which was not read).

exposure.measurement: Self-report at Wave 1 only. Current = uses every day or some days; former = ever used, even 1 or 2 puffs, and not now; never = never used. Exploratory sub-division by every day vs some days, age at first use (under 25, 25 to 44, 45 or over) and experimental vs established use (used 'fairly regularly' or not).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Exposure is baseline status only; the authors state that time-varying exposure was not considered (Limitations). Device generation and flavors were not available for the first wave. In the exploratory analyses the highest incidence was in groups with every-day current use, first use before age 25, and established use (eFigure 2, values not read).
exposure.polysubstance: Cigarette smoking history adjusted as: never; former (quit under 5, 5 to 20, 20 or more years ago); current (under 5, 5 to 20, 20 or more pack-years). Ever use of cigars, cigarillos, pipe, hookah; ever use of heroin, inhalants or hallucinogens. Marijuana, second-hand smoke, childhood smoke exposure and smokeless tobacco were added only in sensitivity analyses (results in a supplement, not read).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Adults who had never used an e-cigarette (not even 1 or 2 puffs), n = 14,213.
comparison.matching: None; Poisson models adjusted in two steps: (1) age, sex, race/ethnicity; (2) plus education, US census region, cigarette smoking history, other combustible tobacco, ever use of heroin, inhalants or hallucinogens, body mass index, and self-reported hypertension, high cholesterol, heart failure, heart attack, stroke and diabetes.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Within-category smoking intensity (the top pack-year category is open-ended, and former smokers have time since quitting but not pack-years), occupational and household exposures, income, allergy and family history, marijuana and second-hand smoke in the main models, and any change in e-cigarette or cigarette use after baseline.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Ever use of heroin, inhalants or hallucinogens: 4.0% of people who had never used e-cigarettes and 15.8% of those who currently used them (Table 1); adjusted for.

outcomes.instruments: Self-report at each wave of a diagnosis of COPD, emphysema, chronic bronchitis or asthma by a physician or other health professional in the past 12 months; incident if first reported over follow-up in someone without a history at baseline. A composite counts any of the four.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors state the survey items have been validated against direct clinical observation and widely used (references 38 to 40, not read). No lung function or medical records were used.
outcomes.operationalization: Incident respiratory condition = first self-reported diagnosis over Waves 2 to 4.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; five outcomes, three e-cigarette contrasts, two subsample analyses and six sensitivity analyses.

analysis.effect_sizes: Cases: asthma 804, emphysema 336, COPD 573, chronic bronchitis 948; 1,460 people (6.8%) with at least one. Multivariable incidence rate ratios against never use, ever / former / current: any respiratory condition 1.28 (95% CI 1.10-1.48) / 1.28 (1.09-1.51) / 1.31 (1.08-1.59); chronic bronchitis 1.33 (1.12-1.59) / 1.31 (1.08-1.58) / 1.33 (1.06-1.67); emphysema 1.54 (1.12-2.12) / 1.42 (1.01-2.01) / 1.69 (1.15-2.49); COPD 1.62 (1.28-2.04) / 1.66 (1.29-2.12) / 1.57 (1.15-2.13); asthma 1.24 (1.01-1.53) / 1.19 (0.95-1.50) / 1.32 (1.01-1.72). Multivariable-adjusted rates per 1,000 person-years, any respiratory condition: never 20.41 (18.65-22.17), former 26.12 (22.34-29.89), current 26.68 (21.83-31.52) (editors' calculation: about 2.0 against 2.6 to 2.7 new diagnoses per 100 people per year). The age-sex-race-adjusted ratios were much larger (any condition 2.14 ever; COPD 5.03; emphysema 4.02) and fell once smoking and the other covariates were added. Restricted to people with good or better self-rated health (n = 18,649): former 1.21 (1.00-1.47), current 1.43 (1.14-1.80); to people with no chronic condition at baseline (n = 14,865): ever 1.20 (0.99-1.45), former 1.11 (0.90-1.37), current 1.40 (1.09-1.79).
analysis.covariates: See comparison.matching. Multiple imputation by chained equations (5 imputations) for missing exposure and covariates; Wave 2 sample weights.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned; analyses were run from February to July 2020. Six sensitivity analyses are described (extra adjustment for second-hand smoke, marijuana, childhood smoke exposure and smokeless tobacco; listwise deletion; replicate weights; Wave 4 panel weights; excluding people who ever smoked cigarettes; excluding all other tobacco), with results only in a supplement (eTable) that was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: Results for the sensitivity analyses and the dose-response (intensity, age at first use, established use) analyses are in the supplement only; the text says they were similar or highest in every-day, early-starting, established use without numbers.
analysis.power: Adequate for the composite (1,460 cases) and the single conditions in the whole sample; the 'no chronic condition' subsample has 808 cases, and the never-smoker analyses rest on few people who currently used e-cigarettes and had never smoked (401).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In US adults followed for up to about four years from 2013-2014, those who had ever used e-cigarettes at baseline (including people who had tried them briefly) had about 28% higher rates of newly reported respiratory diagnoses than those who never had, after adjustment for smoking history and other factors (rate ratio 1.28, 1.10 to 1.48); the ratio was similar for former use (1.28) and current use (1.31), was smaller than the unadjusted-for-smoking ratios, and for asthma the former-use estimate had an interval that included 1 (0.95 to 1.50). Among people with no chronic condition at baseline the former-use estimate was 1.11 (0.90 to 1.37) and the current-use estimate 1.40 (1.09 to 1.79).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Key Points and Conclusions state that e-cigarette use was associated with increased risk of respiratory disease 'independent of' cigarette smoking and other tobacco use, and that people who use them 'may experience increased rates'; the Discussion adds that the results strengthen the evidence for a role of e-cigarettes in lung disease and may inform counselling, and cites animal studies as showing plausibility of causation. The same paper states that causality could not be established, that exposure was baseline-only, and that smoking was adjusted by broad categories. The similar ratios for people who had only tried e-cigarettes briefly or had stopped (former use) and for current use are not discussed as a possible sign of confounding.

timeline.event: Bhatta and Glantz, PATH waves 1 to 3, composite respiratory outcome: the authors report 31% higher risk with former use and 29% with current use of e-cigarettes after adjustment; the same cohort, so not an independent replication (described in this paper's Discussion; not read).

A cross-sectional study of 705,159 respondents to the US Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System 2016 and 2017 reported 75% higher odds of COPD in people who currently used e-cigarettes and had never smoked cigarettes (described in this paper's Discussion; not read).
Berlowitz et al.: cardiovascular outcomes in the same cohort (card sc_berlowitz_2022).

replication.where_it_stands: The direction (higher rates of self-reported respiratory diagnoses in people who vape than in people who never have, after adjustment) is reported by two analyses of the same PATH cohort and a cross-sectional survey; independent cohorts with objectively measured lung outcomes were not read for this batch. Whether it reflects the products or the smoking history that precedes them is the open question.

funding.funder: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and US Food and Drug Administration Center for Tobacco Products (grants P50HL120163, U54HL120163-01 and 1K01HL154130); American Lung Association Public Policy Research Award (PP-702811). The printed role-of-funder statement says the funders had no role in design, conduct, analysis, writing or the decision to submit.
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: Kathuria is a section editor for tobacco dependence treatment in UpToDate. Blaha reports FDA grants during the study and personal fees from Regeneron, Novartis, Novo Nordisk, Bayer, Akcea, 89Bio, Zogenix, Tricida, Gilead and Amgen outside the submitted work. Robertson reports FDA and NIH grants during the study. Benjamin reports NIH and American Heart Association grants during the study. Stokes reports grants from Ethicon, a subsidiary of Johnson and Johnson, outside the submitted work. No other disclosures.
funding.affiliations_note: Boston University, Johns Hopkins, Vanderbilt, the American Heart Association Tobacco Regulation and Addiction Center and the University of Louisville. No tobacco or e-cigarette manufacturer funding is declared; the conflicts listed are pharmaceutical and device-company ties and a federal regulator's grants.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort that records e-cigarette use at every wave with frequency, device and nicotine content, smoking history in full (pack-years and years since quitting), and objectively measured lung function and imaging; with analyses in people who never smoked and in long-term former smokers separately, marginal structural models for time-varying use, and a comparison against people who stopped smoking without vaping.

domains.note: People who currently used e-cigarettes were far more likely to have smoked (84% against 28% of those who never used them) and to have used other drugs and tobacco; smoking history was adjusted by broad categories only, with an open-ended top pack-year band and no pack-years for former smokers, so residual confounding by smoking is plausible and would raise the e-cigarette group's rate. The reverse-causation sensitivity analyses (healthy subsamples) address only one direction, and results in never smokers are in a supplement not read.
Single baseline self-report; 'former' includes people who tried 1 or 2 puffs; later changes ignored; device and nicotine unknown.
Retention 73.5% by Wave 4, with exclusion of people lost by Wave 2; weighted to the Wave 2 sample.
People who start, stop or switch products after baseline are classed by baseline status; the authors note this limitation.
Multiple imputation of exposure and covariates; the authors say listwise deletion gave similar results (supplement not read).
Self-reported diagnoses, not adjudicated or checked against lung function; validity is cited, not shown.
No plan stated; sensitivity and intensity results only in a supplement; five outcomes without correction.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E overall is no milder than the worst domain, and residual confounding by smoking history is a serious concern in a group that is mostly current or former smokers. The cohort is large and national, the follow-up is prospective, the incidence is analysed rather than prevalence, and the authors tested reverse causation and several alternative weights; but the main effect is modest (rate ratios about 1.2 to 1.7) and the same size in people who had only tried e-cigarettes. It may be cited for the rate ratios and absolute adjusted rates as reported, as an association in a US cohort of 2013-2018; not for a causal effect, for a particular product, or for any conclusion about lung function or severe disease.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7662143 (all sections, Tables 1 to 3, figure legend, author notes, funding and conflict-of-interest statement, reference list; the Figure is an image and was not extracted; the supplement (eTable, eFigures 1 and 2) was not read)

key_findings.finding: 21,618 adults analysed: 14,213 never, 5,076 former (11.6% weighted) and 2,329 current (5.2%) e-cigarette use at baseline; 7,405 (16.8%) had ever used. Retention of the baseline cohort 83.2% (Wave 2), 78.4% (Wave 3), 73.5% (Wave 4).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Methods › Study Setting, 1st paragraph; Results › Baseline Characteristics and e-Cigarette Use Behavior, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Former use was defined as ever having used an e-cigarette, even 1 or 2 puffs, and not now; current use as every day or some days.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, footnote b; Methods › Assessment of e-Cigarette Use, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Baseline smoking: 16.0% of people who currently used e-cigarettes had never smoked cigarettes (401 people) against 72.1% of those who had never used them; 22.0%, 28.2% and 18.5% of the current-use group were current smokers with under 5, 5 to 20 and 20 or more pack-years; mean pack-years 13.4 (current use), 11.6 (former use), 5.6 (never used).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, rows 'Cigarette smoking status' and 'Pack-years'

key_findings.finding: New diagnoses during follow-up: asthma 804, emphysema 336, COPD 573, chronic bronchitis 948; 1,460 respondents (6.8%) with at least one.
key_findings.locator: Results › e-Cigarette Use and Incident Respiratory Conditions, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Multivariable-adjusted incidence rate ratios against never use for any respiratory condition: ever 1.28 (95% CI 1.10-1.48), former 1.28 (1.09-1.51), current 1.31 (1.08-1.59). Adjusted rates per 1,000 person-years: never 20.41 (18.65-22.17), ever 26.06 (22.63-29.49), former 26.12, current 26.68 (21.83-31.52).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, 'Any respiratory condition' rows; Results › e-Cigarette Use and Incident Respiratory Conditions, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Multivariable-adjusted incidence rate ratios, ever / former / current e-cigarette use: chronic bronchitis 1.33 / 1.31 / 1.33; emphysema 1.54 / 1.42 / 1.69; COPD 1.62 / 1.66 / 1.57; asthma 1.24 (1.01-1.53) / 1.19 (0.95-1.50) / 1.32 (1.01-1.72). Adjusted rates per 1,000 person-years, never vs ever: COPD 6.48 vs 10.49; emphysema 3.74 vs 5.76; bronchitis 12.18 vs 16.23; asthma 10.73 vs 13.31.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, rows for each condition

key_findings.finding: The age-, sex- and race/ethnicity-adjusted ratios for ever use were 2.14 (any condition), 4.02 (emphysema) and 5.03 (COPD); they fell to 1.28, 1.54 and 1.62 after adjustment for smoking history and the other covariates.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, rows 'Age-, sex-, and race/ethnicity-adjusted IRR' and 'Multivariable-adjusted IRR'

key_findings.finding: Among people with good, great or excellent self-rated health (n = 18,649): former 1.21 (1.00-1.47), current 1.43 (1.14-1.80). Among people with no chronic condition at baseline (n = 14,865): ever 1.20 (0.99-1.45), former 1.11 (0.90-1.37), current 1.40 (1.09-1.79).
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results › e-Cigarette Use and Incident Respiratory Conditions, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Exploratory analyses: the highest rates were in groups with every-day current use, first use before age 25 and established use; no significant interaction with sex; six sensitivity analyses (including excluding people who smoked cigarettes or used other tobacco) gave similar results to the main analysis. Values are in the supplement, not read.
key_findings.locator: Results › e-Cigarette Use and Incident Respiratory Conditions, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Statistical Analysis, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Authors' stated limits: self-reported exposure and diagnoses; observational data with relatively short follow-up, so causality could not be established; no time-varying exposure or confounding; device characteristics (generation, flavor) unavailable; lung function not measured. They also describe reverse causation (people with early symptoms switching to e-cigarettes or quitting) as a bias that could hide an association.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph; Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the asthma ratio for current use as 1.31 (95% CI 1.01-1.71); Table 2 gives 1.32 (1.01-1.72). The abstract's ratios for good self-rated health (former 1.00-1.46, current 1.14-1.79) also differ in the last digit from Table 3 (1.00-1.47, 1.14-1.80).
reporting_issues.locator: Abstract › Results; Table 2; Table 3
reporting_issues.consequence: Immaterial; cite the table values.

reporting_issues.issue: The sample for the composite outcome is 21,618 in the text and 21,640 in Table 2. The samples for single conditions are 25,202 (bronchitis), 23,686 (emphysema), 23,236 (COPD) and 20,914 (asthma): by the stated rule (excluding people with that condition at baseline) each should be at least as large as the composite sample, yet the asthma sample is 726 smaller than the composite, and the paper does not explain.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Baseline Characteristics, 1st paragraph; Table 2, condition headings
reporting_issues.consequence: The selection of participants for the asthma analysis cannot be reconstructed; the flow chart is in the supplement (not read).

reporting_issues.issue: For three conditions the former and current case counts do not sum to the ever-use count (bronchitis 274 + 144 = 418 vs 419; emphysema 92 + 62 = 154 vs 155; asthma 224 + 119 = 343 vs 344).
reporting_issues.locator: Table 2, rows 'No. of incident cases'
reporting_issues.consequence: Off by one (probably from multiple imputation of exposure); immaterial.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract prints '11 017 (491%)' men (49.1% in the Results) and a Results age band '66-64 years' (55-64); a sentence on the sample weights is repeated word for word in the Statistical Analysis section.
reporting_issues.locator: Abstract › Results; Results › Baseline Characteristics, 1st paragraph; Methods › Statistical Analysis, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; no effect on results.

reporting_issues.issue: The Key Points and Conclusions say the association is 'independent of' cigarette smoking and other tobacco, but this rests on categorical adjustment (with open-ended top pack-year band and no pack-years for former smokers) and on supplement-only sensitivity analyses; the former-use ratio (which includes 1 or 2 puffs) equals the current-use ratio.
reporting_issues.locator: Key Points; Conclusions; Methods › Covariates
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should say 'after adjustment for smoking history', not 'independent of smoking', and should not call it an effect of e-cigarettes.

design_detail: Analysis article (BMJ 2015;351:h4863, published 15 September 2015), two authors. Three printed pages headed 'Page 1 of 3' to 'Page 3 of 3', plus a key-messages box on a page headed 'Page 4 of 3': an untitled opening and four headed sections (Defining the role of e-cigarettes; Quality of the evidence; Uncertainty around harms; Where next for policy on e-cigarettes?), 27 references, a competing-interests statement and a provenance note (not commissioned; externally peer reviewed). No data, methods or search. It questions the evidence behind Public Health England's 2015 evidence update (McNeill et al., 2015, its reference 1) on the safety of e-cigarettes and their effectiveness for stopping smoking, including the origin of the '95% less harmful' figure, which it traces to one meeting of 12 people who built a multicriteria decision analysis of their opinions (Nutt et al., 2014, its reference 12). The 2015 report, the 2014 paper and every study cited are known here only as this article describes them. Commentary appraised with the editors' checklist, as for the 2020 editorial on the same figure (card sc_eissenberg_2020).
can_establish: What two public health academics argued in September 2015 about the evidence behind the 2015 report: where the 95% figure came from as they describe it, who funded and attended the meeting behind it as they report it, which comparisons and outcomes they say the report left out (people who do not smoke as a comparison, dual use, young people, bystanders, poisoning, labelling), and the precautionary standard they propose.
cannot_establish: How much less harmful vaping is than smoking (the article offers no estimate and presents no data); whether the 2014 rating exercise and the 2015 report are as described (neither was read); whether the reported ties of the meeting's funders and members affected the ratings (the article does not claim to show that, and its sources for the ties are a company register, web pages, a book and a company report, none read); and anything published after September 2015.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (analysis article). The rating exercise it describes: a single meeting of 12 people convened to develop a multicriteria decision analysis (MCDA) model synthesising their opinions on the harms of different nicotine-containing products, summarised in a research paper (Nutt et al., 2014); according to the authors, the rationale for choosing the panel was not provided (Quality of the evidence, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; the authors choose the evidence.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The evidence is chosen to question one report. The 27 references include news reports (BBC, Guardian), statements of organisations, a company register entry, two pages of the Tobacco Tactics website, a book, a tobacco company's sustainability report, an article in The Conversation and a PhD thesis, alongside a Cochrane review, a systematic review, a cohort study, an online panel survey, a US adolescent cohort and a US poisoning report. No study of toxicant exposure or short-term health measures in people who switched from smoking to e-cigarettes is cited or discussed.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable.
exposure.polysubstance: Dual use (smoking while using e-cigarettes) is discussed as a pattern the 2015 report rarely mentions (Defining the role of e-cigarettes, 2nd paragraph).

comparison.controls: No comparison of its own. The article sets out, as the position of those concerned about e-cigarettes, that non-smoking should be included as a comparison alongside smoking, because e-cigarettes, while lacking some of the most harmful substances in cigarettes such as tar, contain others such as formaldehyde and diverse flavourings (Defining the role of e-cigarettes, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: None. The MCDA exercise is described only as a model synthesising the opinions of 12 people on the harms of nicotine-containing products; the article gives no criteria, scores or weights and does not say how the 95% figure was obtained from the model.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Harm' in the 95% figure is, as described, the output of a decision-analysis model of expert opinion, not a measured rate of disease or death.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own. Numbers in the text, as cited: 12 people at the rating meeting; 76 studies in a 2014 systematic review, a third (34%) published by authors with conflicts of interest; two randomised trials in the 2014 Cochrane review on stopping smoking, evidence rated low or very low quality; two thirds of people who use e-cigarettes also smoke (no source given); dual use above 80% after 12 months among people who vaped daily in one cohort study; over one fifth of 11 to 15 year olds in England had ever used e-cigarettes and 73% of the young people surveyed who had tried them did not smoke; over 2,400 poisoning cases in the United States to February 2014.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: The article argues one side and presents only the uncertainties and omissions it sees in the 2015 report; the exposure and short-term evidence that a comparison with smoking could rest on is not discussed (editors' note), and no reply from the report's authors or from the 2014 paper's authors is given.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: No data. The article argues that the 95% figure featured in the 2015 report came from one meeting of 12 people who modelled their opinions by multicriteria decision analysis, not from a detailed review of evidence with modelling; that the meeting's sponsor and a supporting organisation had, through their chief executive and chief scientific adviser, reported links to tobacco companies (sources: a company register, two web pages, a book and a company report); that the panel's selection was not explained and included several known e-cigarette advocates, some declaring industry funding; that the 2014 paper itself listed the lack of hard evidence for the harms of most products on most criteria as a limitation; and that the 2015 report discussed none of this. It adds that the report did not cite a 2014 systematic review that found no firm conclusions could be drawn on safety, rarely mentioned dual use, and consistently took the most optimistic position on limited evidence (bystanders, poisoning, labelling, young people).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The key messages (p. 4 of 3) say that Public Health England's endorsement of the safety and efficacy of e-cigarettes rests on uncertain evidence, that the evidence that they help people stop smoking is weak, that recent evidence questions the conclusion that they are not a gateway to smoking, and that until better evidence is available public health strategies should follow the precautionary principle; the policy section calls the report flawed. Gaps: (1) showing that a figure rests on expert opinion, and that its authors flagged the lack of hard evidence, does not show that the size of the difference is wrong: the article offers no alternative estimate and does not discuss the exposure measurements on which a comparison with smoking could rest; (2) the paragraphs on the meeting's funders rest on a company register, Tobacco Tactics web pages, a book and a company report, are worded as reported, and do not show that the ties changed the ratings; the article itself quotes the 2014 paper's statement that its sponsor had no role in the process or the writing and was not present at the workshop, and the book's statement that its conclusions were developed independently of BAT; (3) the gateway point rests on one US cohort's association between ever using e-cigarettes and starting to smoke within a year, an association whose causal reading is disputed; (4) the two-thirds dual-use figure has no source. In the authors' favour, the position they set out concedes that e-cigarettes lack some of the most harmful substances in cigarettes, such as tar, and they say no research so far is conclusive and agree with England's chief medical officer that evidence on long-term use is lacking.

timeline.event: Nutt et al., European Addiction Research: the multicriteria decision analysis from one meeting of 12 people on the harms of nicotine-containing products; its authors list the lack of hard evidence for the harms of most products on most criteria as a limitation (as quoted here; no reference record; not read).

Pisinger and Døssing, Preventive Medicine: systematic review of 76 studies of health effects of e-cigarettes, concluding that no firm conclusions on safety could be drawn (as described here; no reference record; not read).
Public Health England evidence update (McNeill et al., 2015) with the headline that e-cigarettes are 95% less harmful than cigarettes (as described here; no reference record; not read).
This article (September): questions the basis of the figure and of the report's other conclusions.
National Academies report: describes concerns raised by this article (continued use of a product with its own risks, more use of conventional tobacco, engagement with the tobacco industry).
Editorial by six authors giving the same account of the figure's origin (July 2013, 12 experts, 12 products, 14 criteria) and quoting the same limitation from the 2014 paper.

UK evidence update with the same first author as the 2015 report: judges the at-least-95% estimate still broadly accurate for the short and medium term, notes that such summaries can be simplistic and misread, and on the pages read gives no source or calculation for it.
Commentary arguing that vaping is substantially less harmful than smoking, written about a different review; it does not mention the 95% figure or this article.

replication.where_it_stands: An early, openly argued critique. Its account of where the figure came from is the same as the 2020 editorial's, and both quote the same limitation sentence from the 2014 paper, which has not been read here: the two critics agree, but they are not independent checks of the 2015 report. No reply from the report's authors or the 2014 paper's authors is in this article or in the other sources read; whether the true difference in harm is large or small is something neither this article nor the rating exercise can show.

funding.funder: No funding statement is printed.
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: the authors have read and understood BMJ policy on declaration of interests and have no relevant interests to declare.
funding.affiliations_note: Martin McKee, professor of European public health, London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine; Simon Capewell, professor of clinical epidemiology, Department of Public Health and Policy, University of Liverpool. Provenance as printed: not commissioned; externally peer reviewed. One of the 27 references is the first author's own earlier article (reference 7).

what_would_settle_it: A published, repeatable account of how the 95% figure was derived (criteria, weights, scores and the evidence for each), repeated by an independent panel chosen by stated rules with declared interests and updated for current products; and long-term cohorts that count disease and death in people who only vape, people who smoke, people who do both and people who use no nicotine.

domains.note: No search or criteria; 27 references chosen to question one report, many of them news items, web pages and organisational documents.

Limits of the evidence the report relied on are named (two trials in the Cochrane review, low or very low quality), but the evidence used against the report (one US adolescent cohort, a poisoning report, a PhD thesis on nicotine and brain development) is not appraised; the funders' ties rest on a company register, web pages, a book and a company report; the two-thirds dual-use figure has no source.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: One of 27 references is the first author's earlier article (reference 7), cited for the list of bodies that disagree with the report.

The funders' ties are worded as reported and the gateway point as a question of prematurity, but the key messages and the policy section ('flawed' report) state conclusions more firmly than an argument from a few sources supports.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how harmful e-cigarettes are compared with smoking
domains.note: Only the uncertainties and omissions of the report are presented; evidence on lower toxicant exposure in people who switch, and any estimate of the size of the difference, are absent. The statements of independence from the 2014 paper and the book are quoted, but no reply from the report's authors.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to an analysis or opinion article (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The article is openly argued, externally peer reviewed and declares no relevant interests, and its central factual point, where the figure came from, can be checked against the 2014 paper it names (not read here). It is one side's case and not an appraisal of the evidence. Cite it for what its authors argued in 2015, and for their account of the figure's origin as theirs, never for the size of any harm; a claim resting only on it stays at draft.

key_findings.finding: The authors write that one might expect the prominently featured '95% less harmful' figure to rest on a detailed review of evidence supplemented by modelling, but that it comes from a single meeting of 12 people convened to develop a multicriteria decision analysis (MCDA) model synthesising their opinions on the harms of different nicotine-containing products, whose results were summarised in a research paper (Nutt et al., 2014; reference 12, not read).
key_findings.locator: Quality of the evidence, 3rd paragraph, 1st and 2nd sentences

key_findings.finding: They quote that paper as conceding, as a limitation, the lack of hard evidence for the harms of most products on most of the criteria, and state that none of the links or limitations they describe is discussed in the 2015 report.
key_findings.locator: Quality of the evidence, 4th paragraph, last two sentences

key_findings.finding: On funding and membership of the meeting, as the authors report it: one sponsor was a company called EuroSwiss Health, about which an internet search revealed little beyond funding the meeting, one of several companies registered at the same address in a village outside Geneva with the same chief executive, who is reported to have received funding from British American Tobacco (BAT) for a book on nicotine as harm reduction (the book states its conclusions were developed independently of BAT) and endorsed BAT's public health credentials in its 2013 sustainability report; the paper also acknowledged support from Lega Italiana Anti Fumo, whose chief scientific adviser was one of the 12 and declared funding from an e-cigarette manufacturer but not funding he is reported elsewhere to have received from Philip Morris International. The rationale for selecting the panel is not provided; it included several known e-cigarette champions, some declaring industry funding in the paper, and some people not known for expertise in tobacco control; Public Health England's tobacco lead attended. The authors quote the paper's statement that the sponsor had no role in any stage of the process or the writing and was not present at the workshop. Sources for the ties: a commercial register entry, two Tobacco Tactics web pages, the book and a BAT report (references 13 to 17; not read).
key_findings.locator: Quality of the evidence, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; references 12 to 17
key_findings.note: Reported ties, worded by the authors as reported; a reason to read the 2014 paper closely, not evidence about harm.

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that where risks are uncertain the precautionary principle should apply, so that, without scientific consensus that a substance is not harmful, the burden of proof falls on those taking an action; that the report's headline, “best estimates show e-cigarettes are 95% less harmful to your health than normal cigarettes”, left little room for uncertainty about long-term risks; and that the report did not cite a 2014 systematic review (Pisinger and Døssing, reference 11, not read) which found serious methodological problems in many of its 76 studies, a third (34%) by authors with conflicts of interest, and concluded that no firm conclusions on safety could be drawn, while adding that e-cigarettes could hardly be considered free of harm.
key_findings.locator: Quality of the evidence, 2nd paragraph (begins on p. 1)

key_findings.finding: On stopping smoking, the authors note that the 2014 Cochrane review included only two randomised trials, both with important limitations, and rated the evidence low or very low quality by GRADE, and that the 2015 report's authors conceded the weakness of the evidence.
key_findings.locator: Quality of the evidence, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors set out the position of those concerned about e-cigarettes: although e-cigarettes lack some of the most harmful substances in cigarettes, such as tar, they contain others such as formaldehyde (a carcinogen) and diverse flavourings, so non-smoking should also be a comparison; reduced smoking, as opposed to quitting, may not reduce the overall risk of death (a 16-year Copenhagen cohort of 19,732 people, reference 8, not read); two thirds of people who use e-cigarettes also smoke (no source given), a pattern the report rarely mentions; and in one cohort dual use among people who vaped daily remained above 80% after 12 months (reference 9, not read).
key_findings.locator: Defining the role of e-cigarettes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
