key_findings.finding: On young people: over one fifth of 11 to 15 year olds in England had ever used e-cigarettes and 73% of the young people surveyed who had tried them did not smoke (a 2015 Health and Social Care Information Centre release, reference 18); nicotine may disrupt brain development (a PhD thesis on rodent and human cortical networks, reference 19); and a US study published after the report found that adolescents who had ever used e-cigarettes were more likely to report starting combustible tobacco over the next year (reference 21), so the report's dismissal of a gateway is called premature. The authors add that none of the research so far is conclusive and longer-term studies are needed.
key_findings.locator: Uncertainty around harms, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that the report equated a lack of evidence of risk to bystanders with evidence of no effect; omitted concerns about product safety (forged safety certificates shown in a December 2014 television documentary) and the lack of evidence on the risks of long-term dual use; quoted a US report of over 2,400 poisoning cases to February 2014 as saying none caused serious harm although that report mentioned a death attributed to suicide, without citing its conclusion that e-cigarettes can cause acute adverse health effects; and said the accuracy of nicotine labelling raised no major concerns although product information is known to be inaccurate. They call the report's most striking feature its consistent adoption of the most optimistic position on the limited evidence.
key_findings.locator: Uncertainty around harms, 2nd, 3rd and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Policy and key messages: the authors hope the restrictions on e-cigarettes in the 2016 European Union Tobacco Products Directive will limit the negative effect of what they call a flawed report, call for advice free from any suspicion of influence by vested interests, and agree with England's chief medical officer that e-cigarettes for stopping smoking should be licensed medicines and that evidence on their long-term use is still lacking. The key messages state that the endorsement of safety and efficacy rests on uncertain evidence, that evidence that e-cigarettes help people stop smoking is weak, that recent evidence questions the conclusion that they are not a gateway, and that public health strategies should follow the precautionary principle until better evidence is available.
key_findings.locator: Where next for policy on e-cigarettes?, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (the 2nd ends on p. 3); Key messages box (page headed 'Page 4 of 3')

key_findings.finding: The article offers no estimate of its own of how much less harmful e-cigarettes are than cigarettes, presents no data, does not discuss measurements of toxicant exposure or short-term health measures in people who switched from smoking, and reports no reply from the 2015 report's authors or the 2014 paper's authors.
key_findings.locator: Whole text (editors' reading)

key_findings.finding: Interests as printed: the authors have read and understood BMJ policy on declaration of interests and have no relevant interests to declare. Provenance: not commissioned; externally peer reviewed. No funding statement.
key_findings.locator: Competing interests; Provenance and peer review

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% wording is quoted as the report's headline message, widely quoted in the media, with no page and no indication of whether it comes from the report itself or from its press material.
reporting_issues.page: pp. 1-2 of 3 (Quality of the evidence, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The exact wording and stated basis of the figure in the 2015 report remain unverified here; the report has not been read.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that two thirds of people who use e-cigarettes also smoke carries no reference.
reporting_issues.page: p. 1 of 3 (Defining the role of e-cigarettes, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Not usable as a figure; it is the authors' assertion here.

reporting_issues.issue: The ties of the meeting's sponsor and supporting organisation are sourced to a company register, two Tobacco Tactics web pages, a book and a company report, and are worded as reported; the article itself quotes the 2014 paper's statement that its sponsor had no role and was not present.
reporting_issues.page: p. 2 of 3 (Quality of the evidence, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; references 13 to 17)
reporting_issues.consequence: Treat the ties as reported, as a reason to read the 2014 paper closely, and not as established facts or as a reason to discard the figure.

reporting_issues.issue: The text attributes the dual-use cohort to 'McNeill and colleagues', while reference 9 lists Hitchman as first author; the full author list of the same paper, printed as reference 6 of Mendelsohn et al. (2022), ends with McNeill, who is also the first author of the 2015 report.
reporting_issues.page: p. 1 of 3 (Defining the role of e-cigarettes, 2nd paragraph); p. 3 of 3 (reference 9)
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the claims; cite the cohort by its first author if it is ever added.

verification.source_read: PDF PDFs/Nicotine/McKee_2015_ECigaretteEvidenceRockOrSand.pdf in the senior author's DrugEncyclopedia uploads (BMJ 2015;351:h4863; pages headed 1 to 4 of 3: all text, the key-messages box, competing interests, provenance and the 27 references), text extracted once with pdftotext -layout; pages 1 and 2 checked on the rendered image for column order and paragraph breaks; none of the cited sources read

design_detail: Commentary (Drug and Alcohol Review 2022;41(7):1493–1498; received 12 May 2022, revised 19 June 2022, accepted 25 June 2022), four authors. About two and a half printed pages of text in six numbered sections (introduction; vaping and smoking cessation; vaping as a gateway to smoking; comparative harms of vaping and smoking; net public health effects of vaping; conclusion), one figure (US high-school smoking and vaping trends, drawn from CDC youth survey data), 54 references and a conflict-of-interest statement; no funding statement. No data, methods or search. Its target is the 2022 report to the Australian Department of Health by Banks and colleagues, 'Electronic cigarettes and health outcomes: systematic review of global evidence' (its reference 1, not read), the report on which the 2023 journal article in this library is based (card sc_banks_2023); the 2023 article appeared later and is not discussed. Every study cited is known here only as this commentary describes it. Commentary appraised with the editors' checklist.
can_establish: What four Australian authors argued in 2022 against the Australian report's conclusions and methods: that it did not compare the harms of vaping with those of continuing to smoke, did not weigh net population effects, underrated the trial evidence on stopping smoking, read the link between youth vaping and later smoking as causal while setting aside observational evidence on quitting, and gave weight to self-reported nicotine-only cases in the 2019 lung-injury outbreak; and which evidence they cite for each point.
cannot_establish: Whether the report's conclusions are wrong (the commentary appraises none of the evidence it cites and describes no search); how much less harmful vaping is than smoking, or what vaping does to rates of heart disease, lung disease or cancer (it cites no study of disease incidence, and its cancer figure is a modelled estimate as cited); and whether the 2023 journal article answered or changed any of the points (not discussed).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; the authors say they summarise evidence inconsistent with the review's main findings (Introduction, 4th paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The 54 references are chosen to set out evidence against the report. For the health effects of switching from smoking, seven of the nine human studies or reviews cited for cardiovascular and respiratory benefit (references 35, 36 and 38 to 42) and one of the two cell studies (reference 44) share authors: at least one of Polosa, Caponnetto, Cibella, Campagna, Morjaria and Caruso appears in each author list as printed; the two others are a four-week switching study (reference 37) and an online survey of airway infections (reference 43). Cancer risk is cited to two studies that, by their titles, estimate risk from emissions (references 49 and 50); youth trends to US survey data and simulation models; quitting to trials, a network meta-analysis, reviews of cohort studies and population surveys. No study of the incidence of heart attack, stroke, chronic lung disease or cancer in people who vape is cited.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed, except that the lung-injury paragraph turns on whether people who reported using only nicotine products had also used THC products (Comparative harms, 10th paragraph).

comparison.controls: No comparison of its own. The commentary argues that a meaningful assessment of the risk of vaping nicotine compares it with the much greater risk of continuing to smoke, because most people who vape frequently are current or former smokers who could not stop by other methods (Comparative harms, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). The journal version of the review it critiques takes people who neither smoke nor vape as the main comparison and gives its reasons (card sc_banks_2023).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: None.
outcomes.operationalization: Harm is argued from the toxicant content of aerosol against smoke, exposure biomarkers, short-term cardiovascular and respiratory measures after switching, cell studies and modelled cancer potency; the net public health effect from simulation models; effectiveness for quitting from trials, meta-analyses and surveys.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own. Figures as cited: the 2021 Cochrane review, moderate-certainty evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes increase quit rates compared with nicotine replacement therapy (RR 1.53); one trial in people unable to stop smoking by conventional methods, relative risk 6.4 (95% CI 1.5 to 27.3, p = 0.01) at 6 months against nicotine replacement; a network meta-analysis of 171 trials ranking vaping the most effective single treatment, with a wide interval; people who vape daily two to eight times more likely to stop smoking than people who smoke and do not vape; fewer than 1 in 100 adults in Australia who had never smoked vaped in the previous 12 months (2019); smoke contains over 7,000 toxic chemicals against fewer than 100 detectable chemicals in aerosols; 14% of EVALI patients denied using THC; lifetime cancer risk from vaping estimated at less than 0.5% of that from smoking; no evidence of harm in studies up to 2 years in the Cochrane review (few studies); in one US model 1.8 million premature deaths avoided and 38.9 million life-years gained from 2013 to 2060; in one UK estimate 50,000 additional people stopped smoking with a vaping product in 2017. Figure 1 labels, read from the image: past-30-day smoking among US high-school students 22.3% in 2004 and 1.9% in 2021, a decline of '1% per year' from 2004 to 2013 and '1.4% per year' from 2013 to 2021; past-30-day vaping 27.5% at its 2019 peak and 11.3% in 2021.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.selective_reporting: By its own statement the commentary sets out only evidence inconsistent with the review. Harms rated in the review's 2023 journal version (card sc_banks_2023), such as dependence, poisoning, burns and acute rises in heart rate and blood pressure in people who smoke, are not discussed, and no cited study is appraised.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: No data. The commentary argues, from 54 references, that the report did not compare vaping with continuing to smoke; did not consider net public health effects (all but one of the simulation models cited find benefits exceed harms); rated the trial evidence on quitting as limited where the 2021 Cochrane review rated it moderate certainty; used 'evidential double standards', reading observational associations between youth vaping and later smoking as causal while setting aside observational and population evidence on quitting, although in the authors' reading adjusted studies and population trends point to a common liability or to diversion from smoking; and gave weight to the 14% of lung-injury patients who reported only nicotine products, a self-report the authors consider unreliable. On harm it cites lower toxicant content and exposure, short-term cardiovascular and respiratory improvements after switching (mostly from studies sharing authors), cell studies and a modelled cancer risk, and it says that human studies on cardiovascular outcomes are limited and that the effect of inhaled flavourings is largely unknown.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion (p. 1495) states that, contrary to the review, the evidence suggests vaping nicotine is an effective aid to stopping smoking, substantially less harmful than smoking tobacco, diverting young people away from smoking, and likely to bring a major net public health benefit if widely available to adults in Australia who smoke. Gaps: (1) 'substantially less harmful' rests on exposure, short-term and modelled evidence, the kinds the review set aside for clinical outcomes, and no study of disease incidence is cited; (2) the diversion claim rests on population time trends and survey comparisons, associations of the kind the authors say the review over-read for the gateway; (3) the statement that lower biomarkers in people who switch confirm harm reduction is cited to two studies that, by their titles, compare exposure between groups, one of them cross-sectional (references 30 and 31); (4) the sentence on in vitro and animal studies cites two human studies (references 39 and 40, by their titles) and no animal study; (5) the overlap of authors behind most of the switching evidence is not mentioned. The 2023 journal version of the review states that the uptake findings were similar after adjusting for factors including risk-taking (Results › Smoking behaviour, 1st paragraph, in the saved PMC text read for card sc_banks_2023), which the commentary, written about the 2022 report, does not address. In the authors' favour, they acknowledge the wide interval of the network meta-analysis, the mixed results of observational cohorts, limited human evidence on cardiovascular outcomes, possible risk from nicotine in people with heart disease, the unknown effects of flavourings and the small number of trials followed to 2 years.

timeline.event: BMJ analysis questioning the evidence behind the 2015 English report and the origin of its 95% figure; not cited by this commentary.
National Academies report: the starting point of the Australian review's umbrella part (card sc_banks_2023); not cited by this commentary.

Cochrane review update (Hartmann-Boyce et al., 2021): moderate-certainty evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes increase quit rates compared with nicotine replacement therapy, RR 1.53 (as cited here; no reference record; not read).

Banks et al., report to the Australian Department of Health, 'Electronic cigarettes and health outcomes: systematic review of global evidence' (dated 7 April 2022 in reference 13 of the 2023 article): the target of this commentary (reference 1 here; no reference record; not read).
This commentary (received May, accepted June 2022).
UK evidence update stating that vaping carries a small fraction of the risks of smoking; published after this commentary was accepted and not cited by it.

Journal article based on the 2022 report: keeps 'limited evidence' for quitting with clinical support and 'strong evidence' for uptake of smoking by young people who vape; its text and reference list, as saved for card sc_banks_2023, do not cite this commentary.

replication.where_it_stands: A published critique of the Australian review that argues mainly about the question and the comparison (relative harm against continuing to smoke; net population effect) and about evidence standards, not with new data. On disease, it and the review do not disagree about rates of heart attack, stroke or cancer, which neither has; they disagree about which comparison and which kinds of evidence should count. No reply from the review's authors has been found: the 2023 journal article does not cite it.

funding.funder: No funding statement is printed.
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: Dr Colin Mendelsohn was a board member of the Australian Tobacco Harm Reduction Association (ATHRA), a registered health promotion charity, from October 2017 to January 2020, and Dr Alex Wodak is a board member of ATHRA. ATHRA accepted unconditional seed funding from the vape retail industry to get established; the funding ceased in March 2019. Mendelsohn and Wodak were directors of ATHRA in March 2018 when it received a donation from Knowledge Action Change Communications, a private sector public health agency in the UK; the donation was sourced from a surplus arising from the Global Forum on Nicotine conference in May 2017. Knowledge Action Change Communications is legally separate from Knowledge Action Change (KAC). KAC has received two grants from tobacco companies: in 2012 a small development research grant from Nicoventures (then owned by British American Tobacco) to evaluate a nicotine delivery device in Scottish prisons, conducted with the Scottish Prison Service and publicly declared; and in 2018 a grant from the Foundation for a Smoke-Free World, which is funded by an annual grant from Philip Morris International, specifically for preparing The Global State of Tobacco Harm Reduction report; under the Foundation's bylaws and pledge agreement, Philip Morris International and the tobacco industry are precluded from any influence over how the Foundation spends its funds or focuses its activities. Mendelsohn is the author of the book Stop Smoking Start Vaping (Aurora Press) and has never received payments from electronic cigarette or tobacco companies; Wodak has never received payments from electronic cigarette or tobacco companies. Professors Wayne Hall and Ron Borland have no interests to declare.
funding.affiliations_note: Affiliations as printed: general practice, Sydney (Mendelsohn); St Vincent's Hospital Sydney, Alcohol and Drug Service (Wodak); University of Queensland, Centre for Youth Substance Abuse Research, Brisbane (Hall); School of Psychological Sciences, University of Melbourne (Borland). None of the four appears among the authors printed in the reference list (lists are cut after six names). Recorded as a reason to read closely, not to discount: the commentary argues for wider access to vaping for adults who smoke, and two authors held governance roles in an association that took vape-retail seed funding until March 2019; both state they have never received payments from e-cigarette or tobacco companies, and the other two authors declare no interests.

what_would_settle_it: On the comparison: long-term cohorts that report disease and death separately for people who only vape, people who smoke, people who both smoke and vape, people who stopped smoking with and without vaping, and people who never used nicotine, so that the comparison with smoking and the comparison with no nicotine can both be read from the same data. On evidence standards: a rule set in advance, applied to both quitting and starting to smoke, on which designs count as causal evidence and how residual confounding is handled. On the lung-injury outbreak: product testing linked to cases rather than self-report.

domains.note: No search or criteria; the authors set out the evidence they find inconsistent with the review.

Cited studies are described, not appraised. Some statements carry no citation (most people who vape frequently are current or former smokers; faster declines in adult smoking in the UK and US); the biomarker statement cites two group comparisons of exposure; the in vitro and animal statement cites two human studies; the overlap of authors behind most of the switching evidence is not noted.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the four authors appears among the names printed in the 54 references (author lists are cut after six names).

Firm wording ('highly implausible', 'confirmed', 'diverting young people') rests on associations, time trends and modelling; some limits are acknowledged (wide interval, mixed cohort results, limited cardiovascular evidence, unknown effects of flavourings).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how harmful vaping is compared with smoking and with using no nicotine
domains.note: Only evidence favouring vaping for adults who smoke is presented, by design; harms such as dependence, poisoning, burns and acute rises in heart rate and blood pressure are not discussed, and the comparison with people who use no nicotine is not addressed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used, as for the other critiques in this monograph (cards sc_eissenberg_2020 and sc_mckee_2015). The commentary is openly argued, says it sets out only evidence inconsistent with the review, and declares its authors' interests in detail; it is one side's case and appraises none of its sources. Cite it for what its authors argue about the review's question, comparison and evidence standards, never for the size of any harm or benefit; a claim resting only on it stays at draft.

key_findings.finding: The commentary critiques the review of vaping by Banks and colleagues funded by the Australian Department of Health, cited as the 2022 report to the Department (reference 1), whose stated aims were to examine contemporary evidence on the health outcomes of nicotine and non-nicotine e-cigarette use and to integrate it with systematic reviews on smoking uptake and cessation to guide policy and practice.
key_findings.locator: 1 Introduction, 1st paragraph; reference 1

key_findings.finding: In the authors' view the review failed its aims because it did not compare the relative risk of the harms of vaping with those of cigarettes, did not consider the net public health impact of vaping, ignored evidence that vaping is effective for stopping smoking, and confused causation and correlation for youth vaping and cigarette smoking. They add that it used 'evidential double standards', accepting a causal reading of observational associations for the gateway hypothesis while rejecting similar observational evidence on cessation, and took a sceptical attitude to trials showing that vaping helps people stop smoking. They state that they summarise evidence inconsistent with the review's main findings.
key_findings.locator: 1 Introduction, 2nd to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Against the report's conclusion of limited evidence that, in the clinical context, freebase nicotine e-cigarettes may be more efficacious than nicotine replacement therapy, the authors cite the 2021 Cochrane review (moderate-certainty evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes increase quit rates compared with nicotine replacement, RR 1.53), other meta-analyses that agree but differ in confidence, one trial in people unable to stop by conventional methods (relative risk 6.4, 95% CI 1.5 to 27.3, at 6 months), a network meta-analysis of 171 trials ranking vaping the most effective single treatment (they note its wide interval calls for larger trials), two reviews of higher-quality cohort studies after mixed cohort results, population surveys in Australia, the US and the UK, people who vape daily being two to eight times more likely to stop, and faster declines in adult smoking where vaping is more common (no source given for the last).
key_findings.locator: 2 Vaping and smoking cessation, 1st to 7th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Against the report's claim of strong evidence that e-cigarettes increase uptake of smoking in people who do not smoke, particularly young people, the authors argue that the association is most likely explained by a common liability to risk-taking; that more rigorous prospective studies adjusting for shared risk factors found the association largely disappears (one paper cited, reference 18); that population studies suggest vaping diverts young people from smoking, with US youth smoking falling faster from about the time vaping became popular (Figure 1, from CDC survey data: past-30-day smoking in high-school students 22.3% in 2004 and 1.9% in 2021); that most young people who vape smoked first and most vaping by people who have never smoked is experimental and transient; and that fewer than 1 in 100 adults in Australia who had never smoked vaped in the previous 12 months in 2019.
key_findings.locator: 3 Vaping as a gateway to smoking, 1st to 5th paragraphs (the 1st begins on p. 1493); Figure 1

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the review does not address relative risk, and that a meaningful assessment of the risk of vaping nicotine should compare it with the far greater risk of continuing to smoke tobacco, because the vast majority of people who vape frequently are current or former smokers who could not stop by other methods (no source given).
key_findings.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: They write that harm reduction from vaping rests on substantially lower exposure to toxins and carcinogens in vapour than in smoke (references 28 and 29) and is confirmed by considerable reductions in biomarkers of harm in the blood, urine and saliva of people who switch (references 30 and 31); that smoke contains over 7,000 toxic chemicals and solid particulate matter while vaping aerosols generally have fewer than 100 detectable chemicals, most at far lower concentrations (reference 29); that chemicals found in vapour but not in smoke do not appear to pose a significant hazard when inhaled (a 2020 UK Committee on Toxicity statement); and that the effect of inhaled flavourings is largely unknown and could carry risk, with no harm shown so far and ongoing monitoring needed.
key_findings.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 3rd to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular: most effects of vaping are consistent with the known effects of nicotine (transiently raised pulse and blood pressure, cardiac contractility, arrhythmogenesis); nicotine may pose some risk in people with existing cardiovascular disease; cardiotoxic constituents of smoke are absent from vapour or much lower (one review, reference 34). Human studies on cardiovascular outcomes are limited; two studies showed sustained falls in blood pressure in people who switched to vaping and one showed better vascular function after 4 weeks. Respiratory: vaping is likely to be far less harmful to the lungs (a narrative review), with improved symptoms, lung function, asthma, COPD, mucociliary clearance and fewer respiratory infections reported in people who switched. In vitro and animal studies are said to find effects generally far smaller than from smoke.
key_findings.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 6th to 9th paragraphs; references 34 to 45
key_findings.note: Seven of the nine human studies or reviews cited (references 35, 36, 38 to 42) and one of the cell studies (44) share authors; the in vitro and animal sentence cites references 39 and 40, which are human studies by their titles.

key_findings.finding: The authors call it highly implausible that nicotine vaping caused the 2019 US EVALI outbreak, which they say was strongly linked to vitamin E acetate added to black-market THC vaping oils and disappeared after it was removed from the illicit supply chain (CDC, reference 46); they argue that the 14% of patients who denied using THC and had vaped nicotine do not prove a link with nicotine products, because many patients who denied vaping THC were later found to have done so and no other causal agent has been identified in nicotine e-liquids (references 47 and 48; no numbers given).
key_findings.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 10th paragraph

key_findings.finding: On the basis of the reduced number and dose of carcinogens in vapour, lifetime cancer risk from vaping has been estimated at less than 0.5% of that from smoking (references 49 and 50, which by their titles estimate cancer potency or lung cancer risk from emissions and particle measurements); the Cochrane review detected no evidence of harm in studies up to 2 years, although the studies were few and longer ones are needed.
key_findings.locator: 4 Comparative harms of vaping and smoking, 11th and 12th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that the key public health question is the net population effect, a function of the harm difference between vaping and smoking, effectiveness for stopping smoking and uptake by people who smoke and who do not; that numerous modelling studies, with one exception, conclude benefits considerably exceed harms, evaluating net effects under a wide range of assumptions about uptake, quitting and the reduction in harm compared with smoking; one US model estimated 1.8 million premature deaths avoided and 38.9 million life-years gained from 2013 to 2060, and one UK estimate put the additional people who stopped smoking with a vaping product in 2017 at 50,000.
key_findings.locator: 5 Net public health effects of vaping, 1st to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: contrary to the review's conclusions, the authors write, the evidence suggests that vaping nicotine is an effective aid to stopping smoking, that vaping is substantially less harmful than smoking tobacco, that it is diverting young people away from smoking, and that vaping by people who smoke is likely to have a major net public health benefit if widely available to adults in Australia who smoke.
key_findings.locator: 6 Conclusion

key_findings.finding: The commentary does not mention the 95% figure or any other overall estimate of relative harm apart from the modelled cancer estimate, cites no study of the incidence of heart attack, stroke, chronic lung disease or cancer in people who vape, and does not engage with the reasons for the review's choice of comparison group or its exclusion of biomarker studies (both stated in the 2023 journal version, card sc_banks_2023).
key_findings.locator: Whole text (editors' reading)

key_findings.finding: Interests as printed: two authors were or are board members of the Australian Tobacco Harm Reduction Association, a registered health promotion charity that accepted unconditional seed funding from the vape retail industry until March 2019 and in March 2018 a donation from Knowledge Action Change Communications (legally separate from Knowledge Action Change, which has received a 2012 grant from Nicoventures, then owned by British American Tobacco, and a 2018 grant from the Foundation for a Smoke-Free World, funded by Philip Morris International); one author wrote the book Stop Smoking Start Vaping; both state they have never received payments from electronic cigarette or tobacco companies; the other two authors have no interests to declare. No funding statement.
key_findings.locator: Conflict of interest

reporting_issues.issue: The biomarker sentence says reduced biomarkers of harm in the blood, urine and saliva of people who switch confirm harm reduction, but the two studies cited (references 30 and 31) are, by their titles, comparisons of nicotine, carcinogen and toxicant exposure between groups, one of them cross-sectional.
reporting_issues.page: p. 1494 (4 Comparative harms, 3rd paragraph; references 30 and 31)
reporting_issues.consequence: Read as evidence of lower exposure in group comparisons, as cited, not of lower harm or of change within people who switched; the studies were not read.

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence on in vitro and animal studies cites references 39 and 40, which by their titles are human studies (a randomised cessation trial and a follow-up of people with asthma who switched); neither of the other two (44 and 45) is, by its title, an animal study.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement about animal studies has no animal study behind it in the text.

reporting_issues.issue: 'Those who vape daily are two to eight times more likely to quit' is cited jointly to three studies (references 14 to 16), one of which is, by its title, a time-series analysis of national prevalence; which study gives which figure is not said.
reporting_issues.page: p. 1493 (2 Vaping and smoking cessation, 7th paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The range cannot be traced to a study from this text.

reporting_issues.issue: 'More rigorous prospective studies' in which the vaping-smoking association largely disappears are cited to a single paper (reference 18).
reporting_issues.page: p. 1494 (3 Vaping as a gateway, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: One re-analysis as cited, not a body of studies; not read.

reporting_issues.issue: The phrases attributed to 'the Banks review' ('limited evidence ... may be more efficacious' for quitting; 'strong evidence' for uptake of smoking) come from the 2022 report (reference 1); the 2023 journal version words these judgments differently (limited evidence that freebase nicotine e-cigarettes with clinical support are as efficacious as, or in Box 4 more efficacious than, nicotine replacement; strong evidence that young people who have never smoked or do not smoke and who use e-cigarettes are about three times as likely as those who do not to start smoking and to become regular smokers).
reporting_issues.page: p. 1493 (2 Vaping and smoking cessation, 1st paragraph; 3 Vaping as a gateway, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The critique should be described as a critique of the 2022 report; it cannot be assumed to quote the 2023 article.

verification.source_read: PDF PDFs/Nicotine/Mendelsohn_2022_CriticalAnalysisECigaretteReview..pdf in the senior author's DrugEncyclopedia uploads (Drug Alcohol Rev 2022;41:1493–1498: all six sections, Figure 1, the conflict-of-interest statement and the 54 references), text extracted once with pdftotext -layout; pages 1493 to 1496 checked on the rendered image (Figure 1 labels read from the image); none of the cited sources read, including the 2022 report it critiques. For the comparison with the 2023 journal article, the saved PMC text used for card sc_banks_2023 was searched.

design_detail: Systematic review with individual-participant-data (IPD) meta-analysis updating a 2007 review: randomized crossover or parallel trials of a single short bout of physical activity against a passive control in people abstaining from smoking for at least 2 hours and not using nicotine replacement or taking part in a cessation programme. Raw data were obtained for 19 of 20 eligible studies (7 parallel, 12 crossover; 14 published, 5 theses); two-stage and one-stage random-effects models of the post-intervention rating adjusted for baseline. Searches from 2004 to 31 May 2011, English only; not registered.
can_establish: Whether, and by roughly how many points on a 7-point scale, a single short bout of exercise lowers self-rated desire to smoke immediately afterwards compared with sitting, in laboratory studies of people abstaining for a few hours.
cannot_establish: How long the effect lasts (craving was rated only immediately or 5 minutes after the bout), whether exercise helps people stop or stay stopped, the effect in people in a quit attempt or using nicotine replacement (excluded), or an effect free of expectation (participants could not be blinded and the trials were not appraised for bias).

sample.recruitment: Searches of SportDiscus, MEDLINE, PubMed, Web of Science, EMBASE and PsycINFO, the Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group register and thesis databases, reference lists, SRNT abstracts 2007-11, list-serves and authors: 544 database records and 27 from other sources, 411 after duplicates, 58 abstracts, 36 full texts, 20 eligible, IPD for 19 (Figure 1, p. 29). The primary studies had 10 to 84 participants each; their characteristics are only in Table S1 (not read).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomized crossover or parallel trials of acute physical activity against control, with strength of desire to smoke (SoD) or desire to smoke (DtS) on a 7-point scale and at least 2 hours of abstinence before baseline; published or unpublished. Excluded: people in a cessation programme or using NRT (because baseline craving may be low), other craving measures, no control group, insufficient or no abstinence (p. 27; Figure 1).
sample.demographics: Not reported in the main text (Table S1 not read); one study's mean age of 36 years is described as older than in the other studies (p. 34).
sample.attrition: One eligible study (8 participants) was left out because its IPD could not be obtained; four participants dropped from one published data set were restored from the raw data (pp. 28, 30). Attrition within trials is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: English only from 2004, with earlier studies taken from the 2007 review; titles screened by the first author alone (p. 28). Seventeen of the 19 included studies list at least one of the review's authors (editors' count from the reference list); the review is a collaboration of those authors pooling their raw data.

exposure.measurement: Supervised single bouts in a laboratory: moderate walking (8 studies), running (2), moderate cycling (9), vigorous cycling (2), light cycling (1) and isometric exercise (3); intensity set by perceived exertion or heart rate (p. 29).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: single bouts of 5 to 40 minutes (p. 29); at least 2 hours without smoking before baseline; three-arm designs collapsed to two arms (exercise arms pooled; passive arms pooled).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 2 hours without smoking before baseline (inclusion criterion); actual durations and verification are in Table S1, not read.

comparison.controls: Passive conditions: sitting (16 studies), sometimes with an audio recording, a cognitive task, a video or body scanning; body scanning was coded as control although both studies of it found it lowered craving (pp. 29-30, 34).
comparison.matching: Within-person crossover or randomized parallel groups; baseline craving adjusted for.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (randomized).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed.

outcomes.instruments: Single-item 7-point ratings of desire to smoke ('I have a desire for a cigarette right now') and strength of desire ('How strong is your desire to smoke right now?'); two studies' 0-5 ratings were rescaled to 1-7 (pp. 27-28).
outcomes.validity_norms: Widely used single items (Tiffany & Drobes; Mood and Physical Symptoms Scale), treated as continuous although ordinal (p. 28).
outcomes.operationalization: Post-intervention rating adjusted for baseline, taken immediately or 5 minutes after the bout (p. 29).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; two outcomes with several sensitivity analyses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not possible for participants, who knew whether they exercised; not discussed.

analysis.effect_sizes: Baseline-adjusted differences in scale points (called standardized mean differences in the abstract and Results; the Methods derive mean differences and the one-stage model reports a mean difference). Two-stage random effects: SoD -1.91 (95% CI -2.59 to -1.22), 15 studies, 797 observations, I2 94.2%, Q 240.35; DtS -2.03 (-2.60 to -1.46), 17 studies, 837 observations, I2 92.0%, Q 201.02. One-stage: SoD -1.89 (-2.52 to -1.26 in Table 2; -2.53 in the text), SD of the random effect 0.850, 95% mid-range -3.56 to -0.22; DtS -2.03 (-2.54 to -1.51), SD 0.722, mid-range -3.45 to -0.62. Parallel trials only: SoD -1.78 (-3.17 to -0.40), I2 96.5%; DtS -2.27 (-3.82 to -0.72), I2 96.8%. Moderate intensity only: SoD -2.20 (-2.89 to -1.51), 13 studies; DtS -2.14 (-2.71 to -1.57), 16 studies. Published against unpublished: SoD -1.91 (-2.85 to -0.97) and -1.90 (-2.88 to -0.91); DtS -2.13 (-2.88 to -1.38) and -1.81 (-2.71 to -0.91). Single studies ranged from -0.22 to -4.54 (SoD) and -0.27 to -4.27 (DtS).
analysis.covariates: Baseline craving; in the one-stage model a fixed effect for study and a random intercept for participant.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; PRISMA was followed.
analysis.selective_reporting: Both outcomes were analysed even where only one had been published (from the raw data). Moderators other than intensity were not analysed, although the authors call that analysis necessary.
analysis.power: Not addressed; heterogeneity very high (I2 89.7% to 96.8%).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Every included trial favoured exercise, with a baseline-adjusted difference of about 2 points on a 7-point craving scale immediately after a short bout, but with very large differences between studies, from a fraction of a point for isometric exercise to more than 4 points in a study with high baseline craving.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes there is “strong evidence that physical activity acutely reduces cigarette craving” (p. 26) and reports standardized mean differences. Gaps: (1) the effects are differences in scale points, not standardized; (2) strong evidence is asserted without any appraisal of trial bias, for unblinded self-ratings, from trials mostly run by the review's authors; (3) the Discussion calls the decrease moderate and the Conclusions call the effects large; (4) the claim that the reduction matches or exceeds that with NRT and glucose cites a review of nicotine receptor partial agonists (ref. 4) and the 2007 review; (5) nothing is shown about duration beyond minutes or about quitting.

timeline.event: Taylor, Ussher & Faulkner, systematic review of the acute effects of exercise on cravings (narrative synthesis), which this review updates.
Roberts et al., aggregate-data meta-analysis with 9 and 10 studies for the two craving measures and similar results (as described, p. 34); it shares most primary studies with this review.
This IPD meta-analysis.

replication.where_it_stands: The main pooled estimate of the immediate effect of a bout of exercise on craving. Agreement with the 2012 aggregate meta-analysis is not independent replication (shared studies). Quitting outcomes and the duration of the effect are outside its scope.

funding.funder: Internal institutional funds (Declarations of interest, p. 35).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no other direct or indirect support and no connection with the tobacco or pharmaceutical industries (p. 35).
funding.affiliations_note: Exeter, Peninsula College of Medicine and Dentistry, St George's London, Moffitt Cancer Center, Toronto, Surrey, West of England and Sheffield. Seventeen of the 19 included studies list at least one review author (editors' count), a conflict of a non-financial kind that the paper does not discuss.

what_would_settle_it: A registered randomized trial in people in a quit attempt comparing short bouts of exercise with an active attention control, with craving rated repeatedly for several hours afterwards and lapses recorded, run by investigators independent of the original trials.

domains.note: Population (temporarily abstaining people who smoke, no NRT), intervention (short bouts of physical activity), comparator (passive control) and outcomes (SoD, DtS) specified.
No protocol or registration mentioned.
Randomized crossover and parallel trials, with the case for IPD from randomized trials set out (p. 27).

Six databases, a trials register, thesis databases, reference lists, conference abstracts, list-serves and authors, with the search string given; but English only without a stated reason (the date limit is explained as an update). Item 4 applied as written, as for other cards (decision p-amstar2-item4).
Titles screened by the first author alone; only abstracts were examined by two authors (p. 28).
IPD were obtained from the primary authors; who checked the data is not described.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail

Two-stage and one-stage random-effects IPD models adjusted for baseline, with crossover designs modelled with participant random effects; the mislabelling of mean differences as standardized does not change the method.

domains.note: Sensitivity analyses by design (parallel only), intensity and publication status, none by risk of bias.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The conclusion of strong evidence does not discuss bias in unblinded self-ratings or the authors' own studies.
I2 and Q reported; baseline craving, age and mode of exercise discussed; a moderate-intensity subgroup analysed (pp. 32-34).
Unpublished studies were included and compared with published ones, but no funnel plot or small-study test was done.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and absence of industry links stated; authorship of the included studies not discussed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 can only be judged from Table S2, which was not read. Critical items 2, 4, 9, 13 and 15 are not met, so confidence is critically low whatever item 7 shows. This concerns how far the pooled number can be trusted as an unbiased summary: the IPD methods are sound and every trial points the same way, but the trials were not appraised, the outcome is an unblinded self-rating taken minutes after exercise, and most trials come from the review's own authors.

key_findings.finding: Nineteen randomized trials with raw data (7 parallel, 12 crossover; 14 published and 5 theses); bouts lasted 5 to 40 minutes; studies had 10 to 84 participants; craving was rated immediately before and immediately after the bout, or 5 minutes after it in three studies; all controls were passive.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study characteristics and quality assessment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 1

key_findings.finding: Two-stage random-effects IPD meta-analysis: strength of desire -1.91 (95% CI -2.59 to -1.22), 15 studies, 797 observations (440 exercise, 357 control), I2 94.2%; desire to smoke -2.03 (-2.60 to -1.46), 17 studies, 837 observations (463 exercise, 374 control), I2 92.0%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Strength of desire; Desire to smoke; All eligible studies › Two-stage random-effects meta-analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 30); Tables 2 and 3 (p. 32)

key_findings.finding: One-stage model: strength of desire -1.89 (-2.52 to -1.26 in Table 2), SD of the random effect 0.850, so 95% of studies' true effects are expected between -3.56 and -0.22 points; desire to smoke -2.03 (-2.54 to -1.51), SD 0.722, range -3.45 to -0.62.
key_findings.locator: Results › One-stage individual participant data meta-analysis; Tables 2 and 3
key_findings.note: The text gives the lower limit for strength of desire as -2.53 (reporting issue 3).

key_findings.finding: Every study favoured exercise; the smallest effects came from the three studies of isometric exercise, two of whose intervals for strength of desire included zero (-0.55, -1.13 to 0.02; -0.22, -1.03 to 0.58), and the largest from a study with the highest baseline craving (-4.54 and -4.27).
key_findings.locator: Figures 2 and 3 (pp. 33-34); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 34) and last paragraph (p. 35)

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity analyses agreed: parallel trials only -1.78 (-3.17 to -0.40) and -2.27 (-3.82 to -0.72); moderate intensity only -2.20 (-2.89 to -1.51) and -2.14 (-2.71 to -1.57); published and unpublished studies similar (-1.91 against -1.90 for strength of desire; -2.13 against -1.81 for desire to smoke).
key_findings.locator: Results › All eligible studies, 2nd paragraph (p. 30); Parallel arm studies; Studies investigating physical activity of moderate intensity (p. 32); Tables 2 and 3

key_findings.finding: Effect sizes were computed as baseline-adjusted mean differences between groups in post-intervention ratings on the 1-7 scale, although the abstract and Results call them standardized mean differences.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Methods › Data analyses, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 28); Results › Two-stage random-effects meta-analysis (p. 30)

key_findings.finding: Eligibility required at least 2 hours without smoking before baseline and excluded people in a cessation programme or using NRT; the review sought effects on strong cravings such as those of the first hours and days of quitting.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Inclusion/exclusion criteria

key_findings.finding: Quality was reported only as randomization (one study allocated by recruitment order); publication bias was addressed by including unpublished studies, and reporting bias was judged not an issue because both outcomes gave similar results.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study characteristics and quality assessment, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Funded by internal institutional funds; no industry links declared.
key_findings.locator: Declarations of interest

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Results describe the pooled effects as standardized mean differences, but the Methods derive mean differences in post-intervention ratings, the one-stage model reports a mean difference, and the single-study values match raw differences in Table 1 (for example 2.10 against 6.58 points, effect -4.54).
reporting_issues.consequence: The effects are about 2 points on a 7-point scale, not about 2 standard deviations; any comparison with standardized effects elsewhere would be wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives 16, 8 and 14 studies for the strength-of-desire analyses, while the text and Figure 2 give 15, 7 and 13.
reporting_issues.consequence: Study counts differ by one between table and text; the text and forest plot (15 studies) agree with each other.

reporting_issues.issue: The one-stage strength-of-desire interval is -2.53 to -1.26 in the text and -2.52 to -1.26 in Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Rounding-level discrepancy; no effect on interpretation.

reporting_issues.issue: The unpublished strength-of-desire analysis cites refs. 28, 29, 50 and the unpublished Janse van Rensburg study, which has no strength-of-desire data (Table 1, NA), and omits Katomeri 2009 (ref. 27), an unpublished thesis that is in Figure 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Citation error; the pooled figure is presumably for refs. 27, 28, 29 and 50.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the craving reduction after exercise matches or exceeds that with NRT and glucose, citing refs. 4 and 11; ref. 4 is a Cochrane review of nicotine receptor partial agonists for stopping smoking.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison with NRT is unsupported in this paper and should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion calls the decrease moderate, while the Conclusions call the effects large and the abstract calls the evidence strong.
reporting_issues.consequence: Inconsistent wording of the same result.

verification.source_read: PDF /mnt/user-data/uploads/DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/Nicotine/Haasova_2013_PhysicalActivityCravingsIPD_MA.pdf, pp. 26-37 (all pages read in a text extraction; pp. 30, 32 and 33 with Tables 2-3 and Figure 2 checked on the rendered pages, including every negative value); supplementary Tables S1-S2 and Figures S1-S4 not read; final published version

design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis of published placebo-controlled randomized trials of oral nicotine products (gum, inhaler, sublingual tablet, 1 mg lozenge) on withdrawal symptoms and craving. Medline and Embase, the Cochrane NRT trials database, reference lists and colleagues were searched (no dates given); quality criteria served as inclusion criteria; results were tabulated as significant or not for each symptom in the first week of abstinence (vote counting). 27 studies reported effects on at least one symptom; 12 met the criteria (8 gum, 3 inhaler, 1 sublingual tablet, no lozenge).
can_establish: Whether placebo-controlled trials published to 2000 reported significant reductions in specific withdrawal symptoms with oral nicotine products in the first week of abstinence, symptom by symptom.
cannot_establish: How large any reduction is (no effect sizes), effects after the first week, effects of patches or nasal spray (outside its scope), or whether unreported non-significant results would change the counts (blanks in Table 3 mean not tested or not reported).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable at review level. Included trials (Table 2) recruited people who smoked, mostly at least 10 cigarettes a day and wanting to stop; three included volunteers not necessarily wanting to stop (Schneider et al., 1984; Fagerstrom et al., 1993; Lunell et al., 1995) and one smokers waiting to join a clinic (West et al., 1984).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Published randomized trials with a placebo control; product started within 24 hours of the start of abstinence; symptoms assessed over at least 24 hours in the usual environment; a sample stated to be abstinent or nearly so; biochemical verification. All included trials excluded people with psychiatric or acute physical illness or on psychotropic medicines, and mostly included moderate to heavy smoking (p. 116).
sample.demographics: Not reported (Table 2 gives no age or sex).
sample.attrition: Per trial in Table 2, from 1 to 140 people dropped (for example 44 in Gross & Stitzer, 1989, with 40 analysed; 140 in Schneider et al., 1996, with 83 analysed); more dropouts on placebo in three trials (Gross & Stitzer, 1989; Hughes et al., 1991; Schneider et al., 1996).
sample.selection_effects: Published trials only. Lapsers were kept in the analyses in 5 of the 12 trials (Table 2), although the text says most trials included partially abstinent people (reporting issue 1).

exposure.measurement: Assigned product, nicotine against placebo; product use recorded in most trials (Table 2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions (Table 2): 2 mg gum in the gum trials (Hughes et al., 1990, also tested 0.5 and 4 mg; West et al., 1984, compared 2 mg with 0.5 mg), about 6 to 12 pieces a day; inhaler about 6 to 11 a day; one sublingual tablet trial. The authors note that use was typically below the recommended level, except in the tablet trial (p. 120). Oral route; first week of abstinence.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: From the quit day; biochemical verification required, but lapsers were kept in five trials.

comparison.controls: Placebo gum, inhaler or tablet; in West et al. (1984) 0.5 mg gum served as the comparator for 2 mg gum (Table 2).
comparison.matching: Randomized; three crossover or within-person trials (Fagerstrom et al., 1993; Lunell et al., 1995; Molander et al., 2000).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (randomized).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed.

outcomes.instruments: Symptom ratings of several kinds: 4-point severity ratings (Hughes et al.), the Smoker Complaint Scale, Profile of Mood States, visual analogue scales, 5-point mood and physical symptom ratings; craving as urges, desire or missing cigarettes (Table 2).
outcomes.validity_norms: No measure preferred; the authors note that craving ratings fell after quitting in some trials, which suggests measurement problems (p. 120).
outcomes.operationalization: A trial counts as positive for a symptom if it reported a significant difference from placebo in the first week (Table 3).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; nine symptom columns.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Placebo products; blinding integrity not assessed.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. Fractions of trials with a significant effect in the first week (Table 3): irritability 9/9, depression 1/1, anxiety 3/4, poor concentration 5/9, restlessness 2/5, sleep disturbance 1/2, hunger 2/5, total withdrawal 6/7, craving 7/11 (gum 3/7; inhaler 3/3; tablet 1/1). No differences by date, size, inclusion of lapsers, use of baselines or product use (p. 117).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Blanks in Table 3 combine not tested and not reported, so trials may have measured symptoms without reporting null results.
analysis.power: Trials of 15 to 240 people; the authors say any pattern across trials would have to be very marked to show (p. 117).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 12 small placebo-controlled trials, all 9 that reported irritability found less with oral nicotine, 6 of 7 less total withdrawal and 3 of 4 less anxiety; other symptoms were mixed, and craving was lower in all inhaler and tablet trials but in fewer than half of the gum trials.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the strength of evidence for total withdrawal discomfort, irritability and anxiety is high, and the Discussion concludes that oral nicotine dosing forms all reduce the severity of withdrawal (p. 121). Gaps: (1) counts of significant results without effect sizes cannot support a high strength of evidence; (2) anxiety rests on 4 trials; (3) all forms includes the lozenge, for which no trial was found; (4) blanks may hide unreported null results; (5) industry funding is not discussed.

timeline.event: Silagy et al., Cochrane review of nicotine replacement for stopping smoking; in it only 14 of 49 gum trials found significant effects on quitting, but pooling showed a clear effect (as described, p. 120).
This review.

replication.where_it_stands: An early systematic tabulation of withdrawal outcomes in oral nicotine replacement trials, giving directions without sizes. Later Cochrane reviews concern quitting, not withdrawal symptoms; a claim about the size of the effect on withdrawal needs trials that report effects.

funding.funder: SmithKline Beecham (Acknowledgements, p. 121).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement is printed, and the funder's role is not described.
funding.affiliations_note: St George's Hospital Medical School, London, and University of Pittsburgh. The first author is an author of one included trial (West et al., 1984).

what_would_settle_it: A meta-analysis of all placebo-controlled oral nicotine replacement trials that measured withdrawal, including unpublished manufacturers' data, reporting standardized effects for each symptom by day over the first month.

domains.note: People abstaining from smoking, oral nicotine products, placebo, withdrawal symptoms and craving.
None mentioned.
Each criterion (placebo control, start within 24 hours, usual environment, abstinence, biochemical verification) is justified (p. 116).

Two databases with keywords, a Cochrane trials database, reference lists and colleagues, but no search dates, published trials only without a stated reason and no grey literature (item 4 applied as written, decision p-amstar2-item4).
Not described.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Critical items 2, 4, 9 and 13 are not met (7 is met; 11 and 15 do not apply without pooling), so confidence is critically low. The review is transparent in listing excluded studies and tabulating every included trial, which lets readers see the vote counts, but counts of significant results from small trials, some keeping people who smoked again, with blanks that may hide null results, cannot give the size or the certainty of an effect.

key_findings.finding: Of 27 studies reporting effects of oral nicotine products on at least one withdrawal symptom, 12 met the quality criteria: 8 gum, 3 inhaler, 1 sublingual tablet and none of the 1 mg lozenge; meta-analysis was not possible and good data existed only for the first week of abstinence.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Results, 1st paragraph (p. 116)

key_findings.finding: Fractions of trials finding a significant effect in the first week: irritability 9/9, depression 1/1, anxiety 3/4, poor concentration 5/9, restlessness 2/5, sleep disturbance 1/2, hunger 2/5, total withdrawal discomfort 6/7, craving 7/11; included trials had 15 to 240 participants.

key_findings.finding: Craving was reduced in all three inhaler trials and the tablet trial but in only 3 of 7 gum trials.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says that in most studies people were included in the withdrawal analyses even if only partially abstinent, but Table 2 records lapsers included in 5 of 12 trials and excluded, or assumed or presumed excluded, in the other 7.
reporting_issues.consequence: The extent of contamination by smoking is smaller than the text implies, but still affects five trials, all of them gum trials.

reporting_issues.issue: Criterion 1 requires a placebo control, yet West et al. (1984), the first author's own trial, compared 2 mg with 0.5 mg gum.
reporting_issues.consequence: One included trial's comparator contained nicotine, which would bias it towards no difference; it found effects on irritability and depression.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 lists 'Schneider and Jarvik (1985), Schneider et al. (1984)' as one row, while Table 2 lists only Schneider et al. (1984).
reporting_issues.consequence: Two reports of one sample; counted once, as intended, but the source of the result is ambiguous.

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion says oral nicotine dosing forms all reduce withdrawal severity, although no trial of the 1 mg lozenge was found.
reporting_issues.consequence: The conclusion extends to a product with no trial.

reporting_issues.issue: The search dates are not given, and Table 3 prints 'P<01' for one irritability result.
reporting_issues.consequence: The search cannot be reproduced or dated; the typographical error is minor.
